MLT.name: Malta
MLT.summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first for LGBTI legal rights in its region every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and 'X' gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in its region, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance describes the country as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence and tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law. The lag is documented, with an improving record: in May 2018 the civil court awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each after finding the authorities had "knowingly and repeatedly" held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers and suffered insults and "continuous sexual abuse and violence"; since the 2013 gender-law reform, trans and gender-diverse inmates transfer to the female section and now receive individual cells there, though a 2024 University of Malta study still records misgendering by officers and clothing and healthcare gaps.
MLT.outOfScopeNotes:
Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general regional terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

Routine border handling of trans visitors is not documented beyond the asylum-seeker case, and no source describes visa or document scrutiny for trans visitors specifically.

Prison axis: the 2024 study rests on four interviews spanning 25 years; the earlier separate-dormitory segregation is documented from that study alone; no source in this record documents current solitary or special-unit practice for trans prisoners beyond what the study describes, and the abuse documented in the 2018 ruling predates the post-2013 reform practice.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Malta with the compliance breakdown across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime/hate speech and equality-body categories, scored per category on the map's red-to-green scale.

Equaldex data for Malta: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. 84% rate it a 'good place' for gay people; but Maltese rank #1 of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Legal status: same-sex conduct legal since 29 January 1973; civil unions since 2014 and same-sex marriage since 2017; gender change without surgery; full adoption since 2014; open military service; discrimination protections cover sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Academic chapter (Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, 2025, Mary Grace Vella): Malta records one of the lowest SOGIE physical/sexual victimisation rates in the EU27, yet LGBTIQ+ people still report a higher share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

University of Malta dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024): four interviews with current and former transgender inmates at the Correctional Service Agency, covering a 25-year cohort, found gaps in healthcare, legislation and knowledge, alongside problems after release, and found Correctional Service Agency practice out of sync with national gender-identity legislation.

ICJ (30 July 2025): ICJ and partners filed observations in M.S. v. Malta at the ECtHR — an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in Malta in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024; submissions raise ECHR Articles 3/5/13 (non-refoulement, detention conditions, individualised assessment before detention). Direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at Maltese borders.

MaltaToday (15 April 2014): parliament approved the constitutional amendment naming gender identity — Malta the first European state to do so — and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; Transgender Europe was among the first NGOs to applaud gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

sources.title: Seven transgender prison inmates awarded €5,000 each in damages for 'truly disgusting' treatment (Malta Today)
sources.summary: Malta Today (29 May 2018): the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

sources.title: The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency (Oriana Vidal, University of Malta, 2024)
sources.summary: University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

The custody record concerns residents: the seven 2018 claimants stayed in the male section because transfer to the female section would cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, while female inmates and warders were said to be hostile; current practice — transfer to the female section with individual cells, following earlier segregation in a separate dormitory (staff rationale: "the risks of pregnancies") — governs resident inmates, not visitors.

ISL.name: Iceland
ISL.summary:
Iceland ranks first of 121 regions surveyed by Equaldex as a good place for gay and lesbian people, with a 93 per cent rating. Same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women, same-sex marriage is recognised in law, and gender change carries no restrictions. Legal gender recognition operates through a self-determination process introduced by the 2019 reform that replaced the country's earlier, already progressive framework, and non-binary identity is recognised in law.

Statutory protections cover discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity in employment and services, hate-motivated offences, and access to sex-segregated facilities. Equaldex also records a full ban on intersex infant surgery and a ban on conversion therapy. Outright International's Iceland profile, last updated 12 March 2026, describes progressive laws alongside acknowledged gaps and confirms that LGBTI organisations are able to register.

Redress routes are institutional. The Equality Complaints Committee is the official equality and complaints mechanism, and the national emergency service publishes dedicated guidance on hate crime, including an explainer on offences committed from prejudice or hatred and specific guidance for queer people who experience abuse, with reporting routes through the 112 number. The United Kingdom's foreign travel advice confirms that same-sex relationships are recognised in Icelandic law and links to dedicated LGBT+ traveller guidance.

Residual risk is measurable but low in absolute terms. Police-recorded potential hate crimes totalled 16 in 2023, three times the previous year's figure, 11 in 2024 and seven in the current partial year. The queer rights group Samtökin 78 has called for stronger hate-crime legislation as incidents climb, and the emergency service states that queer people are more likely to be victims of violence.

A trans traveller guide reports that most pools in the capital area offer private or gender-neutral changing rooms, that using binary changing rooms is legal and common, and that trans visitors should not have to be worried about their safety.
ISL.outOfScopeNotes:
Three sources in the inventory yielded no usable finding: the Pink Iceland traveller guide, and the two OSCE hate-crime pages covering legislation and the national framework. The changing-room and pool arrangements described for the capital area therefore rest on a single traveller guide that could not be substantiated against the other sources inventoried.

The hate-crime figures for the current year are partial and reported as a running count, so they are not directly comparable with the full-year totals for 2023 and 2024.

The comparative ranking is drawn from Equaldex, a crowd-sourced index, and measures perceptions of the legal and social climate rather than reported incident rates.

Outright International's characterization of progressive laws with acknowledged gaps is not itemised in the inventory, so the specific remaining deficiencies are unresolved here beyond the challenges identified by Icelandic trans activists.

ESP.name: Spain
ESP.summary:
Ley 4/2023, published on 28 February 2023, grants legal gender recognition on self-identification. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry before the Civil Registry, without the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The reform places the state alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in permitting administrative self-declaration.

Gender identity is an explicit aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and courts are applying it. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

No legal rule restricts a trans visitor's use of facilities matching their presentation. The framework remains centred on gender self-determination, in contrast to the United Kingdom, where the EHRC statutory code moves toward single-sex spaces defined on biological-sex lines, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Acceptance is high in major cities and tourist centres, where LGBTQ communities and social venues are established, and more conservative outside them. The UK government's travel advice describes the state as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities, and Intrepid Travel rates it safe and welcoming while advising travellers to know local conditions before going, including venue-by-venue and regional variation.

The national tourism institute markets the country through eight flagship LGBTQ+ destinations and a "Destinations for Diversity" certification denoting open, safe, welcoming and discrimination-free spaces.
ESP.outOfScopeNotes:
Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, and gender-identity-motivated hate crime has no free-standing offence; it operates as an aggravating circumstance applied within other offences, which shapes how cases are charged and reported.

The public-attitude baseline is a December 2016 survey, seven years older than the statute it is read against, and its country rankings have not been refreshed in this inventory.

The historical timeline in this record rests on a tertiary encyclopedic overview rather than primary legislation for the 2005 milestones.

Enforcement evidence is thin: one first-instance misdemeanour fine in Vigo and one adult prison sentence in Valencia with two minors judged separately. Whether the aggravation is applied routinely beyond these cases is not established here.

Official UK travel advice pairs its tolerant-and-progressive framing with standard crime warnings unrelated to gender identity, including that counterfeit money is treated as a serious offence.

sources.summary: Official text of Ley 4/2023 (28 Feb 2023), 'real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantee of LGTBI rights', BOE. Article 43: any person of legal age 16+ may request rectification of the registry gender mention themselves before the Civil Registry - the administrative self-identification route visitors and residents use; law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12-16.

Human Rights Watch (16 Feb 2023): parliament passed the 'Trans Law' - gender recognition now by self-identification through a simple administrative process, ending the prior requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Also expands assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans non-consensual 'normalising' surgeries on intersex children, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and adds anti-discrimination measures in healthcare, employment and housing; recognition possible from age 12 under conditions. Joins Argentina, Ireland, Portugal, Uruguay and peers.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (Jun 2026): disentangles which statute does what - 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Criminal Code; the hate-speech aggravation (Art. 22.4 CP) and Art. 510 CP penalties (1-4 years plus 6-12 month fine) come from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 reformed offences against sexual freedom (Arts. 132, 173, 178-181, 189 bis). Useful for reading actual enforcement: gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence.

Euro Weekly News (9 Jul 2026): practical bathroom-access contrast for travellers - the UK is moving toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the EHRC statutory code (restrictions case-by-case, not a blanket ban), while Spain remains committed to a legal framework centred on gender self-determination. Visitor takeaway: facility access rules differ on either side of the Channel.

Intrepid Travel LGBTQIA+ country guide: rates Spain a safe and welcoming destination for LGBTQIA+ travellers, especially tourist hubs Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting attitudes can be more conservative outside big cities and that same-sex marriage plus protective laws apply. Advises knowing local conditions before going (venues, regional variation).

Turespana (national tourism institute) B2B page: names Spain's 8 flagship LGBTQ+ destinations - Madrid (Chueca), Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, Canary Islands (Maspalomas Pride), Sitges and Torremolinos (La Nogalera) - and the 'Destinations for Diversity' certification for open, safe, welcoming, discrimination-free spaces. Practical destination map for trip planning.

La Razon (Jul 2026): Vigo's Tribunal de Instancia applied the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia for the first time, in a misdemeanour threats case - messages threatening a trans woman sent by WhatsApp; the author was fined EUR 300. First instance-level precedent that gender-identity aggravation is being applied in practice.

Observatorio de delitos de odio (8 Jan 2026, reporting Las Provincias): a juvenile gang in a Valencia park harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison, two minors were separately judged. Documents actual sentence outcomes for gender-identity-motivated violence.

UK Foreign travel advice, Spain (safety and security): official UK government view that Spain is 'a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers' with active communities and social venues, alongside standard crime warnings (counterfeit money treated as a serious offence). Baseline official safety framing for a UK-issued passport holder.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex marriage and full adoption rights since 2005; legal gender change without surgery or sterilisation; LGBTQ military service and MSM blood donation since 2005; Spain recognised as one of the world's most LGBT-friendly countries. Backbone timeline for the record.

BuzzFeed News / Ipsos-style 23-country survey (Dec 2016): Spain ranked most trans-supportive of the 23 - the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, restroom support over 70% (with Argentina and India), and 25% of respondents knew a trans person. Dated public-attitude baseline predating the 2023 law.

ESP.tangentialFactors:
Facility access for trans travellers now diverges between neighbouring jurisdictions: the United Kingdom is moving toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the EHRC statutory code, while the state retains a legal framework built on gender self-determination. The practical difference concerns which side of a border a traveller is on when entering a bathroom.

On gender recognition, the state sits with Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay among countries that have adopted self-identification, and is described in overview sources as one of the world's most LGBT-friendly countries.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.summary:
Visa and border treatment of transgender visitors is set out in the official WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel guidance: visa requirements depend on nationality alone, with gender identity playing no part in the application, and a passport carrying a gender marker that differs from the marker assigned at birth or an 'X' marker is accepted provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited under Dutch law, and since 1 July 2025 a discriminatory motive is written into criminal law as a ground for increasing penalties, alongside expanded rights for victims and protection of victim data. Same-sex marriage is legal, non-binary people are legally recognised, conversion therapy is banned and access to sex-segregated facilities is protected, so a trans traveller's relationship status raises no entry or registration issue.

Official victimisation figures published by the Dutch government show that more than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, rising to 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people. The 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence, and in 2022 one third of discrimination reports reaching the police concerned sexual orientation.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is climbing in measurable terms. Police figures relayed by Transgender Netwerk record 4,800 reports concerning LGBTQIA+ people last year, 7.5% above 2024 and 81% above the 2,654 recorded in 2022. Reports specifically about transgender people rose 51% within a single year, from 264 to 399, while COC describes the trend as extremely worrying and notes that only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination followed last year's reports.

Pride-period conditions carry their own documented incident load. During the opening of WorldPride Amsterdam in July 2026, more than 70 people filed discrimination reports through the RITA platform, most of them festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and participants in the Pride Walk; RITA states that these reports represent only a fraction of the total. Mayor Halsema told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents will be handled as a priority during World Pride, with police, enforcers and organisers agreed to act quickly, and recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators leaving the scene before intervention.

Practical reporting infrastructure is extensive for the event. Amsterdam broadened its Safer Spaces reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. The capital remains among the safer large European cities for ordinary street crime, and the combination of legal protection, priority police response and multiple physical reporting channels gives a trans visitor clear routes to assistance.
NLD.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether hate-crime law covers gender identity is unresolved across sources: Equaldex records hate-crime protections as covering sexual orientation only, while the government's own July 2025 measures make any discriminatory motive a ground for increased penalties in criminal cases. The scope of the aggravating-factor rule as applied to gender identity is not specified in the available material.

RITA has stated that the 70-plus discrimination reports filed at the opening of WorldPride 2026 are only a fraction of the total, so no reliable count of incidents during the event exists. Recent Pride baselines of 25 to 45 reports are themselves reported figures rather than measures of underlying incidence.

Official Dutch victimisation statistics for transgender people (17% experiencing physical or sexual violence) and the report trend (transgender-specific reports up 51% in a year) come from different collection systems and cannot be directly compared. The discrepancy between 4,800 reports and six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year is unexplained in the source material.

NJCM records that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and that the placement guidelines under drafting by DIZ were unpublished as of February 2024. The current status of those guidelines and of the minister's response to the advice is not documented in the available inventory.

sources.title: NJCM adviseert demissionair Minister voor Rechtsbescherming over plaatsing van transgender gedetineerden (Nederlands Juristen Comité voor de Mensenrechten)
sources.summary: The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM), criminal-law working group, announced (site date 22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which NJCM calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the relevance of CPT standards, pointing to the full letter (PDF) to Minister Weerwind (21 Feb 2024).

sources.title: Advies plaatsing transgender gedetineerden — brief aan de Minister voor Rechtsbescherming (NJCM Werkgroep Strafrecht, 21 februari 2024)
sources.summary: NJCM letter to Minister Weerwind (Leiden, 21 Feb 2024) documenting Dutch placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees — and DJI (Prison Service) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP (municipal records) together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while DIZ said it was (unpublished) drafting guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling (21 Mar 2016, 15/4323/GB) on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 Oct 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624, trans woman facing placement in a men's prison) and The Hague appeals court (29 Jun 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108, trans man in a women's prison) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asks the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

USA.name: United States
USA.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 makes all federal identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth: the X marker was eliminated, the passport agency stopped processing markers not matching birth sex, and new applications list only M or F per supporting documents — mismatched documents have left trans travellers stranded abroad, passports have been confiscated or blocked at application, and the ACLU has sued over the policy (Lambda Legal maintains guidance on documentation). In February 2025, under Executive Order 14201, the State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events, flagging applicants internally as 'SWS25', and stated that applicants whose declared gender does not match sex assigned at birth may be permanently banned as fraud.

Entry and screening can be hostile in practice: airport screening (secondary screening, body scanners, pat-downs) risks outing trans travellers; a trans traveller was detained at the border for weeks and then deported in January 2025, and a border officer faces a lawsuit over alleged sexual contact with a trans traveller at a major airport.

Facilities and care are federal flashpoints: the same executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and the January 2025 order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care (EO 14187) has led institutions to pause services — a visitor needing care during a trip may find access reduced. The military ban (EO 14183) and schools order (EO 14190) complete the 2025 federal package; several orders are enjoined or blocked in court, so the operative position shifts with litigation.

Beyond the federal layer, exposure is state-by-state: bathroom bans cover trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in 9 states plus 1 territory, and in some states trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances — a trans student was handcuffed in a women's restroom at a state capitol in April 2025 in what attorneys called the first known arrest under such a law. Kansas invalidated birth certificates and licences not matching birth sex, promoted as a template other states may copy. Dated state-level guidance flags 4 states as do-not-travel for trans people as of July 2026 (Idaho the latest).

Foreign governments now warn their own citizens: at least eight European states, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidance for trans and non-binary citizens entering the US in 2025, following documented detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.summary:
Brazil is one of few countries that pairs a comprehensive legal framework for LGBTI people with persistently high levels of violence against them. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Court removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers SOGI grounds.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have ordered businesses to pay damages for anti-trans conduct. Official guidance affirms the right of trans people to use facilities matching their identity. For a trans traveller, the law of the country is unambiguously protective.

The gap between statute and street is the operative risk. A 2026 country assessment concludes that LGBTIQ people continue to face significant violence and discrimination in practice. A commercial tour operator rates the territory progressive on LGBTQIA+ rights and generally safe while explicitly warning that practical safety problems can still arise for LGBTQIA+ travellers. A foreign-government advisory sets the country-wide baseline at a high degree of caution because of high crime rates and gang-related urban violence.

Night-time and app-based interactions carry the sharpest documented risk. An investigation published in May 2024 describes drink-spiking robberies carried out under the guise of a good-night greeting, with LGBTQIA+ people among the victims in the largest city, where Pride events draw thousands of international visitors. Earlier reporting recorded fatal muggings arranged through dating apps targeting gay men, and robbery schemes of that kind remain the deadliest single pattern for visitors.

Being barred from a venue on the basis of gender presentation is not hypothetical and is litigated. In 2025 the state court of appeals for the largest state upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing; a lower court had awarded R$4,000 in compensation. A parliamentary inquiry in the largest city concluded with 189 recommendations on violence against trans and travesti persons, indicating the scale of the problem at municipal level.
BRA.outOfScopeNotes:
The tour operator guidance is a commercial assessment, not a legal or governmental finding, and its assurance of general safety should not be read as a guarantee for any individual itinerary or nightlife district.

The 2024 investigation into drink-spiking robberies and the 2025 nightclub discrimination ruling concern the largest cities and their nightlife economy; neither establishes conditions in rural or smaller urban areas, which are not described in this inventory.

The National Council of Justice resolutions describe the housing framework on paper. Whether individual units comply with it is not established here, and the Rio de Janeiro state prison study shows direct non-compliance in that state's system as of 2021, so compliance outside that state remains unverified.

Claims about dating-app robbery schemes fatal to gay men are recorded in this inventory only through secondary summary rather than a primary source, and the exact figures for trans officeholders and candidates derive from a single news agency account of the October 2024 municipal elections.

The 2022 analysis on violence-prevention law describes the direction of lower-court and Superior Court of Justice reasoning rather than a final national holding, and the terms of any resulting remedy for individual cases are not specified.

The foreign-government travel advisory in this inventory is dated August 2026 and is a country-wide baseline; it does not rank the safety of specific districts or venues, and its crime framing is not specific to LGBTQIA+ travellers.

sources.title: Resolução CNJ n. 348 de 13/10/2020 (alterada pela Resolução n. 366/2021) — diretrizes para o tratamento da população LGBTI custodiada ou privada de liberdade (Conselho Nacional de Justiça)
sources.summary: Brazil's National Council of Justice (CNJ) Resolution 348 of 13 Oct 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 Jan 2021, is the national framework for where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed: a person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing (Art. 4º); on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference (Art. 7º), and the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it general population or specific wings/cells (Art. 8º); the declared preference is recorded and a later change of placement is possible, with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat (Art. 9º). LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited (Art. 11, VI–VII). The resolution entered into force after publication (120 days, extended to 180 days by Res. 366/2021).

sources.title: Elas também não são mulheres?: Travestis e mulheres transexuais em situação de prisão no Rio de Janeiro (Dilemas — Revista de Estudos de Conflito e Controle Social 17(2), 2024, e60615)
sources.summary: Peer-reviewed census study (Alves-da-Silva & Bonan, Dilemas 17(2), 2024; lead author also of the LGBTI health division of the Rio de Janeiro state penitentiary administration, SEAP-RJ) of travestis and transgender women in prison in Rio de Janeiro state: 138 self-declared travesti/trans-woman inmates were interviewed inside eleven units deemed 'masculine' in the metropolitan region (April–June 2021, via the SEAP's SIPEN database). It documents that in the Rio state system travestis and trans women are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called 'neutral' or 'security' units, and frames male-unit placement as a double punishment combined with recurring basic-rights violations; it also cites the 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics) and national norms (2014; 2020) that let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

BRA.tangentialFactors:
Trans politics is unusually visible and unusually targeted. Nearly 1,000 transgender candidates ran in municipal elections across every state in October 2024, and the number of trans officeholders has tripled since the previous cycle, with candidates reporting death threats, intimidation and interference during campaigns.

Violence-prevention law has been extended to trans women. Lower courts pressed the Superior Court of Justice toward a unanimous position bringing the national domestic-violence statute and the femicide statute to bear in cases involving trans women, embedding trans people within violence-prevention remedies rather than outside them.

Nightlife is where the legal protection and the lived exposure diverge most sharply. Venue refusal cases and drink-spiking robberies both cluster in the late-night economy, the same setting in which Pride events concentrate thousands of tourists and therefore concentrate opportunity for criminals.

Practitioners rate the territory progressive on LGBTQIA+ rights and generally safe at the same time as they flag practical safety issues for LGBTQIA+ travellers, which is consistent with the pattern visible across the wider inventory rather than a contradiction within it.

For historical context on gay visibility, a 2000 essay documents an early-1900s homosexual subculture in a major port city, where a monument site functioned as a meeting place in the era of that city as a continental cultural capital, indicating that visible queer urban life is a long-standing feature rather than a recent import.

A national council of justice resolution (348, 13 Oct 2020, amended 2021) governs custody placement: self-declaration before a judge, a reasoned placement decision after consulting the person's preference, information on male, female and LGBTI-specific units, recorded declared preference with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat, and no use of LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation.

A state/province census (138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed inside eleven units treated as masculine, April–June 2021) found them housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement documented as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations; state/province law has since 2015 granted parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units.

The world's largest Pride parade takes place in the country; a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in the largest city happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.
BRA.blindLocalsOnly:
Same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker procedures form a settled family and entry framework that resident partners and long-term visitors can rely on, and that trans residents can use to establish identity documents without surgical intervention.

The judge must inform the person of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and must ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer a female, a male or a specific unit, and within it the general population or specific wings or cells. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers take priority where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used for disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. The resolution took effect after publication, with a 120-day lead extended to 180 days by resolution 366/2021.

Municipal-level scrutiny exists alongside the national framework: the city council's parliamentary inquiry into violence against trans and travesti persons produced a final report carrying 189 recommendations, which is the resident-facing record of what the municipal authorities were told to fix.
BRA.blindTangential:
Trans politics is unusually visible and unusually targeted. Nearly 1,000 transgender candidates ran in municipal elections across every state/province in October 2024, and the number of trans officeholders has tripled since the previous cycle, with candidates reporting death threats, intimidation and interference during campaigns.

Violence-prevention law has been extended to trans women. Lower courts pressed the national highest ordinary court toward an unanimous position bringing the national domestic-violence statute and the femicide statute to bear in cases involving trans women, embedding trans people within violence-prevention remedies rather than outside them.

Nightlife is where the legal protection and the lived exposure diverge most sharply. Venue refusal cases and drink-spiking robberies both cluster in the late-night economy, the same setting in which Pride events concentrate thousands of tourists and therefore concentrate opportunity for criminals.

Practitioners rate the state/province progressive on LGBTQIA+ rights and generally safe at the same time as they flag practical safety issues for LGBTQIA+ travellers, which is consistent with the pattern visible across the wider inventory rather than a contradiction within it.

For historical context on gay visibility, a 2000 essay documents an early-1900s homosexual subculture in a major port city, where a monument site functioned as a meeting place in the era of that city as a continental cultural capital, indicating that visible queer urban life is a long-standing feature rather than a recent import.

RUS.name: Russia
RUS.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Official assessments from a foreign body conclude that trans people specifically are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution in Russia. Enforcement has produced over a hundred "extremism" convictions for displaying LGBT symbols or participation, bar raids, and the death in custody of a man who ran travel tours for gay customers. Enforcement focuses on public expression and activism rather than private existence, and same-sex activity itself is not criminalised — a discreet visitor is not automatically targeted — but there is effectively no police protection, and detention carries placement by passport sex.

One region, Chechnya, where quasi-Sharia governance applies, is in a separate and graver category of danger for anyone perceived as LGBT.
RUS.outOfScopeNotes:
Official travel advisories from a foreign government (the US State Department) and most Western governments advise against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, due to the risk of wrongful detention, the war in Ukraine, and arbitrary law enforcement.

Unresolved or unverifiable: the travel-advisory page itself could not be retrieved at research time (the underlying highest-level advisory includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers); the death-in-custody case has no published outcome; exact current conviction totals and detention counts are not published, so visitor exposure is assessed from dated records.

SAU.name: Saudi Arabia
SAU.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under its uncodified Sharia legal system, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and the morality police enforce with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned.

Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a Pakistani trans woman died in custody in Riyadh in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. Amnesty International reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the Kingdom — and device inspection at the border is an established risk.

The tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.
SAU.outOfScopeNotes: Missile and drone attacks on infrastructure, and the general risk of detention without charge for any visitor, affect all travellers.

sources.summary: LegalClarity (4 Jun 2026): Saudi Arabia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity with no codified penal code — judges apply an uncodified sharia interpretation; penalties range from flogging and lengthy imprisonment to death in the most severe cases; visitor-facing explainer of the laws, how enforcement works and rules for visitors.

Outright International Saudi Arabia overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminal penalties are based on Shari'a; same-sex relations illegal for men and women; no legal gender recognition; LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute Saudi Arabia profile (MENA Trans Archives): deviating from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence; regional legal-research framing of gender-nonconformity provisions and their enforcement.

Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Saudi Arabia' (fetched 2026): same-sex conduct illegal with penalties including capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging and fines; no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no same-sex relationship recognition; law uncodified on a Wahhabist interpretation of sharia (Quran/Sunnah), with enforcement-case and living-conditions sections. Reference overview.

BBC News: 'Meeno' — Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman — died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh; Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack; family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. Directly relevant to how Saudi enforcement treats trans people.

Gulf News (25 Oct 2021): five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media — cross-dressing/gender-nonconformity enforced as a criminal matter.

Amnesty International (29 Jun 2026, updated 17 Jul 2026): documents visitors imprisoned over social media posts — including a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 Aug 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for posts published before he even arrived in the country. Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground.

UK FCDO Saudi Arabia safety advice (current): same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon; couples should avoid public affection; VisitSaudi states all visitors are welcome and privacy will be respected; being transgender is not recognised — trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care.

A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map (2024/25): Saudi Arabia appears among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan; page also profiles safest destinations (Iceland: self-ID, marriage since 2010).

The Guardian (April 2005) by Brian Whitaker: 'Saudis' tough line on gays' - dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and 'behaving like women' at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes plus up to two years' jail, after a closed trial without defence lawyers; HRW's Scott Long: 'Prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct are flagrant human rights violations.'

AFG.name: Afghanistan
AFG.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban — the nation's current ruling movement — is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. A 2024 Morality Law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; the ruling movement applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that international experts say is escalating into 2026. The prison-housing axis is thin but must not read as neutral: nothing is documented on where trans prisoners are held — no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units, no solitary or segregation practice — while Human Rights Watch / OutRight International (January 2022, 60 interviews) documents wrongful-detention risk, threats, assault and blackmail of LGBTI people since the takeover; in a criminalising regime with no recourse, an undocumented placement practice means a detained trans visitor is held at the regime's discretion amid the documented abuse of queer detainees, not under any protected standard.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.
AFG.outOfScopeNotes:
Armed conflict, terrorism, kidnapping, and the arbitrary detention of foreign nationals for leverage are severe risks for every visitor to Afghanistan, independent of any personal characteristic.

Unresolved or unverifiable: enforcement figures rest on 2022-23 interview-based reports and 2025-26 international flogging counts rather than the regime's own statistics; most accounts predate the 2024 Morality Law's implementation, so current on-the-ground practice is inferred rather than directly documented; no tourist entry pathway exists to test in practice.

Prison-housing axis: there is no evidence at all on birth-sex vs identity placement, trans special units, or solitary/segregation practice — the only prison-relevant finding is general wrongful-detention danger; that gap is treated as danger here, because a regime that criminalises same-sex conduct and abuses queer detainees cannot be assumed to place trans prisoners safely.

sources.summary: EUAA Country Guidance: Afghanistan, section 3.17 'LGBTIQ persons' (profile last updated Jan 2023, in guidance May 2024): treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious/social norms, alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty — the asylum-framework basis for assessing Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU.

EUAA COI Report — Afghanistan Country Focus, section 4.5 (Feb 2026): no legal protections for sexual orientation or gender identity before or after the 2021 takeover; the 'Morality Law' of 31 Jul 2024 specifically prohibits lesbianism, anal intercourse and enabling same-sex relationships; per Amnesty International, same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight report (Jan 26, 2022), 43 pages based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans: Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

OutRight International report (Feb 14, 2023), 22 interviews Sep-Oct 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in-country: Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in early rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations — punishments the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed on social media.

DW feature (Oct 2, 2021): profiles a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the Taliban takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave; documents street attacks on men coded as gay (clothing changed, confinement indoors).

JURIST feature (Nov 8, 2024) summarising the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan (formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen): reports systematic persecution after Aug 2021, noting that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework and that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Translation of Article 22 of the Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice (PVPV) Law, dated 31 Jul 2024: the overseer must prevent listed 'evils' including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery, gambling and other offences.

OHCHR press release (Mar 2026): UN human-rights experts condemn the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment — at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double 2024 — warning women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for 'moral crimes' such as adultery, 'illicit relationships' and 'sodomy'.

Human Dignity Trust country profile (updated Jan 19, 2026): Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Penal Code 2017 provisions on 'sodomy' and 'inciting sodomy' carry up to two years, while the Penal Code's Sharia-reference clause allows the death penalty for same-sex activity.
CNN (Nov 2024): 'LGBTQ Afghans say they face abuse in detention as Taliban crackdown intensifies' — first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.summary:
The United Kingdom has a documented, in-force rollback concentrated on facilities and detention that directly affects trans visitors. Bathroom and changing-room use is now directed by biological sex under the equality watchdog's statutory code — a daily, nationwide civil restriction (the only country above 0.55 in this dataset with a nationally-legislated bathroom restriction). Since the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling, two severe-when-triggered risks apply if arrested: police forces strip-search trans women according to biological sex (with male officers), and trans women are placed in men's prisons — with documented suicide-risk litigation.

Documented trans killings have occurred (2023 and others). The climate is actively deteriorating via court- and equality-watchdog-led rollback rather than executive demonisation — a contrast with the United States.

The traveller-relevant positives are limited: no trans-specific border friction (foreign passports with X or amended markers are accepted), a hate-crime law covering gender identity (in practice theoretical recourse), no criminalisation, and functional institutions. Regional police forces, including the transport police, have published biological-sex search policies. Visitors arrested face the same strip-search and prison-placement rules as residents.
GBR.outOfScopeNotes:
Ordinary city crime in the capital and night-out alcohol incidents affect all travellers.

Unresolved or unverifiable: one police force's searching policy could not be retrieved at research time (an access-restricted document release); litigation outcomes on prison placement and equality-statute revisions are pending, so the operative rules may shift; conviction or prosecution data for the documented killings is not covered by this record's sources.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.summary:
Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons run on a statutory separation with a binary men/women housing model, and assignment matching a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

How the exception is applied in practice is unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from a neighbouring state in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility; critics called her gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. A Verfassungsblog essay from March 2026 argues that trans prisoners need no discriminatory special law and that ordinary anti-discrimination law should govern their placement and treatment.

Airport screening is the other documented point of friction. The trans DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, alleging that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Women-only venues remain contested but the dispute is confined to commercial leisure settings. A guideline from the Deutscher Sauna-Bund issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public argument about registered trans women's access, and Berlin saunas and comparable venues have been working out how to treat trans women since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025 after months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears the self-declaration route would be misused. Trans woman Alessia Dorigo countered that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic, that identity is felt rather than declared, and that she had taken a hard road to it.

Whether the Chemnitz women's prison placement announced in August 2025 was final, and whether any challenge to the July 2026 transfer succeeded, is not established by these sources; the DW and France24 items rest on a single case.

The DW prison description predates the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 January 2025, so the account of routine practice may be outdated, and the statutory citation is specific to one province while placement rules and their application vary by state.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.summary:
Most visitors experience little direct hostility or discrimination in daily contact, particularly in major tourist destinations, and the everyday risk posture for a transgender traveller is low. LGBTQ visibility remains limited, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality lags behind other developed countries.

The statutory framework is the Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, which defines gender identity, obliges the government to publish the annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of SOGI diversity, and establishes the national basic plan. Parliament enacted the law in June 2023 after months of debate, with the text watered down amid a culture-war dispute over transgender issues. No national anti-discrimination statute and no guarantee against violence exist alongside it.

In July 2023 the Supreme Court held that government restrictions on a transgender employee's use of restrooms were illegal, upholding damages against the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work. She had challenged the denial in 2015, and a Tokyo district court ruled for her in 2019 on her important legal interest in living by her self-identified gender, awarding damages.

A separate court ruled that requiring surgery as a condition of changing gender markers on documents is unconstitutional; the case, brought by Gen Suzuki, concerned the sterilising-surgery requirement for legal gender-marker change. Legal gender recognition therefore remains a court-based process from which the surgical condition has been struck.

Bathhouse use is the sharpest day-to-day exposure point. Onsen, sento and super-sento venues can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors, and dedicated guides list LGBTQ-friendly venues, private-bath and co-ed options, and the applicable etiquette; a first-person account published in March 2023 sets out what a trans traveller should expect from venue norms and transition-related questions.

Custody consequences of the lagging framework are documented rather than theoretical. Kasamatsu Prison, a women's facility in Gifu, holds an inmate listed as female on the family register who identifies as a man and has been diagnosed with gender identity disorder; the Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded male clothes and a male hairstyle and, after years with no policy change, issued a formal warning to the prison in September 2023. Placement of convicted trans inmates follows registered sex rather than gender identity.

Pre-trial detention shows the same pattern. Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024 and held for more than 100 days charged with assault: he was detained among men, initially denied hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it, mocked for his transgender identity during interrogations, and permitted to shower away from other detained men only after repeated requests. Human Rights Watch frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face.
JPN.outOfScopeNotes:
The CEDAW shadow report dates from May 2009 and functions as a historical baseline; the inventory supplies no current equivalent measurement of discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care.

The onsen material is traveller-utility guidance rather than legal or official guidance, and it does not establish the legal position of a gender-diverse person refused entry to a bathhouse.

The first-person onsen account is published as of 29 March 2023 with a stated last update of 10 July 2026; that update date could not be reconciled against the publication date from the inventory alone.

Whether the Gifu prison has since adopted a policy on clothing, hairstyle or housing placement for trans inmates is unresolved: the record shows only a formal warning issued in September 2023 after years without change.

The extent to which the Supreme Court bathroom holding applies to private-sector workplaces, transport, hotels and other non-state settings is not resolved by the sources listed.

Legal gender recognition requirements beyond the struck surgical condition, including any remaining court-process conditions, are not detailed in the inventory beyond the ruling on the surgery mandate.

Chambers Global Practice Guide update (Japan LGBTQ status): significant progress including enactment of the SOGI-promotion law, two pro-transgender Supreme Court decisions and one gay-friendly Supreme Court decision, while full marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain absent — legal-status update useful for framing institutional protection.

CEDAW NGO shadow report on LBT persons in Japan (May 2009): situation characterised by invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation; lesbians, bisexual women and transgender persons face discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention — dated baseline for institutional-protection claims.

sources.title: Prison warned over treatment of transgender inmate | The Asahi Shimbun
sources.summary: Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.

sources.title: Japan Should End Abusive Detention Conditions for Transgender People | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. For the prison-housing axis, it documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.

JPN.localsOnly:
Residents face discrimination in education, employment, housing and health care on the basis of being lesbian, bisexual or transgender, with limited governmental attention to those sectors as recorded in the 2009 CEDAW shadow report.

The SOGI-promotion Act imposes continuing obligations on the state: it requires publication of annual implementation status for policies promoting understanding of SOGI diversity and sets the national basic plan that governs official approaches to LGBT issues, giving residents a statutory basis on which to assess government performance.

Employment protections have a concrete anchor in public service. The Supreme Court's 2023 holding that a national ministry violated public-service law by restricting a transgender woman's bathroom access, following a 2019 first-instance victory on her important legal interest to live by her self-identified gender, supports claims by public-sector employees; its reach beyond public service is not established here.

Companies operate under duties discussed in professional guidance on LGBTQ status in Japan, including alongside the SOGI-promotion law, while full marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain absent from the statute book.

For incarcerated residents, placement follows the family register. Treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level: in the Gifu case the bar association sought male clothing and hairstyle for an inmate who identifies as a man, and after years without policy change escalated to a formal warning in September 2023.
JPN.blindSummary:
Most visitors experience little direct hostility or discrimination in daily contact, particularly in major destinations, and the everyday risk posture for a transgender traveller is low. LGBTQ visibility remains limited, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality lags behind other developed states.

The statutory framework is the Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, which defines gender identity, obliges the national government to publish the annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of SOGI diversity, and establishes the national basic plan. The legislature enacted the law in June 2023 after months of debate, with the text watered down amid a culture-war dispute over transgender issues. No national anti-discrimination statute and no guarantee against violence exist alongside it.

In July 2023 the supreme court held that government restrictions on a transgender employee's use of restrooms were illegal, upholding damages against a national ministry for barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work. She had challenged the denial in 2015, and a first-instance court ruled for her in 2019 on her important legal interest in living by her self-identified gender, awarding damages.

a separate court ruled that requiring surgery as a condition of changing gender markers on documents is unconstitutional; the case, brought by a named plaintiff, concerned the sterilising-surgery requirement for legal gender-marker change. Legal gender recognition therefore remains a court-based process from which the surgical condition has been struck.

Bathhouse use is the sharpest day-to-day exposure point. Public baths can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors, and dedicated guides list LGBTQ-friendly venues, private-bath and shared-bath options, and the applicable etiquette; a first-person account published in March 2023 sets out what a trans traveller should expect from venue norms and transition-related questions.

Custody consequences of the lagging framework are documented rather than theoretical. a women's prison in the province holds an inmate listed as female on the family register who identifies as a man and has been diagnosed with gender identity disorder; the provincial bar association demanded male clothes and a male hairstyle and, after years with no policy change, issued a formal warning to the prison in September 2023. Placement of convicted trans inmates follows registered sex rather than gender identity.

Pre-trial detention shows the same pattern. a prominent transgender activist was arrested in March 2024 and held for more than 100 days charged with assault: he was detained among men, initially denied hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it, mocked for his transgender identity during interrogations, and permitted to shower away from other detained men only after repeated requests. an international human-rights organisation frames this as part of the state's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face.
JPN.blindOutOfScope:

The bathhouse material is traveller-utility guidance rather than legal or official guidance, and it does not establish the legal position of a gender-diverse person refused entry to a public bath.

The first-person bathhouse account is published as of 29 March 2023 with a stated last update of 10 July 2026; that update date could not be reconciled against the publication date from the inventory alone.

Whether the provincial prison has since adopted a policy on clothing, hairstyle or housing placement for trans inmates is unresolved: the record shows only a formal warning issued in September 2023 after years without change.

The extent to which the supreme court bathroom holding applies to private-sector workplaces, transport, hotels and other non-state/province settings is not resolved by the sources listed.

Legal gender recognition requirements beyond the struck surgical condition, including any remaining court-process conditions, are not detailed in the inventory beyond the ruling on the surgery mandate.

THA.name: Thailand
THA.summary:
The Immigration Bureau operates 'Welcome Pride by Immigration', launched 5 August 2024 to mitigate the concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender. It is the entry-friction measure a trans visitor most needs to know about before arrival.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, following the bill's final Senate reading in June 2024, making Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. Marriage equality closes the practical gaps that previously excluded couples from property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims.

Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID or passport, and title prefixes remain locked to the sex assigned at birth. Advocates at the 2025 'Pride in Action' forum urged the government to expedite a gender-recognition law after marriage equality, and Human Rights Watch found no route for transgender people to obtain legal documentation reflecting their gender identity, with even affirmative measures such as first-name changes leaving discretionary power with officials.

Thai law has no hate-crime designation. When a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April 2025, after she refused his request for sex, the community called it a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is handled as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no data collection. LGBTQ+ groups called urgently for new hate-crime protections in the aftermath.

Detention carries specific exposure. The Department of Corrections has separated LGBT prisoners from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; one trans woman stopped by police, expecting to be placed with men because her documents still carried the title Mr., was instead held in the separated wing. Elsewhere, transgender women usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary confinement.

Social acceptance runs ahead of the legal framework. Trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than is typical in the West, and gender variance is visible in mainstream culture.
THA.outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition is still pending after marriage equality; no enactment date or draft status is established in the available sources.

The enforcement record of the 2015 anti-discrimination law is described as incomplete, but the sources do not quantify complaints, rulings or penalties.

The status of the Min Buri LGBT prison pilot after its 2016 announcement is not resolved in the inventory, and the proposal for an exclusively-LGBTQ facility has no reported outcome.

The Outright International country overview underpinning the legal-status read was last updated 12 March 2026; other items date from 2017, 2021 and 2025, so the currency of individual claims varies.

The 2025 Pattaya killing is documented through community and press accounts; the inventory does not report the judicial outcome or whether any charge beyond the ordinary offence was brought.

sources.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)
sources.summary: NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police and expecting to be 'thrown in prison with all the men because I still have the title of Mr.,' was instead held in the separated wing. The government was also discussing what could be the world's first exclusively-LGBTQ prison facility (the Min Buri pilot), while accepting that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary. Of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities.

sources.title: Exclusion or protection? Activists skeptical about LGBT prison (Coconuts Bangkok)
sources.summary: Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'
