SVN.name: Slovenia
SVN.summary:
Slovenia is among Central and Eastern Europe's most progressive destinations for trans visitors, with a cleaner documented profile than its neighbours. Legal gender recognition is depathologised (no surgery or psychiatric-diagnosis requirement), and a 2022 reform abolished local jurisdiction in the gender-change procedure — reducing involuntary outing through local bureaucracy. Comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers gender identity, same-sex marriage is legal (2022, via the Constitutional Court), and no far-right party is in government.

No severe traveler-axis incidents surfaced in research: no mob violence against trans people, no trans-tourist rape, no European Court case of police abuse, and no documented foreign-trans-detention case — unlike several neighbours (Greece's Thessaloniki mob, Italy's tourist-rape and Milan police beating, Czechia's trans-foreigner extradition mishandling, Poland's foreign-trans-woman-in-male-detention). The main caveats are a far-right youth campaign ("Two Sexes, One Truth"), an underreporting/trust gap in hate-crime reporting, and thinner detention-placement evidence for a small country.
SVN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is very low.

sources.summary: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: Slovenia is regarded as among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights - same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations registerable - with comprehensive antidiscrimination laws enacted since 2016 explicitly covering sexual orientation and gender identity.
thin: no usable finding

Ministry of the Interior notice of 29 October 2022: the local-jurisdiction step in legal gender-change procedures was abolished on the recommendation of the Advocate of the Principle of Equality, so transgender persons are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of transgender identity in their local environment.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): Legebitra documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents in 2023. After Pride, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate while the Prime Minister took three days to react and the Interior Minister made no statements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the Health Ministry officially confirmed to the Interdisciplinary Council for Gender Recognition that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition and formally asked the Interior Ministry to amend the relevant Civil Registry Act sub-article. The review also notes the death at 73 of a founder of Slovenia's grassroots LGBTI movement.

US State Department 2023 report on Slovenia: no laws criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and there were no reports of state-condoned violence, but authorities recorded violence incidents without tracking case numbers and local NGOs called violence against LGBTQI+ persons prevalent and under-reported. In June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the Ljubljana Pride route, marchers had eggs thrown at them and rainbow flags were burned on video.

ENACT national report of January 2025 (EU CERV-2023 project): civil society provides LGBTI hate-crime victims counselling, advocacy and safe spaces, but LGBTI persons using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles. The report documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.

UPI report of 25 July 2006: Slovenia passed a law legalising same-sex marriage but restricted the ceremony to the two partners plus a local community registration official - no friends or relatives. Gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the move as a concrete step while criticising the law as 'insufficient'.

Inquirer/AFP (Dec 2015): Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family' four days before the referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament in March - the referendum (later lost) followed a conservative challenge.

SVN.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
SVN.localsOnly: The depathologised LGR regime and the 2022 local-jurisdiction reform are resident-facing administrative law.

SRB.name: Serbia
SRB.summary:
Serbia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors despite no criminalisation. The most acute documented traveler-axis risk is police: in February 2024 the interior ministry began investigating officers who beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during a Belgrade apartment raid. About 105 sexual-orientation/gender-identity-motivated incidents were recorded in 2024, and Pride marches require heavy police protection.

The country is outside the Schengen border-free travel area, so border checks apply to foreign travellers.

The bottom line for visitors: police-brutality risk and weak protection make it a high-risk destination despite no criminalisation, with the major-tourist city "conditionally" manageable under situational awareness.
SRB.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and border-corruption affect all travellers; the country is not inside the Schengen border-free travel area, so border checks apply to foreigners.

sources.summary: Balkan Insight (27 Feb 2024): Serbian authorities investigating allegations that police officers assaulted two LGBT people — a probe into police violence against LGBT citizens (outcome: investigation opened).
Da se zna! (2 Sep 2025): presentation of the association's 8th annual hate-crime report, 'Transphobia and Homophobia in Serbia 2024' — the standing civil-society incident register for the year.

APT (Association for the Prevention of Torture) Serbia country page, national-preventive-mechanism recommendations: the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela, Belgrade, shall let transgender women at intake choose a female officer for searches/body inspection rather than a male or combined search — a concrete custodial-rights finding for trans detainees.

HRW World Report 2025 (Serbia/Kosovo chapter): intolerance and violence against LGBT people remained significant concerns in Serbia in 2024; state response to July-August protests (activist arrests, smear campaigns) highlighted rule-of-law weaknesses.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Serbia: trans people face testosterone supply shortages (Testosteron Depo); a publication analysed 70 instances of politicians' hate speech (April 2023-April 2024); the Pride Info Centre was attacked in January and announced closure in September after 20+ attacks since 2018, none properly sanctioned; a Zoomer survey found three-quarters of trans/non-binary people fear job interviews due to anticipated discrimination.

US State Department 2018 Human Rights Report for Serbia: human-rights issues include government corruption, violence against journalists, and 'crimes including violence targeting Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Intersex (LGBTI) individuals'.

HRV.name: Croatia
HRV.summary:
Croatia is broadly workable with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its regional neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in the research. The Dalmatian coast's international-tourism culture (Dubrovnik, Hvar, Split) is broadly open, and Zagreb, the capital, has the region's most established gay scene.

The framework is weaker than many peer nations': legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID, covering only some documents; there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of a host who refused to accommodate a gay couple shows enforcement works.

The Catholic-conservative climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. The country, an EU and Schengen member, sits inside the border-free travel area, so border friction for most travellers is low.
HRV.outOfScopeNotes: General tourist-season crime and border checks for non-EU nationals affect all travellers. The clean documented profile reflects research coverage; absence of documented cases is not proof of absence of risk.

sources.summary: Zagreb Pride documentation report (2018) on Croatia's implementation of CoE Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5: hate-crime legislation and under-reporting of homophobic/transphobic crimes, hate speech case studies, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, same-sex partnership recognition, employment discrimination, and compiled hate-crime data with case studies.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Croatia: a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking (2018 incident); anti-gender disinformation escalating - a Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation with no LGBTI organisations invited; the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before.

Croatian legal journal (Igrec, 2026, Elektronicki zbornik radova Veleuilista u Sibeniku 20(1-2):191-206): analyses how police/customs/court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming persons under Croatian law — built on the 2013 legislative amendment allowing gender-marker registration WITHOUT altering sex characteristics, working through the Criminal Procedure Act, Police Powers Act, Customs Act and prison-sentences law with case studies of search difficulties. Documents the post-2013 legal framework in practice.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Croatia (SOGI section): minority representatives say anti-discrimination provisions (employment, housing, education, health) are not consistently enforced; NGOs report the judiciary's uneven handling of discrimination cases and limited justice access, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial; hate-crime investigations flagged as inadequate. Official-source evidence on enforcement gaps despite formal protections.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex conduct legal since 1977; life partnerships since 2014 while the 2013 constitutional referendum banned same-sex marriage; full same-sex adoption rights since 2022 (final court ruling); open military service; hate-crime legislation; Pride events incl. Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac, Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March; legal gender recognition framework. Reference backbone for the record's dated milestones.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers (legal since 1977, partnership/protection laws) — but PDA may draw unwelcome responses in lesser-populated cities and gay venues are 'virtually non-existent outside Zagreb', now improving with new venues in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Visitor-facing nightlife/PDA guidance.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Croatia (2024, reporting period 2023): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds.

CroL (May 2014, Croatian): Split got an LGBT Centre (second in Croatia, first in Dalmatia) a month before the 4th Split Pride (7 June 2014), run by association Risp-et; organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families (marriage, joint adoption) and said institutions create 'second-class citizens'; mayor Ivo Baldasar attended the press conference. Documents organised community infrastructure on the coast.

CroL (Oct 2014, Croatian): presentation of LGBTIQ+ centre 'Druga Rijeka' in Rijeka — founded to develop the community in Primorsko-goranska county and network with national/international organisations, backed publicly by mayor Vojko Obersnel and cultural institutions; goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy. Second major community centre documented.

HRV.localsOnly:
The partial, non-self-ID LGR regime (since 2015, covering only some documents) is resident-facing.

Enforcement gaps documented for residents: official human-rights reporting flags inconsistent enforcement of anti-discrimination provisions and inadequate hate-crime investigations, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial.

The country is broadly workable with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its regional neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in the research. The coast's international-tourism culture is broadly open, and the capital has the region's most established gay scene.

The framework is weaker than many peer nations': legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID, covering only some documents; there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of a host who refused to accommodate a gay couple shows enforcement works.

The Catholic-conservative climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. The country sits inside the border-free travel area, so border friction for most travellers is low.
HRV.blindOutOfScope: General tourist-season crime and border checks for non-nationals affect all travellers. The clean documented profile reflects research coverage; absence of documented cases is not proof of absence of risk.

An official human-rights report on the country says minority representatives report that anti-discrimination provisions (employment, housing, education, health) are not consistently enforced; NGOs report the judiciary's uneven handling of discrimination cases and limited justice access, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial; hate-crime investigations flagged as inadequate.

A travel guide reports the country widely accepts LGBTQIA+ travellers — but public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less populated cities and gay venues are virtually non-existent outside the capital, now improving with new venues in coastal and interior towns.

A local news report covers the presentation of an LGBTIQ+ centre in a second major city — founded to develop the community in the surrounding county and network with national and international organisations, backed publicly by the mayor and cultural institutions; goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy.

EST.name: Estonia
EST.summary:
Estonia is broadly workable with a strong progressive trajectory but a social climate that lags the law. It was the first Baltic and post-Soviet country to legalise same-sex marriage (2024), approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan in 2025 (with particular attention to trans people), joined 16 EU states in urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBT laws, and held Tallinn Pride in 2025. There are no documented severe traveler-axis incidents — no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality, or foreign-trans-detention case.

The notable gap is legal gender recognition: it remains medical-gatekept (it requires a diagnosis and is "complicated, arbitrary"; a reform bill stalled), and surveys show Estonians are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (62% avoid holding hands; 40% avoid certain locations for fear of assault).

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
EST.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime very low.

sources.summary: ERR News: Estonia approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan (approved by Economy Minister Erkki Keldo, developed over ~2 years by the Equality Policies Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications; photo-dated Tallinn Pride 31 May 2025). Sets targets across education (inclusive curricula, physical/mental safety of LGBTIQ students and staff), healthcare, employment and legal-framework reform, anchored on 'Estonia should be a great place for LGBTIQ people to live'. Trans-relevant: legal framework to be updated to support gender identity/expression protections.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): all same-sex relations legal nationwide; Estonia became the first Baltic state with marriage equality in June 2023 (incl. joint adoption; opposition filed 700+ amendments to block it, failed). Public support for marriage equality 53% (75% among 20-somethings) in 2023 vs 34% in 2012. National LGBTI equal-opportunities action plan approved 2025 with special attention to trans wellbeing; advocacy continues for self-determination-based legal gender recognition and hate-speech/hate-crime laws. LGBTI orgs can register.

Equaldex data for Estonia: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, no censorship; legal gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis; no nonbinary recognition; no hate-crime protections; employment discrimination prohibited on SOGI; housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only; conversion therapy not banned; bathroom access protected. Estonians rank #1 of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

F&M Global Barometer of Transgender Rights time series for Estonia (2011-2024): legal gender recognition exists but requires physiological alteration and psychiatric diagnosis; hate speech/crime legislation does not include gender identity; workplace/housing/healthcare anti-discrimination laws include gender identity; no known murders of gender-identity minorities.

TGEU/ILGA-Europe compliance report (2018) on Estonia's implementation of CoE Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5: covers hate crimes and data collection, safety of LGBT people deprived of liberty, hate speech, association, expression, transgender-specific health and private-life issues, employment, education, housing, sports and asylum.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Estonia: joined 16 EU states urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBTI laws; Foreign Minister publicly supported Tallinn Pride and missions flew rainbow flags; in December Estonia adopted a national action plan to strengthen LGBTI equality across education, healthcare, employment and the legal system.

LTU.name: Lithuania
LTU.summary:
The country is broadly workable, at the lower end, with one of Europe's most restrictive legal-gender-recognition situations. Lithuania's Civil Code grants the right to medically change gender in principle, but no legal framework regulating the procedure has existed for 17 years — a deadlock the Constitutional Court refused to resolve in September 2025, perpetuating what an ECtHR body called a "distressing legal uncertainty."

Socially, a conservative climate is well documented: an MP called LGBT people "degenerated" and "spreading diseases" (his immunity was revoked), "traditional family values" groups disrupt peaceful protests, and an ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to assembly. Trans people report systemic workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation, and psychological abuse.

There is no criminalisation, and the national Pride in 2024 drew a large crowd of 15,000.
LTU.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

sources.summary: LGL (Lithuanian Gay League) news (Sept 2025): the Constitutional Court refused to address Lithuania's 18-year trans rights gap - a significant setback; the Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

LGL news (Aug 2025): could courts finally end 17 years of legal limbo for transgender rights? - the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the question of the laws' compliance with the Constitution to the Constitutional Court.

LRT (Sept 2025): Lithuania's Constitutional Court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
LRT (May 2025): trans people in Lithuania detail workplace harassment - open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

LGL news (April 2024): the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly - inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs at an LGL assembly; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson, 'The Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania - Summary of the National Review 2024': second national review (after 2019) covering public attitudes, the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and negative public attitudes; notes the lack of a legal framework and strategic approach.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Lithuania: systemic lack of targeted LGBTI hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule complicated by his MEP immunity.

PinkNews (Sept 2013): Lithuania's parliament to consider five anti-gay and anti-trans bills - a ban on gender reassignment ('gender is determined genetically from the very moment of conception'), a same-sex adoption ban, fines up to €1,800 for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

PinkNews (July 2009): Lithuania's parliament passed a 'Section 28-style' law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors ('Law on the Protection of Minors'), overriding President Adamkus's veto 87-6; Amnesty called it 'a huge step backwards'.

LVA.name: Latvia
LVA.summary:
Latvia is broadly workable with no legal framework for gender recognition — trans people cannot legally change their gender marker, leaving those who have transitioned in a legal limbo. The most documented institutional failure is the European Court of Human Rights' ruling in Hanovs v. Latvia (2024), which found the country failed to prosecute a homophobic hate crime, violating the prohibition of inhuman treatment and the right to private life.

On the positive side, an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to an LGBTI asylum-seeker in 2025, showing some institutional capacity for protection.

There is no criminalisation, and bathrooms are unrestricted.
LVA.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

sources.summary: LSM feature (27 Jun 2025): civil unions for same-sex couples in force since 1 July 2024; transgender and nonbinary Latvians still lack targeted legal change — a trans immigrant describes how legal transition would invalidate his marriage and residency status, and coalition MPs say trans rights 'have not emerged as a major issue yet'; Latvia was the first EU country to elect an openly gay head of state (2023).

ECtHR press release, Hanovs v. Latvia (18 July 2024): the Court unanimously found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after a 2020 homophobic attack - no criminal charges were brought despite the aggressor admitting anti-gay slurs; the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Latvia: an administrative court overturned denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker; the Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in the Khanov hate-crime case after the ECtHR ruling; two people attacked in Daugavpils, with the Prosecutor General ordering the investigation reopened after police closed it; former MEP Mamikins' homophobic posts investigated (he fled to Russia).

Strasbourg Observers analysis (Nov 2024) of Hanovs v. Latvia: further clarification of states' positive obligations in homophobic-attack cases - states must thoroughly investigate and punish hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; notes the troubling pattern of Eastern European states failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

ILGA-Europe Latvia page: includes the July 2024 ECtHR judgment in Hanovs v. Latvia - the Court found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after Latvian authorities declined to prosecute a homophobic assault on a gay couple in Riga as a hate-motivated offence.

PinkNews (May 2007): Archbishop of Riga Cardinal Janis Pujats called homosexuality 'total corruption in the sexual arena' and 'an unnatural form of prostitution', demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage and crowds of 40,000-50,000 to counter Pride, calling Pride a 'foreign-inspired action'.
Xinhua (June 2018): around 8,000 people marched in Baltic Pride 2018 in Riga - the annual event rotated among Baltic capitals; organised by Mozaika under the motto 'See Diversity! See Freedom!'.

TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.summary:
Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

The consequence axis of an arrest is severe and current: Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex — a transgender man was held in a women's prison — and a 2024 system-level profile documents LGBTI+ prisoners facing arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation in solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, frequent transfers, and complaints that are ineffective and can lead to further violence, with no policy or staff training to address LGBTI+ needs in a system described as built on a binary, heteronormative model. The December 2025 death of a transgender prisoner in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison moved the question to formal state-level contestation: rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to “detention practices affecting transgender prisoners,” accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers describe four trans inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, a delayed medical response, investigators entering only two days later and witness statements not taken, and the case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025. For a trans visitor — already profiled and detained for identity checks — arrest means placement by registered sex in a gendered facility under practices documented as segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched housing, in a system where the most recent custody death is under contested official handling.
TUR.outOfScopeNotes:
The October 2025 draft law is not yet passed — its enactment outcome is unresolved and under active government consideration. General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to Turkey. No source in the record documents marriage or partner-travel exposure for visitors separately from the general criminalisation risk described above.

Prison axis: no Turkish statute or regulation codifying trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in this record — the registered-sex placement finding rests on the December 2025 reporting, the segregation-and-isolation practice on the 2024 Prison Insider/CISST profile, and the December 2025 death's circumstances are contested with the investigation outcome unresolved.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a draft legislative package would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague claims of protecting 'the family' and 'public morals' — framing the Erdoğan government has repeatedly used to legitimise stigmatisation; sets the reform backdrop as authoritarian drift. Key legislative-risk evidence for 2025-26.

Kaos GL (Feb 2026): the LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations in 2025 — about two-and-a-half times 2024 — dominated by detention (299 detention decisions: 256 on record, 43 off the record), plus systematic privacy attacks; frames hostility turned into state policy. Quantified annual evidence.

bianet (Aug 2025): Istanbul police detain ~20 trans women for ID checks amid profiling concerns - stopped on the street, while shopping or in cafés in Beyoğlu, held at Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released after 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks; legal experts argue GBT checks violate ECHR Article 5; one detainee: 'They didn't fine us, but they documented us. The new law hasn't even passed yet, but they're already enforcing it on us.'

Turkish Minute (26 Feb 2026): covers the Kaos GL 2025 report — hundreds of cases documented via media monitoring and civil-society complaints; six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings; transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Second reporting of the annual data.

Truth Justice Memory Center (Aug 2025): monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week — violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025; senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepened homophobia and transphobia, and discrimination against LGBTI+ people and their allies was entrenched. Event-monitoring evidence.

sources.title: Rights groups urge probe into 'suspicious' death of transgender prisoner in Turkey (Stockholm Center for Freedom)
sources.summary: SCF (18 Dec 2025): transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkish rights groups (coordinated from Human Rights Association / IHD branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakir, Mersin and Aydin) demanded an independent investigation and changes to 'detention practices affecting transgender prisoners'. Kaos GL-cited accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers say four transgender inmates were collectively sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators only entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; opposition MP Sevda Karaca (EMEP) raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. The case documents that Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex (a trans man was held in a women's prison) and that trans-prisoner custody conditions were formally contested at the state level in late 2025.

sources.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
sources.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

TUR.localsOnly:

The documented custody practice is resident-facing: trans prisoners held by registered sex in gendered facilities (a trans man in a women's prison), the documented pattern of strip searches, solitary-style isolation, restricted healthcare, frequent transfers and ineffective complaints, and the December 2025 death of a transgender prisoner at Sincan Women's Prison all concern residents in state custody — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
TUR.blindSummary:

DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.summary:
Denmark is a historically progressive destination. It was the first European country to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration (2014), has banned conversion therapy (2023), offers nonbinary gender markers, and has comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering gender identity. There is no rollback movement, and Copenhagen ranks among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities.

One documented visitor-relevant weakness: the Danish Institute for Human Rights flags that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time of reporting — relevant to a visitor who is targeted.
DNK.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

One source claims Denmark has no conversion-therapy ban yet (bill revived August 2026) while the summary records a 2023 ban — the discrepancy is unresolved. The resident-discrimination statistics above cover residents, not visitors, so their bearing on visitor risk is scope-limited.

sources.summary: Context/Thomson Reuters (25 Sep 2024): Denmark's self-ID law (gender change without medical evaluation, in force since 2014) is credited by activists with cooling the trans debate; Denmark was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989) and ranks among the world's best for LGBTQ+ rights.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex couples may marry and adopt; discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics is prohibited; trans people self-determine legal gender markers and non-binary people can choose an 'X' passport marker; Aug 2024 the government announced a plan to strengthen multi-parent (3-4 parent) families.

TV 2 Denmark (10 Sep 2024): the Supreme Court held it is not a human-rights violation for a trans inmate to serve in a men's prison department — the leading Danish authority on trans placement in custody.

Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT+ barometer: 38% of homosexuals and bisexuals report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance; hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity/expression or sex characteristics recurs annually.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): UN Committee Against Torture 8th periodic review found some trans people, QTIBIPOCs and migrants report denial of access to spaces and services and threats; anti-trans discourse intensified as Parliament debated lowering the legal-gender-recognition age limit; committee urged psychosocial counselling and intersex remedy.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025: in July a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen; 40% of LGBTI students aged 15-25 reported self-harm in the past year, two to three times their classmates' rate; Denmark signed a UN resolution against intersex discrimination (March).

WanderSafe 2026 Copenhagen guide: among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities — first country to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989), marriage 2012, gender self-declaration since 2014; Danish Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment/services; no conversion-therapy ban yet (bill revived Aug 2026).

F&M Global Barometers Denmark profile: gender-identity-based arbitrary arrest freedoms affirmed every year 2011-2024; workplace anti-discrimination laws have covered gender identity since 2015, with fair-housing gender-identity protection throughout the period.

HuffPost (5 Feb 2013): Guatemalan trans woman Fernanda Milan became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark — refused return over gender identity, citing police attacks and threats for her trans activism — an early marker of Denmark's asylum treatment of trans claimants.

DNK.localsOnly: The self-declaration LGR regime (2014, nonbinary markers) is resident-facing; the 2024 Supreme Court prison-placement ruling — a trans woman who legally changed her gender without surgery must serve in a men's prison and be strip-searched by male staff, held not to violate the European Convention on Human Rights — and the LGR-age-limit debate concern residents. Resident discrimination data: 38% of homosexuals and bisexuals report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance; 40% of LGBTI students aged 15–25 reported self-harm in the past year; and a migrant trans woman was murdered in a Copenhagen hotel in July 2025.

NOR.name: Norway
NOR.summary:
Norway is very safe for trans visitors, with strong legal protections and official responses, but with a more acute violence context than its Nordic neighbours. There is no criminalisation, bathrooms are unrestricted, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction; anti-discrimination law covers gender identity; and the police operate a dedicated hate-crime unit with the security service providing annual Pride threat assessments.

Offsetting facts: a terrorist shot and killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022 (the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years); police-reported hate crimes against queer and trans people rose sharply in 2023 (up 18% overall, with trans-specific reports nearly doubling); and though the security service reports a significant decline in threats for 2025 Pride, hate-speech and intimidation risks persist.
NOR.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US travel update; general urban crime is very low.

A source was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401), so the 2020 hate-speech ban's adoption details rest on the underlying news report. Underreporting means the official hate-crime figures understate the real level, which remains unverifiable.

sources.summary: Official Norwegian health-rights page (Gender Recognition Act): legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity — self-declaration decided at the tax office — from age 16 alone, 6-16 with parents, under-6 only for documented congenital DSD; a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad. For this record: the official, no-medical-intervention document-change route.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Norway: reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity/expression and antisemitism; Zaniar Matapour sentenced to 30 years (the strictest penalty) for the 2022 Oslo Pride mass shooting; a drag bingo event sparked online threats; a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (2020) covers Norway outlawing hate speech against trans people (amendment to the Penal Code).

NRK (May 2024, Norwegian): record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims report little trust in police, and a dedicated hate-crime group encourages reporting. For this record: rising reports with a documented, quantified drop in case clearance.

UiO C-REX research blog (Sept 2024): transphobic hostility in Norway manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists — the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 Kristiansand march advocated 'crushing the gay lobby', and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as 'degeneracy'. For this record: organised ideological anti-trans hostility as a movement phenomenon, not street-level risk for ordinary visitors.

UiO C-REX (June 2025), HATECYCLE study of 3,000+ survey responses from LGBTQI people: only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police — barriers include mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, and many who did report described dismissive treatment. For this record: official statistics undercount anti-LGBTQI hate crime by a wide margin.

OSCE/ODIHR frameworks page for Norway: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework. For this record: the statutory definition behind Norway's hate-crime counting.

Nordisk Post (Apr 2025): Norway's Police Security Service (PST) reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. For this record: current threat-level assessment from the security service.

Life in Norway resource page (updated Nov 2020): Norwegians generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people; Norway was among the first countries with anti-discrimination laws; directory of national resources (FRI, Skeiv Ungdom, Transgender Association, Oslo Pride). For this record: social-climate context and the support-directory landscape.

SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.summary: Sweden is very safe. The one documented everyday-facility friction: a national swimming-pool chain's guidelines restrict trans persons' changing-room access — lawyers say this may violate discrimination law, so a trans visitor using such facilities may face exclusion. Brå (the crime-prevention council) reports roughly 6,700 LGBTQI-related hate-crime reports. Bathrooms as such are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and there is no rollback movement.
SWE.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

One source could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so the parliamentary-approval step rests on the underlying summary of that entry. Whether the changing-room guidelines breach discrimination law is unresolved — only a legal opinion is on record.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry (April 2024) covers Sweden's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and medical procedures performed on genitalia.

TGEU report of 16 July 2025: Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025, simplifying the procedure but falling short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining.

Swedish-language SVT report of October 2025: swimming-pool giant Medley stops trans people from choosing changing rooms - the article explains why trans customers may no longer pick changing facilities at the chain, a direct everyday-facility access setback documented for trans visitors.

Brå (National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13: supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives - the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025): a bill would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure. In November the Church of Sweden decided new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, passing 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council.

Open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (4 February 2016, vol 13, pp 119-129): traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014 - the historical record behind current service conditions.

FIN.name: Finland
FIN.summary: Finland is very safe for trans visitors. There are no documented severe trans-specific incidents (no tourist-rape, mob-violence or police-brutality case); bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction. Record-level hate-crime reporting exists, but no incident series involving trans visitors is documented.
FIN.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US update issued for outbound citizens; general urban crime is very low.

Official statistics register suspected offences as reported in police files — the legal code has no hate-crime category, so the true motive-based level is unverifiable from official figures. No marriage or partner-travel exposure for visitors beyond the general legal-equality baseline is documented in this record.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Finland: record 1,808 suspected hate crimes in 2025 (+13% since 2023), with sexual orientation and gender identity recurrent motives (12% of cases); Finland's first conversion-practices case prosecuted as assault (convictions in March); Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices (125-49) in March, though a full ban remained pending.

Finland's Police University College (Polamk, Nov 2025): record 1,808 suspected hate-crime offenses reported in 2024 — highest figure ever recorded; defamation and assault the most common types. The sexual-orientation/gender-identity-or-expression category climbed 72 -> 68 -> 126 -> 140 -> 215 -> 241 across the six reported years. The Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, so motive is only recorded in police reports — meaning SOGI-motivated incidents are counted via reported suspicion, not charge.

The Guardian (21 Mar 2025): Finland (with Denmark) updated its US travel advice for transgender citizens after reports of border ordeals following the US 'two genders' executive order — Denmark advises trans travellers to contact the US embassy in Copenhagen before departure over document issues. Signal for the record: Finland's government publicly sides with trans travellers facing document-based refusals abroad; issued as outbound advice, not destination risk.

Investigate Europe, 'The Cruel Condition' (10 Sep 2025): Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden explicitly wrote infertility requirements into law for legal gender recognition; at least 11,000 people subjected to such conditions across the six countries investigated, Sweden first (1972, in force 40 years); the last requirement was phased out at end-June 2025 — Finland's statutory sterilisation-era requirement is history, but the legacy cohort is documented.

Yle (28 Feb 2018): Parliament approved a citizens'-initiative-inspired change to the Maternity Act recognising both women in same-sex partnerships as mothers from the moment of the child's birth — second-parent registration fixed at birth rather than via adoption.

Yle (1 Mar 2017): same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal in Finland; the western Finland register office alone had ~41 same-sex couples scheduled to marry in the first week — the operative date for all marriage-equality claims about Finland.

Yle (19 Sep 2013): the 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative for same-sex marriage collected 162,000+ certified signatures — largest Finnish initiative ever, far above the 50,000 threshold forcing parliamentary consideration; organiser target had been 250,000. The process route that produced the 2017 marriage law.

TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.summary:
Taiwan is a progressive Asian destination — it was the first in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage (2019), the government is investing US$8.76 million to double gender-neutral public bathrooms by 2029, and a trans march in Taipei drew 3,000 participants in 2025. There are no documented severe incidents (no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, or organised dating-app predation).

The main gaps are legal-gender-recognition reform stagnation — a 2008 Ministry order still requires sex-reassignment surgery to change one's gender marker (blocking an estimated 90% of trans people, with only case-by-case court exceptions), and the government has been "floundering" on reform — and a rising anti-gender discourse movement that has produced online waves of hostility. A trans woman was outed during a police identity inspection (the Viva case), and Taipei has held a vigil for victims of anti-trans violence.

For a visitor, bathrooms are unrestricted (and being proactively expanded to gender-neutral), there is no criminalisation, and border/immigration poses no trans-specific friction. Taipei City has trans-friendly service guidelines.
TWN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; earthquake/typhoon risks affect all travellers.

sources.summary: Taiwan Insight (Feb 2026): 'What about trans rights? Taiwan's ongoing struggle for self-ID' - the 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery to change legal gender blocks an estimated 90% of trans people from obtaining matching national ID; every ID-requiring aspect of daily life (clinics, airport security) becomes a potential site of distress and discrimination; the Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013.

Taiwan Insight (Jan 2026): the Taiwanese government continues to flounder on transgender rights in 2025 amidst continued transphobia - no tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction; pending conscription-criteria changes could actively harm trans people; anti-gender movement activity rising, with organisations supporting Trump's anti-trans policies and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Taipei Times (Aug 2024): the Ministry of Environment will invest NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide (623 to 1,246 by 2029); of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents reporting discrimination, 17% occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

Focus Taiwan (Nov 2025): 'Most Taiwan all-gender restrooms do not meet standards: Rights group' — an LGBTQ+ rights group finds only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.summary:
South Korea is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

The consequence axis of an arrest is largely undocumented: no source in this record describes how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice — and no civilian trans-prisoner case surfaced. The one documented trans-in-state-placement case is military rather than civilian: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; the Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty — a harsh institutional default corrected by the courts only after death. For a detained trans visitor, civilian-prison placement is simply unknown: in a legal system where legal gender recognition is possible and courts have repeatedly ruled for trans people, recourse would likely exist, but the placement practice itself is unverified — not a verified midpoint and not verified safe.
KOR.outOfScopeNotes:
Foreign-tourist taxi scams and shopping complaints rose 71% in 2024 — general, not trans-specific.

One source — a supreme-court family-register decision — could not be retrieved at research time, so that ruling's detail rests on its summary. No border-screening or document-handling practice specific to trans visitors is documented in this record.

Prison axis: no South Korean rule, regulation, case or practice is documented on civilian trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, no solitary/segregation practice; the only state-placement case on record is the military discharge case (an administrative discharge, not a prison-housing case). Where a detained trans visitor would be housed in the civilian system is unverified, and that gap cannot be read as evidence of either identity-based placement or mistreatment.

sources.summary: Seoul Central District Court, final 2 Jul 2024 (no appeal): police advising a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights; symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state, recognising the infringement.

Yonhap (8 May 2024): a court (Yeongdong) ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery to change legal sex status — five plaintiffs assigned male at birth, on hormone therapy for years; the court held demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals.

The Hankyoreh (21 Mar 2024): youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong research presented 20 Mar 2024 shows trans teens avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed — a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reports holding it in and leaving school early; researchers urged law and institutional reforms for safer school environments.

Korea Herald (28 Nov 2023): the state human rights watchdog NHRCK flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalisation' — the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): civilian same-sex conduct legal but criminalised in the military under Military Criminal Act Art. 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023; legal gender recognition possible; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; LGBTI organisations can register.

Peer-reviewed nationwide survey (Epidemiology and Health, 27 Jun 2025): 585 transgender and non-binary young adults mapped key milestones and stigmatization across life stages — documents pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

HRW World Report 2025, South Korea chapter (events of 2024): overall relatively positive record with free media and civil society, but persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people; chapter also covers the December 2024 martial-law crisis and assembly freedoms.

misterb&b gay travel guide to South Korea safety (July 2026): broadly positive for visitors to Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighborhoods but requiring contextual understanding - military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition, no national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

HRW (4 Aug 2017, 'South Korea: Supreme Court Affirms LGBT Rights'): documents LGBT registration litigation — an NGO won at Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017, with the government appealing to the Seoul High Court and Supreme Court; HRW criticises years of bureaucratic obstruction of LGBT group registration.

Custody-axis framing: the only trans placement case inside the country's custody system on record is a military conscript case — a conscript's discharge, death, posthumous reinstatement and line-of-duty recognition — rather than a civilian prison case; the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel (the military criminal code, article 92-6, up to two years' imprisonment) and the exclusion of transgender people from military service are resident-conscript-facing, not visitor-facing.

IND.name: India
IND.summary:
India demands real caution from trans visitors, with a complex mix of constitutional protection and real practical gaps. Same-sex acts were decriminalised in 2018, courts are protective, and same-sex marriage is not legal although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units — the partner-travel baseline. Police abuse is documented: a trans woman was groped by a railway-protection constable to 'check gender', airport security discriminated against a trans student at Chennai (CISF), and passport authorities have demanded unwarranted medical exams. A new penal code removed safeguards protecting trans people from sexual violence. Enforcement is uneven — only 11 of 36 units (states and territories) have protection cells.

The police abuse, the enforcement gaps, and the airport and passport friction place it in the middle of the scale, with courts protective. Huge subnational variation is expected: liberal metros like Bangalore and Kerala are materially safer than conservative rural north and central states.
IND.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime (theft, scams, sexual harassment of women tourists) is a documented concern in India affecting all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

The harsher documentation regime's enforcement is not yet observable; the freshness note records its passage in March 2026. Subnational variation is expected but only coarsely documented (11 of 36 units have protection cells).

Parliament passed it in March 2026.

CHN.name: China
CHN.summary:
China demands real caution — authoritarian but not criminalising: there is no criminalisation of trans identity, no bathroom-restriction law, and courts can provide some protection, but there are no anti-discrimination protections. The most directly visitor-specific finding is airport discrimination: a Thai trans YouTuber was singled out and subjected to discriminatory treatment at a Chinese airport. Displaying rainbow symbols inside venues has been disallowed — relevant to a visitor planning visible expression — and a foreign drag queen's tour was cancelled, showing foreign gender-nonconforming performers can meet repression while working here.

The most severe documented case — forced psychiatric commitment with electroshock 'conversion' therapy under family pressure, where a resident won unprecedented compensation — targeted a resident, not a tourist, showing the medical system can be weaponised; it does not scale directly to a visitor.
CHN.outOfScopeNotes:
General government surveillance, internet censorship, and arbitrary-detention risks affect all travellers to China; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

The policy drift is ongoing and its trajectory unresolved; no border-screening practice specific to trans visitors beyond the airport incident is documented; and a major news investigation on conversion practices could not be retrieved, so its findings rest on its summary.

sources.summary: The Thaiger (27 May 2025): Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong alleged Chinese immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video on Instagram with 'No one should be treated differently, no matter what their gender is.' Direct visitor-facing evidence of how a visibly trans traveller was treated at a Chinese border post.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT investigation (Dec 2024) covers transgender 'conversion' practices in China.

The Guardian (21 Nov 2024): performance artist Ling'er, 28, won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment — the first time a trans person had successfully challenged such treatment in China; she said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights.

Human Rights Watch (25 Jun 2026): around Pride month, platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes — HRW reads the censorship wave as illustrating a deteriorating rights situation for LGBT people in China (deepening repression restricting expression and association).

Radio Free Asia (28 Jan 2024): the CCP's crackdown against 'foreign ideologies' has made LGBTQ+ activism 'all but extinct' on the mainland — displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer allowed even inside venues, and in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. Ongoing harassment of queer expression in public space.

Foreign Policy (Jan 2025): gender transition in China is treated as 'a family affair' — even adults need parental consent to undergo gender-affirming surgery and change their legal gender (and must prove parental death if applicable); families are forced to resolve disagreements about the procedure internally. Practical barriers to care for trans residents and long-stay visitors.

Outright International overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): China's long-standing 'don't encourage, don't oppose, don't promote' posture has grown restrictive — the Cybersecurity Law and related rules censor LGBTI content deemed to 'disrupt social order'; LGBTI organisations cannot register, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and same-sex conduct has no legal protection.

CNN (3 Jan 2025): cancellation of nationwide shows by famous transgender dancer Jin Xing led some in China to fear a wider LGBTQ+ crackdown — the case of China's most visible trans star becoming a bellwether for the tightening climate.

SWI swissinfo (20 Aug 2026): a Zurich drag artist on tour in China found the space for queer subcultures shrinking first-hand — documenting how even foreign gender-nonconforming performers meet repression while working in China.

CNN (3 Mar 2016): broadcast regulator SAPPRFT guidelines banned depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour', including same-sex romance, from Chinese television screens — the media-censorship baseline that has persisted and now extends to social platforms.

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.summary:
Malaysia is dangerous — one of the few countries that criminalises gender expression per se. All 13 states and the Federal Territory prohibit "a man posing as a woman" under Sharia law (up to 3 years in jail, a fine, and caning). While these laws technically apply to Muslims, the enforcement climate affects all trans people: religious police conduct systematic raids on trans events — tipping off media in advance and sharing detainees' faces with tabloids (public outing and humiliation). Three trans women were killed in fewer than two months in 2019.

The political climate is shifting toward Islamist parties (a deputy minister urged the "deviant culture" label for LGBTQ; state-backed "rehabilitation" programs; dating-site blocking). For a non-Muslim foreign trans visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing law doesn't directly apply, but being caught in a raided venue, facing the enforcement climate, or being subject to Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping, applies to all including tourists) are real risks. There is no legal gender recognition.
MYS.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and Islamic-law compliance (alcohol, dress codes for religious sites) affect Muslim and non-Muslim travellers in different ways; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile — Malaysia (live page in cache): federal Penal Code section 377 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping), alongside Sharia enactments across the states prohibiting 'cross-dressing' or 'males posing as females' — including the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering 'sodomy' and 'sexual intercourse against the order of nature'. Situates Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise, with active litigation listed alongside the Mauritius and Namibia cases.

Human Rights Watch report (10 August 2022) 'I Don't Want to Change Myself', based on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 across seven states plus journalists and lawyers: every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity ('a man posing as a woman'), while the federal penal code punishes oral/anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events/media content were censored. The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows enforcement reach — 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt her over 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection.

Human Rights Watch (25 June 2019): a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb — the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity ('The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself').
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Aug 2023) covers growing LGBTQ fears in Malaysia as Islamists shatter reform hopes.

The Diplomat (10 December 2025): on 28 November police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B — the largest such raid since 2022 — with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, suspending 17 civil servants identified among them. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed; over 130 remained held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang. Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (DNS failure); the underlying Human Rights Law Centre case summary covers the Malaysian High Court denying a request to declare Sharia law prohibiting cross-dressing unconstitutional.
NOTE: The UNDP/Asia Pacific Transgender Network publication on Malaysia (image-based PDF; no text extractable).

International Commission of Jurists (July 2020): Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons; the ICJ condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees. Documents state-sanctioned targeting of trans people in the federal territories.

Malaysia4U legal guide (updated July 2026): sections 377A/377B criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; state Syariah offences (liwat, musahaqah, cross-dressing) apply only to Muslims (max 3 years, RM5,000 fine, 6 strokes). The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted. No same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human Rights Watch (24 September 2014) 'I'm Scared to Be a Woman': since the 1980s every one of Malaysia's 13 states has passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all 13 bar Muslim men from 'dressing as women' and three also bar 'women posing as men' — enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over 20 times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department (a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery), and prison terms of four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Follows the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge (Court of Appeal decision then expected 7 November 2014).

MYS.tangentialFactors: Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping) applies to all including tourists — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.

Political influence has grown for religious-conservative groups, and official rehabilitation programs for LGBT people exist.

For a foreign trans visitor who does not follow the country's religion, the religious offence does not apply directly, but same-sex conduct is a national criminal offence with severe penalties, applying to residents and international visitors alike. There is no legal gender recognition.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.summary:
Singapore is broadly workable — far safer than its neighbour Malaysia, with no criminalisation of trans identity, no religious police, and one of the world's lowest crime rates. Section 377A (which criminalised sex between men) was repealed in 2022, and the prison service reports no assaults against its 10 transgender inmates — unusually positive for axis-H. Singapore is also a regional medical hub with gender-affirming care available.

The main gaps: legal gender recognition requires genital surgery (expensive and restrictive), there is no anti-discrimination law (the 2025 Workplace Fairness Act explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity), and over 65% of trans Singaporeans report negative workplace experiences. A radio code still groups homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" as lifestyles barred from the airwaves. Progress has "stalled" since the 377A repeal, with discrimination "quietly tolerated."

For a visitor: efficient border processing, very low street crime, unrestricted bathrooms, and no trans-specific police friction. The atmosphere is conservative but quietly accommodating in practice.
SGP.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is extremely low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

sources.summary: MPSC report (Feb 2025): transgender community faces several key challenges to health and well-being. These include (1) the difficult process of legal gender recognition, which has a prohibitive cost due to the required genital surgeries; (2) discrimination, abuse and restrictions facing transgender students; (3) discrimination against transgender persons in the employment sector; (4) discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings that discourag

Outright International Singapore overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal for men and women; legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations cannot register — registration remains the structural gap despite decriminalisation.

Straits Times (15 Nov 2023): the Singapore Prison Service reported 10 transgender inmates currently behind bars and no recorded cases of assault against transgender inmates — a rare official datum on trans prisoners in the system.

Pink Dot SG (8 Jan 2025): the new Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it stops short of covering LGBTQ+ workers — gender identity/expression are not protected grounds, leaving workplace exposure for trans staff.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature (June 2023) covers Singapore's LGBT community feeling safer as the end of the 377A ban brings change.

South China Morning Post (3 Jul 2025): a clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden 'lifestyles' sparked calls for review — a former radio DJ and actor argued the grouping 'has no place in a post-377A Singapore'. Media-regulation residue after decriminalisation.

F&M Global Barometers Singapore country profile: interactive scores across unified/gay/transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index, 2011–2024, covering de jure protections and lived experience — score values are served dynamically and are not extractable from the fetched text.

Intrepid Travel 'Is Singapore LGBTQIA+ friendly': describes a thriving LGBTQIA+ social scene — gay-friendly bars (e.g. Backstage Bar in Chinatown), pop-ups and exhibitions — alongside practical guidance on solo travel and room sharing for its own trips. Visitor-facing operator guidance.

SGP.tangentialFactors: The radio code grouping homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" is a climate signal; the 2022 repeal of 377A removed partner-related criminal exposure for visitors.
SGP.localsOnly: The surgery-required LGR regime, the Workplace Fairness Act exclusion, and the 65% negative-workplace-experience figure are resident-facing; the prison-service data concerns resident inmates.

A law that criminalised same-sex conduct was repealed in 2022, and official prison data report no assaults on trans prisoners. Legal gender recognition requires genital surgery and is costly; no national anti-discrimination law protects gender identity, and a 2025 workplace fairness statute explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity; many trans residents report negative workplace experiences.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.summary:
Iran is one of the world's most severe environments for trans people — but with a unique bifurcation. Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty, and a trans woman was raped in Ministry of Intelligence custody (the documented case of Ghazal Marzban in Evin Prison, 2023). The Tehran City Council ordered trans people to avoid "busy" areas of the capital. Trans people who have not had surgery face immorality and indecency provisions (imprisonment, fines, lashes) and documented forced-transition pressure — 6Rang describes "40 years of forcing gay people to choose between transitioning and death."

However, transsexuality IS legally recognised in Iran (under a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini), and gender-affirming surgery is state-funded — making Iran one of the few countries in the region with any legal recognition of trans identity, and a trans medical-tourism hub. A post-operative trans visitor with matching documents is in a structurally different and better position than a pre-operative or non-binary visitor, or anyone perceived as same-sex-active — who face the death penalty, state-custody sexual violence, and forced-transition coercion.
IRN.outOfScopeNotes: General state-surveillance risks, compulsory hijab for all women, and the risk of arbitrary detention for foreign nationals affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub. The protections do not reliably reach custody: documentation shows Israel's response to transgender-prisoner vulnerability has been isolation or segregation from the general prison population rather than placement in facilities matching gender identity, and trans women have at times been held in men's prisons — but courts have intervened case-by-case, most notably an October 2019 ruling that ordered the prison service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing Netanyahu coalition and the Israel-Hamas war aftermath have weakened protections, though the National Security Committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.
ISR.outOfScopeNotes:
Security risks from the Israel-Hamas conflict (rockets, terrorism, border areas) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Custody axis: no statute or prison-service regulation on trans-prisoner placement is documented — the isolation/segregation pattern rests on a 2015 journal article and the corrective intervention on a single October 2019 court case, with the follow-up petition's outcome unreported — and whether case-by-case judicial relief would extend to a detained foreign visitor is not established.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary:
Argentina has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — the 2012 Gender Identity Law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, and funds transition healthcare. Buenos Aires is "one of the safest major cities in Latin America for LGBTQ+ visitors."

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the Milei government: the president has called "gender ideology" "child abuse," issued decrees modifying the Gender Identity Law, and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Police institutional violence against trans and travesti women is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, searches only on travestis). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the Milei decrees.
ARG.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (robbery, scams) in Buenos Aires affects all tourists; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (Apr 10, 2025): interviews in Buenos Aires (Apr 4, 2025) with trans activists — including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán (stabbed to death 2015) and Lohana Berkins — saying President Milei's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence; the situation described as 'chaotic, desperate'.

Agencia Presentes (Mar 19, 2026): the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — a record year, averaging one every 38 hours, marking an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.
