ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.summary:
The UAE is one of the most thoroughly documented trans-traveler-hostile countries in the world. At the border, trans visitors have been X-rayed to check their genitals (Israeli trans women, detained and denied entry at Dubai airport), deported for having a male passport (Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon at Expo 2020; Gigi Gorgeous), denied entry despite valid UAE visas (Indian trans person), and sentenced to prison for "dressing in a feminine way" (Singaporean trans woman, 1 year in Abu Dhabi). A Brazilian trans woman was arrested in her Dubai apartment by plainclothes police accusing her of drug trafficking.

The state "employs various legal mechanisms to explicitly acknowledge and penalize nonconformity with traditional gender roles" and actively targets "non-Emirati tourists." There is no legal gender recognition.

However, the UAE does not have the death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike Saudi Arabia or Iran), no documented custodial death of a trans person (unlike Saudi), and some trans visitors do enter successfully if their passport gender matches their presentation. The targeting is triggered by passport/presentation mismatch, not blanket.

VICE (Mar 21, 2022): Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon (2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up) was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand before her Expo 2020 appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.summary:
South Africa has one of the world's most progressive constitutional frameworks for trans rights — it was the first country to ban discrimination on sexual orientation (1996), has a legal gender recognition procedure (the Alteration of Sex Description Act, 2003), marriage equality (2006), and an Equality Act prohibiting unfair discrimination on gender. The Equality Court recently ruled in favour of a trans inmate who was denied gender expression and healthcare in prison (the Mokoena case, November 2025), affirming the constitutional right to gender-affirming healthcare for inmates, and Correctional Services has developed a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners.

But there is a wide gap between law and lived reality. LGR is administratively difficult, expensive, and inconsistently implemented ("the Mariana Trench of transphobia"). A trans woman was brutally attacked in a Tshwane tavern (January 2025); a Grindr-hostage ordeal was reported (December 2024); and anti-transgender violence has been documented within the public health system. There is a legal debate about whether businesses can refuse trans people facility access under the Consumer Protection Act.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, private healthcare available, and Cape Town and Johannesburg have established queer scenes. The violence targets local trans communities, not tourists.
ZAF.outOfScopeNotes: South Africa's high general crime rate (violent crime, carjackings, muggings) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

GroundUp (6 Aug 2025): Correctional Services has a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners but rights organisations doubt implementation; Lawyers for Human Rights represents a trans prisoner (NM) challenging conditions — pre-echo of the Nov 2025 Equality Court win.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): Civil Union Act in force 2006; since 2003 trans/intersex people can amend sex markers under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act (medical requirements pathologise identity; reform toward self-determination pending); 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; violence disproportionately hits black lesbian/trans/gender-nonconforming people in townships.

MambaOnline (6 Jan 2025): 23-year-old trans woman Aobakwe Mahlobo (make-up artist, Soshanguve→Winterveld) survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 Dec 2024, left with severe facial injuries and physical/emotional scars — she spoke out publicly; illustrates violent hate-crime risk against visible trans women in social venues.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.summary:
Indonesia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented trans-traveler death in custody and a presidential decree classifying LGBTQ+ as a national security threat. Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard trans activist from Peru, died in Bali police custody in 2022 after arrest at Bali airport on his honeymoon (family alleges police beating; police deny violence).

In Aceh province, Sharia law criminalises same-sex relations with public caning (applies to all persons in Aceh, including tourists). A new penal code effective January 2026 effectively criminalises all same-sex conduct nationally. President Prabowo in October 2025 classified "promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" as a national security threat alongside terrorism — and vigilante mob attacks on trans women escalated after this decree (10 attacks documented in Bogor between March and July 2026). Police conduct discriminatory raids on gay gatherings (75 arrested in Bogor in June 2025).

BUT: Bali is a major tourist hub where many trans visitors enter discreetly without incident; Indonesia has no death penalty; and Rodrigo's death is disputed (police deny violence) rather than clearly documented state torture.
IDN.outOfScopeNotes: Drug laws are severe (Rodrigo was arrested on drug charges); general terrorism/crime risks in certain regions affect all travellers.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Aug 2022) covers Indonesian police denying violence in the death of Harvard trans activist Rodrigo Ventocilla in Bali.

Harvard Crimson (Sept 2022): Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; on a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody, and his mother alleges police beat him — a documented death-in-custody case involving a trans traveler.

The Diplomat (14 August 2026, Robin Vochelet): vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law — President Prabowo Subianto's October 2025 presidential decree listing nonmilitary threats framed LGBTQ+ people within national defense policy. Article ties the violence and the official framing together as one escalation.

ABC News (15 August 2026): attacks on trans women 'did not suddenly appear' — analysis ties the surge to officials' latest verbal attacks and to the October 2025 presidential defense decree treating LGBT people as national-defense 'risks'. Academic commentator: the regulation shifts rhetoric 'into the official doctrine of national defence policy... risks that must be monitored and controlled'.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2025) covers Aceh province publicly caning two men for a same-sex relationship.

Outright International country page (updated 12 March 2026): Indonesia's new penal code took effect 2 January 2026 (signed December 2022) and penalises all consensual extra-marital sex between adults (reported as up to 2 years' imprisonment). Since same-sex marriage is not permitted, this effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with prosecution reported as selective — the current-law baseline for this record.
Human Dignity Trust country profile: two provinces of Indonesia (Aceh and South Sumatra) criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; national-level provisions target morality.

Amnesty International (June 2025): police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor on Sunday 22 June 2025, arresting 75 people (74 men, 1 woman) after public reports of a 'gay party'. Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called it 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' and said the gathering violated no law — evidence of venue-based raids targeting LGBT gatherings near Jakarta.

HRW (7 July 2026) 'Indonesia: Surge in Abuse Against LGBT Students': HRW has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016, following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia; Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organization, documented 94 cases. Officials in early July called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

HRW report (10 August 2016) 'These Political Games Ruin Our Lives': the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities 'mental illnesses' and recommended psychological 'rehabilitation', while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent — the origin point of the institutionalized anti-LGBT posture the record describes.

IDN.tangentialFactors: The new penal code (January 2026) criminalising all same-sex conduct nationally, and Aceh's Sharia caning provision (applying to tourists), are direct risks for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.summary:
Pakistan is dangerous for trans travellers — legally progressive on paper but severely undermined in practice. The 2018 Transgender Persons Protection Act is described as one of the most progressive pieces of legislation internationally, but the national religious court (the Shariat Court) gutted it in 2023, declaring provisions "un-Islamic". Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead in Karachi, the largest city of the country, 267 violence cases were documented in one state/province (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), and police commit a documented "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." The jirga (tribal) system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (the Zina Ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions). No trans-traveller-specific border friction or death in custody is documented. The 2020 rules introduced a neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but how document markers are treated at border crossings is undocumented.

For partner travel, no relationship or partner recognition is documented, so partner-based protections should not be assumed. The severity of social and police violence is the dominant risk.
PAK.outOfScopeNotes:
Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain regions affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the precise criminal status of consensual same-sex conduct — the statutes cited in the sources differ and definitions are unclear — remains ambiguous; no prosecutions were documented.

Unresolved: how identity documents are treated at border crossings ('X' recognition-marker practice is undocumented).

sources.summary: AP (Nov 2024): 'Shooting kills 3 transgender women in Pakistan's largest city' — gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there in a week.

BBC (21 Sep 2025): police found bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi — latest in a continuing pattern of lethal violence; article notes estimates of ~500,000 transgender citizens facing social exclusion and abuse.

Justice Project Pakistan policy brief: despite notable legal advances (Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018), protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice — the central challenge is implementation failure, not absence of law; brief makes custody/police safeguards recommendations.

UK Home Office country-policy note on SOGI, Pakistan, November 2025 (current-status authority): trans/intersex people protected under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 though the Federal Shariat Court declared provisions 'un-Islamic' in 2023 leaving ongoing legal disputes; consensual same-sex acts criminalised under PPC s.377 (2 years to life, definition unclear, male-to-male sex), only men criminalised per Human Dignity Trust (Dec 2024); LGBT+ people unlikely to face state persecution.

Amnesty International (19 May 2023): reacting to the Federal Shariat Court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 — calls the ruling 'a blow to the rights of the already beleaguered group' of transgender and gender-diverse people; Amnesty had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards.

The News, Pakistan (21 Oct 2025): analysis of the gap between law and reality — the 2018 Act affirmed self-perceived gender identity and the 2020 Rules introduced the neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but trans Pakistanis still face bullet-riddled bodies on highways, street harassment, rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion/ridicule at police stations.

Erasing 76crimes (3 Feb 2026, citing the Guardian): a wave of violence has left Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out — describes the Karachi night-time shooting at activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana (three bullets fired through the door, narrowly escaped); also reports Senator Mushtaq Ahmad proposing a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control trans people's official gender identity — an active retrograde legislative push.

Dawn analysis of the Federal Shariat Court verdict of 19 May 2023 (delivered across 12 shairat petitions): the court ruled sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Transgender Persons Act 2018 (gender identity, right to self-perceived gender identity, inheritance for transgender people) do not conform with petitioners' reading of Islamic principles, and speculated the Act could facilitate rape/sexual assault of women by men 'disguised' as transgender women — framing echoing Western anti-trans moral panic.

The Diplomat (Jul 2025): Pakistan's 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was hailed as a legislative turning point — granting right to self-identify and protection from discrimination in education, employment and healthcare — yet the piece documents citizens 'legally recognized, socially forsaken', i.e. statutory rights not matching lived status.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Pakistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Section 377; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.

PAK.localsOnly:
The 2018 Act's third-gender recognition (gutted by the religious court in 2023, under appeal) and the hijra community's legal recognition are resident-facing; the 267 documented violence cases and jirga case-closures describe residents' situation.

Third-gender recognition has existed since 2009, a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety operates in Lahore, and civil society is active — all resident-facing facts a visitor would not directly rely on.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.summary:
The Philippines is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), the SOGIE Equality Bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist. The vacuum extends into custody: transgender women at the capital's main city jail are held by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — where mandatory head-shaving applies on arrival to the male dorm and safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than any gender-matched placement policy — while Davao City Jail answers abuse risk by relocating LGBT detainees to a separate annex; a trans visitor arrested in the Philippines has no documented path to identity-matched custody.
PHL.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical treatment of identity documents at borders is not documented, and the sources do not detail how bathroom and fitting-room policies at venues are enforced.

Custody axis: no national rule on trans-prisoner placement — birth-sex vs identity housing, special units, or solitary/segregation practice — is documented; the male-dorm housing is documented at Manila City Jail and the annex segregation at Davao City Jail only, so practice appears to vary by jail; the head-shaving intake requirement applies to the male dormitory generally rather than to transgender detainees specifically, and the 2022-23 reports are the only custody sources in this record.

sources.summary: Outright/IGLHRC Philippines legal overview (fetched page): lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility updated 2023 to bar SOGI-based discrimination of clients; openly gay/bisexual people allowed in armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017 (uniform policy follows legal gender on birth certificate); Clerical Error Law RA 9048 (2001) blocks administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people (judicial order required) and the 2008 Supreme Court ruling in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan bars legal-gender change even after gender-affirming surgery.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): two killings in days — 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist/activist shot by an unidentified gunman inside a General Santos clinic the same day; Bahaghari says the cases are an urgent reminder to pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill, which has been stuck in Congress for 25 years — no national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Manila Bulletin report (May 2025) covers a foreigner arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas.

Interaksyon (10 Apr 2024): drag artist Taylor Sheesh (Taylor Swift impersonator) was physically struck on stage by a man from the crowd at Bayambang, Pangasinan's Kalutan Concert on 6 April 2024 — she called the attack traumatic and urged passage of the SOGIE Equality Bill; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Rolling Stone Philippines explainer (7 Feb 2025): 25 years of legislative inaction on the SOGIE Equality Bill; patchwork protections that do exist — SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur, Iloilo) and 32 cities/municipalities; Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (SOGIE harassment: P20k-40k fine and/or up to 1 year); Magna Carta of Women and Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic/homophobic/misogynistic slurs and ridicule (fines P1k-10k, up to 30 days, sensitivity seminar).

Rappler: trans Filipinos' legal gender recognition bill would let applicants — including minors with consent — choose markers beyond male/female (X/nonbinary), addressing the lack of a recognition process that drafter Chase Go says drives social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence; the Commission on Human Rights has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'; allies plan to endorse the bill to the 20th Congress (28 July).

WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel guide (2026 data as of 18 Jun 2026): Manila 'Generally Safe' — LGBTQ+ 69, but Trans travellers only 62 ('Exercise Caution'), HIV+ 81; same-sex relations never criminalised, deep gender-diversity traditions (bakla/tomboy), vibrant Pride/nightlife scene and high media visibility, but SOGIE Bill (filed since 2000) stuck, no marriage equality, Catholic Church resistance; accessibility caveat: 80% of Metro Manila's 46 train stations lack step-free entrances, only 5 of 46 LRT-1 stations have elevators.

HRW report (21 Jun 2017), 'Just Let Us Be': documents bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools, with law short on remedies at the time — basis-level evidence of school-setting climate for gender-diverse youth; includes Tagalog summary and recommendations.

sources.title: Inside jails, gay men and trans women ‘wed’ fellow PDLs to escape abuse (Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism, by Aie Balagtas See)
sources.summary: Investigative feature on Manila City Jail: transgender women and gay men are held in the ordinary MALE dormitories (mandatory head-shaving on arrival for the male dorm), where they assume housekeeping/entertainer roles and informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates are widely used by gangs as a survival/protection strategy against abuse. Documents that trans women in Philippine jails are housed by birth sex in male facilities with no gender-matched placement, and that safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than policy.

sources.title: BJMP-Davao transfers LGBT inmates to annex facility for safety (SunStar Davao, by Ian Carl Espinosa)
sources.summary: Official practice documented: BJMP-Davao Community Relations chief Jail Senior Inspector Ellen Rose Saragena said LGBT detainees at Davao City Jail are relocated in batches to the City Jail Annex “to prevent abuse”, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens; three LGBT groupings live in the annex since its establishment. Shows the official Philippine response is administrative segregation of LGBT detainees into a separate annex for “safety”.

PHL.localsOnly:

PHL.blindSummary:

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), an anti-discrimination equality bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist. The vacuum extends into custody: transgender women at the capital's main city jail are held by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — where mandatory head-shaving applies on arrival to the male dorm and safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than any gender-matched placement policy — while another city's jail answers abuse risk by relocating LGBT detainees to a separate annex; a trans visitor arrested here has no documented path to identity-matched custody.

General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Custody axis: no national rule on trans-prisoner placement — birth-sex vs identity housing, special units, or solitary/segregation practice — is documented; the male-dorm housing is documented at the capital's main city jail and the annex segregation at one other city's jail only, so practice appears to vary by jail; the head-shaving intake requirement applies to the male dormitory generally rather than to transgender detainees specifically, and the 2022-23 reports are the only custody sources in this record.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.summary:
Chile has a strong legal framework — a gender identity law allowing self-determination (2019, no medical requirements), marriage equality (2022), a hate-crime law covering gender identity (2012), and a positive Gendarmería protocol that places trans inmates in facilities matching their gender identity and provides healthcare examination (better than most European countries on axis-H). The UN Human Rights Committee commended Chile's police measures to promote LGBTIQ rights.

But 2024 was a "year of regression" (the first rollback since democracy returned in 1990), with lawmakers rejecting nondiscrimination-law reforms and a 2025 Movilh report describing a "breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus" on LGBTIQ+ rights. Documented violence includes a trans person murdered and dismembered ("the biggest hate crime in Chile"), a transphobic hotel attack in Santiago (beating, captivity, death threats), and institutional discrimination against Chile's first trans police officer.

The Supreme Court restored a femicide conviction for the murder of a trans woman (overturning an appeals-court ruling that she didn't "legally qualify" as a woman). For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Santiago is welcoming.
CHL.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (theft, scams) and earthquake risk affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Outright International overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; hate-crime law has included sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances since 2012; civil unions since 2015; comprehensive self-determination-based legal gender recognition passed 2019; third sex option on birth certificates available for intersex children.

Washington Blade (19 Mar 2025): a Chilean advocacy group's annual report judged 2024 a 'year of regression' for LGBTQ rights — stalled equality and trans-rights legislation, blamed on the rise of the ultra-right and government inaction.
NOTE: The MOVILH (Chilean LGBT integration movement) 24th Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity (2025) (image-based PDF; no text extractable).

BioBioChile investigation (2 Jan 2024): profile of Ever, a young trans man murdered in 2023 and hidden for 24 hours — described as Chile's 'biggest hate crime'; the killer, an acquaintance, confessed. The country's benchmark anti-trans homicide case.

Chilevisión (23 Sep 2021): a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour in a transphobic attack at a Santiago hotel; the victim recounts 'he told me he wanted to kill me'. Documented violent-transphobia risk in the capital.

La Tercera: Gendarmería's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees — placement by assumed gender, segmented housing, and entry examinations; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives oversees implementation and trans visitors' access rules.
F&M Global Barometers country profile for Chile: composite scores measuring LGBT rights perception, including a specific Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

El Universal Chile (1 Apr 2025): Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros for discrimination — relegated to administrative tasks, her private life exposed without consent, and support denied. Institutional discrimination case against the national police force.

Movilh achievements page: index of the Chilean LGBT movement's milestone wins — the anti-discrimination law, inclusive 2012 census questions, the 'El amor es amor' marriage campaign, 'Comuna Diversa' local-level work and regional branches — the campaign record behind the current legal framework.

CHL.tangentialFactors: Marriage equality since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary:
Colombia has one of Latin America's strongest legal frameworks — Constitutional Court legal gender recognition since 1993 (no surgery required, based on self-recognition), "trans" and "non-binary" ID markers (November 2025), a Comprehensive Trans Law being legislated (2025), marriage equality (2016), and a Constitutional Court ruling protecting a trans inmate from prison violence. President Petro's government is pro-LGBTIQ+.

But the law-versus-practice gap is extreme and violent. More than 40 trans women were killed in a single year, with armed groups running "social cleansing" campaigns (Caquetá) and posting kill-lists targeting specific LGBTQ individuals ("All will be military targets"). Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was tortured and murdered in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, with a viral video of the assault. The UN Independent Expert urged Colombia to "close the gap between laws and lived realities amid rising violence."

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Bogotá's Chapinero district is a well-established LGBTQ+ area. The armed-group violence is concentrated in conflict regions and targets local communities, not tourists — but the organized targeting is a distinctive, severe concern.
COL.outOfScopeNotes: The US State Department advises reconsidering travel to Colombia due to crime, terrorism, and kidnapping risks; these affect all travellers.

sources.summary: El País (14 Apr 2025): the transphobic murder of Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello (Antioquia, near Medellín) — a 28-second video, viral since 5 April, shows her flailing in a creek unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands before drowning; her mother Sandra Borja: 'They killed her for being who she was.' President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities; the report notes 13 trans people killed in Q1 2025.

CNN (6 Aug 2025): killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case — in Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals ('All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'); describes Millerey's limbs broken before she was pushed into churning water outside Medellín, and frames the repeated killings of LGBTQ people as calculated brutality even amid the country's decades-long civil war.

The Guardian (30 Jul 2024): more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023, and armed groups threaten a further wave of 'social cleansing' in Caquetá — flyer campaigns announce cleansing of 'drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots'. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men; trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work; a friend of interviewee Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): strong formal protections (marriage since 2016, adoption since 2015, ID change without medical exams) versus documented killing — the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025. July 2023: the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution (a crime against humanity); UN Human Rights Committee noted concern.

JURIST (May 2025): UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination Graeme Reid concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities — praised the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality, but warned of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience: widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT individuals must be urgently addressed as killings rise.
Ambito Jurídico (in Spanish): Colombian court protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty - ruling on treatment of trans detainees.

International Business Times (June 2015): Colombia approved a rule change letting trans people change the sex marker on government-issued ID by signing a document before a notary, replacing the old route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric exams — official Reyes called those exams 'profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice'.

COL.tangentialFactors: Marriage equality since 2016 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
COL.localsOnly: The Constitutional Court LGR procedure, the new trans/non-binary ID markers, and the Comprehensive Trans Law are resident-facing; the prison-protection ruling and the >40 annual murders concern residents.

NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through the country's only recorded trans-imprisonment case: Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, and served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', and the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section — placement was discretionary — while an October 2024 investigative panel found the maximum-security placement itself unlawful for a first-time offender under the Nigerian Correctional Service Act. For a trans visitor, the SSMPA's 14-year exposure already applies to tourists; on top of that, detention would land in a prison system with a documented discretionary, unlawfully-assigned placement practice and no recorded housing standard for trans prisoners.
NGA.outOfScopeNotes:
Terrorism (Boko Haram in the northeast), kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Prison axis: no Nigerian law, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in any source in this record; the Bobrisky biography does not record which section she was assigned to, the October 2024 panel finding concerns the lawfulness of a placement rather than a housing standard, and the Reuters report on the proposed cross-dressing ban could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so that bill's status rests on its written summary.

sources.summary: BBC (Aug 2024): the beaten body of Abujan trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. For this record: a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

The Dial (Feb 2025): six months after Abuja Area Mama's killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. For this record: impunity is documented — police response to a trans victim's killing produced no arrests half a year on.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. For this record: current (2026) official foreign-office warning aimed squarely at LGBT+ visitors.

TimesLIVE (Mar 2025): a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; the SSMPA is described by those affected as a 'weaponised' law creating a climate of hostility. For this record: police extortion and violence against perceived-gay people, with the specific bribe amount and injury.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024), marking 10 years of the SSMPA: the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed. For this record: a decade-outcome assessment of the national criminalisation law, not just its text.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Apr 2024): 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians via Grindr and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; community counters with exposure forums (one admin's alert page drawing 43,000 followers) and sting operations. For this record: documented app-based luring crime specifically targeting queer people, relevant to a visitor using dating apps.

UK Home Office CPIN on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026): same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; Sharia law in all 12 northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. For this record: current official UK-government assessment of penalties, including the north/Sharia overlay.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Sept 2022) covers transgender Nigerians fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

HRW report (Oct 2016) 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe': the SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage — it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any 'public show of same sex amorous relationship', and gay organisations, with punishments of 10-14 years' prison; the report documents police torture and arbitrary arrests under it. For this record: the scope and severity of the national law visitors fall under.

KEN.name: Kenya
KEN.summary:
Kenya is a dangerous destination for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the colonial-era Penal Code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a $50 bribe in Mombasa, and 25 trans and intersex people told CNN this kind of police harassment is "common." The Kenya Human Rights Commission's "Lives on the Line" report documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist, Edwin Chiloba, was murdered (his body found in a metal box) — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, Kenya's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The High Court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a Transgender Protection Rights Bill). In May 2026, the High Court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and the Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. "Thousands of gay travelers visit annually through specialized tour operators."

There is no anti-discrimination law and no LGR procedure yet, but the court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill is a positive trajectory.
KEN.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism risks near the Somali border, general crime, and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Kenya (Feb 2025): same-sex consensual sex between men illegal with prison penalty; no laws on gender identity (no legal change pathway); intersex people legally recognised as third gender; LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only in restrictive civic space.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

KHRC 'Lives on the Line' (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

KHRC press release: Eldoret High Court handed transgender Kenyans a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

GATE.ngo on Nairobi Milimani High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026 (Justice Bahati Mwamuye, Petition 27 of Jan 2020): follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a Kenyan man sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

ROU.name: Romania
ROU.summary:
Romania is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: EU/Schengen, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The ECJ ruling means EU-issued LGR documents must be recognised.
ROU.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Oct 2024) covers the CJEU ruling that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights (the Mirzarafie-Ahi case on recognition of UK gender recognition).

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

FRA-commissioned legal study (Feb 2008) by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu: maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners — national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints; a dated baseline for Romania's protection architecture.

ROU.tangentialFactors: No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
ROU.localsOnly: The court-based domestic LGR regime and its inconsistent implementation are resident-facing; the ECJ Mirin ruling directly benefits EU-recognised trans visitors' documents.

BGD.name: Bangladesh
BGD.summary:
Bangladesh is a dangerous destination for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport.

The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).
BGD.outOfScopeNotes: Political instability, mob violence/lynchings, terrorism, and cyclone/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (12 Feb 2025): prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work. For this record: lethal violence against visible trans people continues — case specifics (Rangamati, Feb 2025).

Erasing 76 Crimes (7 Apr 2026) citing JMBF's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — 'a sharp increase' continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder/attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. For this record: the current national incident baseline — magnitude and trend for a visitor assessing exposure.

Global Press Journal: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding. For this record: the 2024 regime-change inflection point where formal rights began rolling back in practice.

Washington Blade (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's ouster (August 2024), Bangladesh's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. For this record: a dated, post-coup security assessment directly relevant to a visitor's risk calculus.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Bangladesh (September 2023, updated April 2026): Section 377 ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within s.377 (ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to 'all genders'). For this record: authoritative statement of the legal ambiguity any visitor's conduct sits inside.

For this record: the legal baseline plus the harassment-not-prosecution enforcement pattern and third-gender recognition.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Oct 2025): after hijras refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles in Narayanganj — a traditional livelihood. For this record: extortion-driven police violence against visibly trans people, including disruption of street livelihoods.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Apr 2024): five transgender/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, per JMBF. For this record: policing of visibly trans people concentrates at transit hubs — the airport itself is a documented hotspot.

UK Upper Tribunal decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal — Home Office country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues (citing fact-finding missions and IRB Canada). For this record: asylum-grade evidence of state-tolerated hostility; international-regime (asylum) source in scope by design.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 Civil Code (Article 37) was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. UGA.name: Uganda
UGA.summary:
Uganda is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," and the US State Department explicitly warns that "the law applies to both visitors and residents." Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes (one woman described being grabbed and shouted at that she needed to die); police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has "spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people." The law also criminalises the "promotion of homosexuality," meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the AHA targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and state violence. The Constitutional Court upheld the AHA in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

Uganda's death penalty is for "aggravated" same-sex (not all same-sex like Iran; not gender expression per se like Saudi), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic state-led crackdown makes this a environment to avoid entirely.
UGA.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (ADF in border areas), violent crime (armed robbery, sexual assault), and civil unrest affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch report 'They're Putting Our Lives at Risk' (26 May 2025): Uganda's 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act — death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', lengthy prison terms for 'promotion of homosexuality' — unleashed arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings; many LGBT people in hiding, with a small group of Ugandan mothers speaking publicly for their LGBT children.

Human Rights Watch (4 Apr 2024): Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act's core provisions — including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years — rejecting public-participation challenges; contrasted with the same court voiding a similar 2013 law on procedure.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (June 2024) covers rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community escalating, per a pressure group.

The Guardian (7 Jan 2024): fear across Kampala after the anti-gay laws — a transgender woman mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false TikTok allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house; notes the death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', international condemnation, and continued political support for the law in parts of Africa.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under the 'Do Not Travel' advisory.

Access Now (15 May 2025): Uganda's anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online — digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, while the companies behind popular apps do too little; shares 2025 case research and safety recommendations — directly relevant to visitor device/app risk under the AHA.

Amnesty International (23 Oct 2024) report 'Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names': the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in Uganda — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the AHA 2023 fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

AP (Feb 2026): 'Ugandan police arrest two women for allegedly kissing in public' — two women detained in Arua after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda: the three most important problems included 'violence and discrimination against marginalized groups (women...; children...; persons with disabilities; and the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender community)' - the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.

UGA.tangentialFactors: The AHA's life imprisonment and "aggravated homosexuality" death penalty apply to visitors — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app entrapment is a direct app-user risk.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.summary:
Egypt is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by Egyptian authorities ("Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here," Cairo 52, 12 incidents 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws (six months + fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (BBC Grindr entrapment) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The Ministry of Interior is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 Universal Periodic Review. The authorities' approach is described as "not only to criminalize LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life."

Egypt has no death penalty for same-sex (unlike Uganda/Nigeria's death penalties), no documented trans-specific tourist killing, and the statutory penalty is six months + fine (not 14 years or life) — but the systematic police entrapment, foreigner-targeting, coerced anal exams, and healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.
EGY.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (Sinai), political instability, and general crime affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Cairo 52, 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (27 Nov 2023): analysis of Egypt's immigration law and case law plus 12 documented incidents (2018-2022) — Ministry of Interior holds broad powers to deny entry or deport anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', applied to travellers perceived as queer. Directly visitor-facing risk.

Cairo 52 (24 Jan 2024): Egypt's Economic Courts have moved from de-facto to EXPLICIT criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Art. 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961; Court of Cassation 1970s interpretations had already removed the financial-exchange requirement (habitual/multiple partners sufficed).

Cairo 52 (12 Dec 2024): a new Ministry of Interior directive to civil-registry heads nationwide closes the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that let transgender Egyptians correct gender markers via governorate committees — legal gender recognition now actively being shut.

BBC investigation, 'How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps': no explicit law against homosexuality, but the 'debauchery' (sex-work) law is used to criminalise the community; police run entrapment via apps with victims describing blackmail and arrests (names changed).

Bedayaa, '10 FAQs about LGBTIQs Situation in Egypt' (Feb 2023): documents rising arrests of homosexuals and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye, and no anti-discrimination policy or law; covers detention conditions and the trans situation as a reference for SOGIESC work.

EIPR security documentation: police arrest patterns — first, entrapment of individuals, especially transgender women, through fake accounts on LGBTQ dating apps and websites; second, Ministry of Interior deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without charges upheld; violations continue inside police stations.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): homosexuality not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and debauchery laws are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences; NO legal protection against discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics.

TIMEP (6 Jan 2025): for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle — transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health; barriers to equitable health services persist since the last UPR, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

Human Rights Watch, 'In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct' (29 Feb 2004): documents the Queen Boat-era crackdown — arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants — the landmark record of state violence against gay men in Egypt.

PER.name: Peru
PER.summary:
Peru is a country that demands real caution for trans visitors, with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence, but no criminalisation of trans identity. The national legislature approved (February–April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated restriction comparable to bans passed in other countries. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed — trans women most affected. In one documented case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025), an unprecedented conviction. An official decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024) before being walked back after mass protests.

For a visitor: no border friction or criminalisation, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure whenever public facilities are used. Same-sex or partner recognition does not exist, so marriage-based protections cannot be assumed.
PER.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: how the bathroom ban is enforced in practice at public facilities and how it applies to visitors is not documented in the sources.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): Congress's committee approved unanimously (for plenary) the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 (presented by Jorge Montoya and Honor y Democracia party) that threatens trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.

IDEHPUCP (PUCP human-rights institute) analysis: the bathroom-restriction article openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites IACtHR Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights; also quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024): report finds hate crimes rose in Peru with trans women most affected; co-author Gianna Camacho (trans human-rights defender/journalist) stresses recorded numbers are only a sub-registry; cites the 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work.

BBC News Mundo (19 Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, trans woman and LGBTI activist — Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history (case reached the Court via the CIDH).

Infobae Peru (15 Dec 2025): officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León sentenced to 17 years for the rape/torture of Azul Rojas — the sentence landing nearly 20 years after the attack; judgment issued by the judiciary after years of litigation.

HRW (19 May 2025): the April-2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' mandates public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people — including trans youth — from facilities matching their identity; vague child-protection articles (art.4 media/advertising ban, art.5) enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content; obscenity-minimum sentence raised 3→4 years; HRW says child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating.

HRW dispatch (27 Jun 2024): Peru's health system walked back anti-trans guidance — authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as 'a step toward dignity' for trans patients in healthcare settings.

Outright International current Peru overview: public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional; April 2025's 'sexual integrity' law restricts restrooms by biological sex; April 2025 NGO foreign-funding law lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order/security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising; Pride marches held annually since 2002 (oldest recorded 1984).

Peru Support Group (Apr 2025): week-in-review of setbacks — Congress approved bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR (Muñante/Montoya) banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; Willax TV's Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed first openly-lesbian congresswoman Susel Paredes ('go use the men's room'); congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at INMP.

PER.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution for trans visitors, with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence, but no criminalisation of trans identity. The national legislature approved (February–April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated restriction comparable to bans passed in other countries. A consumer-protection body dismissed a discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

For a visitor: no border friction or criminalisation, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure whenever public facilities are used. Same-sex or partner recognition does not exist, so marriage-based protections cannot be assumed.

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming. Even the custody consequence axis is comparatively benign: at a 2023 parliamentary hearing the National Rehabilitation Institute's director stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to go to a men's or women's prison, trans women are currently placed in women's prisons, and a dedicated trans sector was planned for a new Montevideo prison — though he conceded the gap: "the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line."
URY.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory. Prison axis: the dedicated trans sector and Punta de Rieles accommodation were commitments announced in July 2023 (commissioner's estimate: ready within two years); nothing in the current sources documents whether delivery has occurred, and no source records special-unit or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners beyond the planned sector.

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.summary:
Qatar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely, with the most severe documented police practice in the Gulf — its region. An international human-rights organisation interviewed four transgender women arrested by the security department between 2019 and 2022 based solely on their gender expression in public places. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her, and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced phone-unlocking to identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison in the capital, Doha; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Same-sex conduct is also criminalised, so a partner travelling with you carries the same exposure. Arrests continued even as this country hosted the 2022 World Cup — a major international sporting event — under international scrutiny.
QAT.outOfScopeNotes:
Migrant-worker abuses and the sponsorship labour system, and general human-rights concerns, affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: how trans visitors are treated at border entry and document checks is not documented in the sources; the documented detentions begin after entry, in public places.

The reported physical detransition rests on a single documented account and could not be independently verified from the current sources.

KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.summary:
Kuwait is dangerous for trans visitors — the least hostile of the Gulf states, but not safe. In 2007, Article 198 of the Penal Code criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" (up to 1 year in jail); within two weeks at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops, and taxis, three were beaten (one into unconsciousness), and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against trans women under this law.

However, in February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down Article 198 as unconstitutional — the only Gulf state to repeal its cross-dressing statute. The repeal has teeth: a cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut won 4,000 KWD in compensation, with the Court of Cassation ruling police had arrested her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime in Kuwait.

But the repeal is incomplete in practice: HRW reports transgender people "continue to face threats and harassment," and in December 2022 security forces carried out mass deportations of LGBT people under "security" measures. For a trans traveler: no criminal exposure for gender expression itself, courts now provide recourse, but police harassment and deportation risk remain real.
KWT.outOfScopeNotes: Migrant-worker labour conditions affect all foreign workers; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

sources.summary: Brian Whitaker's overview essay (2016) on transgender issues in the Middle East: gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable; notes 'The Danish Girl' was banned by censors in Kuwait among other countries; discusses cross-dressing as a crime across the region.

HRW (16 Jan 2008): Kuwait's National Assembly added Article 199 bis to Penal Code Art. 198 — 'indecent act in a public place, or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex' punishable by up to 1 year imprisonment or a 1,000-dinar (US$3,500) fine; the only known targets of the law were transgender people, who can neither change legal documents nor find protection from such policing.

HRW (17 Feb 2022): Kuwait's Constitutional Court struck down the 2007 anti-transgender provision ('imitating the opposite sex') as unconstitutional; HRW urged parliament to repeal the law outright — the ruling removed criminal exposure but not the underlying dress-code policing practice.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry covers the same Kuwait Constitutional Court ruling striking down Article 198.

US State Dept 2023 Country Report on Kuwait (via ecoi): communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information; no candidate ran for National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation — documents censorship and invisibility of LGBT political participation.

HRW World Report 2024, Kuwait (events of 2023): penal code art. 193 still punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to 7 years and adultery by up to 5 years; positive step noted — Feb 2022 Constitutional Court ruling unconstitutional the 2007 art. 198 'imitating' provision.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute (11 Jul 2024): the 2007 amendment criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex' was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei with overwhelming parliamentary support, and abolished by the Constitutional Court in 2022 after an individual targeted by police challenged it — analysis of the steps still needed after abolition.

DAWN MENA (13 Feb 2023, Nora Noralla): a year after the Constitutional Court overturned the anti-transgender law, transgender discrimination continues in practice — the ruling was not a first step toward recognizing transgender rights, with social and employment discrimination persisting.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018): regional study of LGBT activism in 22 MENA jurisdictions incl. Kuwait, based on interviews with 34 activists; six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism.
