BHR.name: Bahrain
BHR.summary:
Bahrain is a place to avoid entirely for trans visitors, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the region. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in this country since 1976 and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression; a foreign government's official guidance notes that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in the capital on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A foreign trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker, showing that corrected identity documents may not be respected by the judicial system.

For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is an indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment. Same-sex conduct is legal, so partner travel is not criminal in itself, but public displays risk the same indecency provisions.
BHR.outOfScopeNotes:
Political repression, restrictions on free expression, and labour concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: a 2016 refugee-board research request cites sources that said homosexuality is illegal, contradicting the 1976-decriminalisation reading — the conflict remains unresolved in the current sources.

Unresolved: how the February 2024 bill — if enacted and enforced — would change documented enforcement practice is not yet documented.

sources.summary: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Bahrain' (continuously updated): legal status 'decriminalised since 1976' per ILGA-sourced infobox, with recognition limits and no SOGIESC discrimination protections. For this record: tertiary overview consistent with the Outright/State Department baseline — orientation source only, not stand-alone evidence.

Cairo 52 (7 Feb 2024): in a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia — including refusal of a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested. For this record: the documented judicial-refusal practice blocking legal transition at first instance.

Cairo 52 country review: Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade — including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International — so local media often serve as the only source. For this record: an evidence-reliability caveat — most findings for this jurisdiction rest on thin, partly remote sourcing.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era law, and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy — but authorities still use 'indecency' and 'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people (the Feb 2024 Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation). For this record: decriminalisation with the residual-arrest pattern — the nuance a visitor's safety turns on.

Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada RIO BHR105575.E (Aug 2016, covering 2011–Jul 2016): reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain' (citing Canada 14 Jul 2016 and Gulf News 5 Feb 2011) plus societal-attitude and treatment-by-authorities research. For this record: a SOURCE CONFLICT — this contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading of Wikipedia/Outright/2023 US State Dept; treat as unresolved, flagged for intake follow-up rather than ground truth.

BHR.comparisons: Bahrain scores above Qatar, Oman, and the UAE because it lacks both a codified gender-expression statute and a documented pattern of systematic targeting.
BHR.blindSummary:
This country is a place to avoid entirely for trans visitors, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the region. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976 and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression; a foreign government's official guidance notes that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in the capital on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A foreign trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker, showing that corrected identity documents may not be respected by the judicial system.

For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is an indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment. Same-sex conduct is legal, so partner travel is not criminal in itself, but public displays risk the same indecency provisions.
BHR.blindOutOfScope:
Political repression, restrictions on free expression, and labour concerns affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: a 2016 refugee-board research request cites sources that said homosexuality is illegal, contradicting the 1976-decriminalisation reading — the conflict remains unresolved in the current sources.

Unresolved: how the February 2024 bill — if enacted and enforced — would change documented enforcement practice is not yet documented.

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, a provision that extends to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the national police force announced arrests of transgender women after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented further arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024 a foreign non-binary traveller arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these countries."

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the same code, so partner travel carries the same exposure; consensual same-sex activity risks prosecution for foreign nationals too. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented rather than hypothetical: in September 2018 a Salalah court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and a fine of OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and publishing the photos, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video — the judicial outcome of the January 2018 police arrests under the Penal Code's Article 22, which penalises appearing in female clothing or demeanour. A gender-nonconforming visitor detected on arrival can therefore be jailed, and nothing in the sources records where inside the prison system such prisoners are held.
OMN.outOfScopeNotes:
Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: the airport account rests on a single traveller's first-hand account and could not be independently verified from the current sources, and whether the anti-trans statute has been applied at border entry for other travellers is not documented beyond that reported incident.

Prison axis: no Omani rule, practice or case is documented on where trans or gender-nonconforming prisoners are housed — nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary or segregation practice. That absence cannot be read as a protected standard in a state that criminalises cross-dressing and has jailed people for it.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Oman's criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression.

Cairo 52 + White Tent joint stakeholder submission (6 Aug 2025) to Oman's 4th-cycle UN UPR: documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states recent legislative developments have deepened criminalisation of gender expression, says Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, and reports Oman ignores earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access; recommends ending criminalisation, adopting anti-discrimination law and permitting legal recognition.

Statute-level extraction from Oman's Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018): Art 265 public indecency (10 days-3 months + OMR 100-300 fine), Art 266 impersonating/entering women-only venues disguised (1 month-1 year), Arts 267-268 producing or sharing content 'violating public morals' offline and online (up to 1 year / 10 days-1 month), plus Cyber Crime Law 2011 Arts 17/31 used against LGBT expression (1 month-3 years + OMR 100-3000); gender non-conformity punished through Art 266(d).

LegalClarity overview (published 3 Jun 2026): Oman criminalises all same-sex conduct with up to 3 years' prison under the 2018 Penal Code, prosecution often triggered by digital evidence discovered during unrelated investigations without a family complaint (Art 49 dual-criminality exception); Art 60 requires deportation for foreign nationals convicted of a felony (permanent) and allows it for misdemeanours (3-15 years); state ISP Omantel enables surveillance; outing carries social AND criminal risk; assembly/advocacy restricted via the Civil Associations Law.

Visitor-facing incident (27 Feb 2023): a genderqueer/non-binary Indian model-activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa says friends cleared immigration but she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers — direct first-hand evidence of border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors.

HRW open letter (13 Jul 2020) to Oman's authorities on arrests/convictions under the 2018 Penal Code's 'imitating the opposite sex' provision: Royal Oman Police announced arrests of 'men in women's clothing' after Snapchat photos from a private Salalah party circulated, and an Asian expat in abaya/niqab at an Al Buraimi women-only park hour — shows active enforcement of the cross-dressing offence against gender non-conformity.

HRW regional report (16 Apr 2018) with MENA laws annex covering Oman: documents that Oman's 2018 penal code (effective that year) added a retrograde provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside regional comparison (Kuwait's 2007 imitation law), and records Oman's existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGBT organising.

Shafiqa Ahmadi, 'Islam and Homosexuality: Religious Dogma, Colonial Rule, and the Quest for Belonging' (Journal of Civil Rights and Economic Development, 2012): distinguishes homosexual acts from homosexual persons; in some Islamic countries acts are criminalised (even by death) while identity alone is not - scholarly context for Oman's legal-religious framework.

sources.title: Playing dress-up: Four cross-dressers jailed in Oman — Roya News
sources.summary: Roya News (19 Sep 2018), on the Public Prosecution's announcement: a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years in jail and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photos of themselves in women's clothes on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video; the sentences fall under the July 2018 Omani Penal Code provision (Article 22), under which 'any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor' may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed up to one year, with additional 'publishing immoral acts on social media' charges. The article notes these follow January 2018 arrests by the Royal Oman Police of a group of men for dressing as women after social-media photos circulated. It documents court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people in Oman, but contains no information on where inside the prison system those convicted were housed.

OMN.comparisons: Oman scores below Qatar because it adds a codified, enforced gender-expression statute and a documented airport outing of an actual trans traveler; it stays above Saudi Arabia only because penalties are lower and no custodial death is documented.

BGR.name: Bulgaria
BGR.summary:
Bulgaria is workable for trans visitors — an EU member with no traveler-facing restrictions, but one of the EU's most hostile social climates. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The European Court of Justice is actively hearing the Shipov case on Bulgaria's refusal to issue ID matching lived gender, and EU free-movement law provides a legal backstop.

The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the Supreme Court of Cassation ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (gender an "unchangeable biological factor"), parliament passed a Russia-style law banning "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools (August 2024), and the EU's FRA survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above EU averages. Hate speech by politicians is routine.

For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and Sofia has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic.
BGR.outOfScopeNotes: Roma minority issues and asylum-system abuses are out of scope.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004 (direct and indirect — housing, education, medication) expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex' including 'sex change'. For this record: the current statutory baseline — old decriminalisation, layered but incomplete protection.

DW (Sep 2025): ECJ Advocate General Richard de la Tour issued an opinion that EU law as interpreted precludes national legislation like Bulgaria's refusing a trans person ID documents matching presented gender — the court concurred with the AG's proposed reasoning. For this record: EU-law pressure to overturn Bulgaria's legal-recognition ban — dated Sep 2025, pending full judgment.

Strasbourg Observers (17 Dec 2024) on Y.T. v Bulgaria: the original 2020 ECtHR judgment found an Article 8 violation over refusal of legal gender recognition, and the Court made clear those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 registry revision (consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria); Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic. For this record: the legal explanation for Bulgaria's recognition ban and its continuing unlawfulness.

Amnesty International (Feb 2015, 'Missing the point'): authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes — legislation exists but bias attacks (spiking in 2013 per the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee) go unpursued; Sofia Prosecution opened some cases. For this record: institutional non-response to bias crime — dated but establishes the pattern later reports inherit.

Human Rights Watch (5 Jun 2017): urges authorities to protect the 10 June Sofia Pride march, noting a group called the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse Sofia from garbage'. For this record: organised far-right hostility to visible LGBT events — dated evidence of the threat environment around public LGBT visibility.

Novinite (June 2011): the 4th annual Sofia Pride parade passed without incidents under heavy police guard, drawing only a 'Family NGO' protest — after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. For this record: historical baseline of pride security dynamics (protection-dependent order).

BGR.tangentialFactors: The 2024 "propaganda" law bans promotion of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools — a climate signal; same-sex relationships have no recognition, relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
BGR.localsOnly: The LGR ban (Supreme Court 2023) and the Shipov ID case are resident-facing; they signal climate but do not directly restrict a foreign passport holder.
BGR.comparisons: Bulgaria scores below Romania (0.67, no propaganda law, less hostile FRA numbers) and level with Serbia (0.64, similar climate, no EU backstop but no propaganda law either).
BGR.blindSummary:
This country is a member of a regional union with no traveler-facing restrictions on trans visitors, but one of the most hostile social climates inside that union. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The union's court of justice is actively hearing a case on this country's refusal to issue ID documents matching a person's lived gender, and the union's free-movement law provides a legal backstop.

The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the supreme court ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (characterising gender as an unchangeable biological fact); parliament passed an August 2024 law, modelled on a similar foreign statute, banning school-level "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation; and a regional rights-agency survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people here avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above the union-wide averages (53% and 29%). Hate speech by politicians is routine.

For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and the capital has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic.
BGR.blindOutOfScope: Ethnic-minority issues and asylum-system abuses are out of scope.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: in August 2024 a law banning representation of LGBTI identities in schools was introduced (spearheaded by a nationalist party leader); the country continues rejecting asylum requests by LGBTI people from two other states and unlawfully detains LGBTI asylum-seekers from a conflict region in closed detention; a performer at the capital's Pride event received death threats; an LGBTI youth organisation faced institutional checks.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex change' under 'sex'. But a constitutional marriage-definition provision bans same-sex marriage, and there is no legal gender recognition. A 2023 regional human-rights court judgment (brought by two same-sex couples) found this country in violation of its obligations on non-recognition of same-sex relationships.

A regional union rights agency's LGBTIQ survey country sheet for this country (2024): 75% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (union-wide: 53%); 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (union-wide: 29%); only 27% are open about being LGBTIQ (union-wide: 51%); 28% felt discriminated against at work or looking for work. Indicates a strongly hostile day-to-day climate.

Foreign public broadcaster (Sept 2025): an advocate general of the regional union's court of justice issued a non-binding opinion that this country must not refuse a trans woman ID documents matching her presented sex ('lived gender identity') - the case concerns a trans woman on hormone therapy refused documents; such opinions are followed by the court in roughly two-thirds of cases.

Regional human-rights court analysis blog (Dec 2024) of a line of cases against this country: the original 2020 judgment found a violation of the convention's private-life article over refusal of legal gender recognition; on revision (July 2024) the application was declared inadmissible for abuse of process, but the court confirmed the country remains obliged (under a later judgment) to provide a framework for legal gender recognition - which it still lacks.

International human-rights organisation report (Feb 2015): the country's failure to adequately investigate and prosecute hate crimes fuels fear, discrimination and violence against asylum seekers, migrants, religious minorities and LGBT people; authorities consistently fail to identify bias motivation.
An international rights group (Jun 2017): urges this country's authorities to protect the capital's pride event and showcase a tolerant side of the country.

News outlet (June 2011): the 4th capital Pride march passed without incidents under heavy police guard - after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 parades; only a 'traditional family' NGO protested.
BGR.blindLocalsOnly: The LGR ban (supreme court ruling, 2023) and the pending union-court ID case are resident-facing; they signal climate but do not directly restrict a foreign passport holder.
BGR.blindTangential: The 2024 "propaganda" law bans promotion of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools — a climate signal; same-sex relationships have no recognition, relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

SVK.name: Slovakia
SVK.summary:
Slovakia is workable for trans visitors. There are no traveller-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues under the free-movement rules of the regional union this country belongs to, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022 a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside an LGBT bar in the capital — classified as the country's first modern terrorist attack. The national authorities responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in the capital.

For a visitor: no legal exposure and functioning institutions, but a real threat of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against transgender recognition. The sources document no marriage or partner-recognition protections, so partner-based expectations should not be assumed.
SVK.outOfScopeNotes:
Roma discrimination (an ethnic minority) is out of scope for this record; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the sources document no marriage or partner-recognition protections for same-sex travellers, so partner-related protections should not be assumed.

Unresolved: border and entry treatment for trans travellers under the free-movement rules of the regional union is not documented in the current sources.

sources.summary: Wikipedia timeline of the 12 October 2022 Bratislava shooting: a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger (the LGBT bar Teplaren was 'plan B') arrived about 18:35 and at 19:11 fired eight shots at Teplaren, killing two and injuring one. The article's investigation, victims and perpetrator sections document the planning, the LGBT-venue target and the aftermath.

Feature of 7 February 2023: Slovakia's trans community remains precarious after the 12 October 2022 terrorist attack on the Bratislava LGBT bar, which rights groups say 'marked a new era' for trans people in the country. Existing transition rules already required surgical sterilisation before changing documents, and the aftermath brought even greater fears about the future.

SVK.comparisons: Slovakia scores above Hungary (0.68 — LGR already banned there plus a propaganda law in force), below Poland (0.72 — no terrorist attack and larger protective infrastructure), and well below Czechia (0.74).

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.summary:
Belarus is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In 2024 the authorities escalated from hostility to active persecution: a Culture Ministry decree reclassified transgender identity itself — "the desire to live and be seen by others as a person of an opposite sex" — as pornography, punishable by up to four years in prison. In September 2024 a wave of arrests targeted the community: the local organisation TG House Belarus documented over 15 LGBTQ+ people detained, including at least eight transgender people, several arrested for merely subscribing to "extremist" resources online.

Detained trans people were beaten and forced to record humiliating "confession videos" circulated on pro-government channels. The human-rights watchdog ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the majority of bias incidents targeted trans people, including "physical assaults, threats, abductions, humiliation, and coerced confessions related to their gender identity by law enforcement officers." National media runs systematic dehumanising propaganda. A post-dating April 2026 law criminalises "propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness" — a new enforcement layer; acts remain legal, protections remain zero.

For a visitor: gender transition technically remains legal, but the 2024 decree and the 2026 law mean a discoverable online presence or simply living visibly as trans can be prosecuted. No documented trans-tourist case exists yet, but police actively hunt trans people, any visible gender nonconformity risks detention, and foreign nationals receive no protection.
BLR.outOfScopeNotes:
General political repression and the post-2020 protest crackdown affect everyone; the score reflects trans-specific risk.

No documented trans-tourist case exists yet, and no source addresses border-screening or document-practice for trans visitors; the April 2026 law post-dates every cited source, so its enforcement practice is unverified. Official hate-crime statistics are unavailable — this nation has not reported to the watchdog ODIHR since 2015 and has no national point of contact — so account-level figures cannot be cross-checked.

Explicitly aimed at LGBT dignity — a persecution vector for visitors and residents alike.

JURIST (28 Sep 2024): TG House Belarus reports 15+ LGBTQ people detained in one month, incl. 8 transgender — most charged with hooliganism, two with pornography; custody abuse (physical and psychological) reported and some fled the country.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.summary:
Ukraine is workable for trans visitors — with the caveat that this scores trans-specific risk, not the general risks of an active war zone. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (medicalised — a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol); civil society, including two support NGOs and other groups such as Gender Stream and Insight, operates openly, and the capital Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in June 2026 even during the war.

For a visitor: a foreign passport is not subject to conscription rules, so border crossing follows standard wartime entry rules, but wartime document checks can out people, and civil-society groups report that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border. There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, societal attitudes lag the regional average, and the healthcare system is war-disrupted (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption reported). No marriage- or partner-travel-specific rule for visitors is documented.
UKR.outOfScopeNotes:
General war risks (missile strikes, infrastructure, mobilisation) apply to all travelers and are out of scope for the trans-specific score; trans residents' draft exposure is context, not the visitor score.

One cited news piece (June 2022) was not retrievable at research time. No source directly documents visitor border-screening practice for trans foreigners, and no marriage- or partner-travel-specific consequences for visitors are recorded.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch essay (15 May 2024) 'When Laws Fail to Protect Trans People': Ukraine-trans war-displacement case work — cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist notes commission hours (8am-8pm) and gatekeeping ('if a doctor says I'm a woman, the state can shrug').
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (June 2022) covers Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.

ZMINA (28 Jul 2026): trans women in Ukraine now find it harder to obtain a diagnosis — stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers; Trans Forum 2026 (Kyiv, early June 2026) discussed the new draft Civil Code's effect on transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation — visitor-relevant documentary friction for trans Ukrainians and those crossing borders.

Gender Stream (Ukrainian NGO): consultations and support — advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline regions to western Ukraine/EU, and helps with processing/reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to legally cross the border; documents that since martial law, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service.

European Parliament written question E-002018/2022 (Jun 2022): on the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, in the context of Parliament's resolution on war's impact on women.

Amnesty International (16 May 2013) report 'Nothing to Report': Ukraine's government must legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on a sexual-orientation/gender-identity basis amid a pervasive climate of homophobia; lawmakers urged to vote down proposals to criminalise; attacks routinely used as pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and peaceful public events.

Erasing 76 Crimes (30 Aug 2016): among three-country advances, a Ukrainian court ordered changes requested by two trans people to their passports and all other documents WITHOUT requiring sterilisation — a concrete legal-gain data point for document amendment.

Human Rights Watch (26 Jun 2012): LGBT activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment — the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; diagnosed concussion and broken jaw, police did not immediately respond despite medical referral; HRW urged investigation into homophobic motive.

UKR.localsOnly:
The medicalised legal-gender-recognition protocol (a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol), the martial-law exit ban on trans women with male passports, and the war-disrupted healthcare (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption) are resident-facing.

Resident data: in 2016 a court ordered the passport and document changes requested by two trans people without requiring sterilisation; a 2012 attack on a resident activist near his home (the second in six weeks) drew no immediate police response; and the monitoring organisation Amnesty International's 2013 report described a pervasive climate of homophobia and urged lawmakers to reject criminalisation proposals.
UKR.comparisons: Ukraine scores far above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) — no criminalisation, no state persecution, functioning NGOs — and below Serbia (0.64) and Moldova (0.65), reflecting wartime institutional strain and weaker legal protections rather than active hostility.

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT “propaganda” law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through a single contested case: a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007) served his sentence at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, where he says he was held alone in unsanitary cells — three years fully isolated from other detainees per a 2025 corroboration — including long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the ward for detainees requiring protection) was refused and no special-unit option existed. He described staff humiliation (forced strip body searches, demeaning roll-call name-calling, bathroom-door intrusion) and said only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The penitentiary administration contested the account, replying that he was held alone at his own written request, that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. For a visitor, the practical lesson is that a detained trans person in Moldova's system faced solitary-style isolation presented as protection, a refused protection-ward transfer, no special-unit option, and an administration that denies mistreatment — in a country that is otherwise the safest in its neighbourhood.
MDA.outOfScopeNotes:
The breakaway region of Transnistria is scored as part of Moldova de jure, but travelers should treat it separately: foreign-controlled, anti-LGBT “propaganda” law, no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travelers. No source addresses border-screening or document-practice for trans visitors, and no visitor-specific incident record exists to independently verify the assessment.

Prison axis: the placement finding rests on a single detainee's account that the prison administration disputes (it says the isolation was at his own written request and no rights were violated), so the disputed details are unadjudicated; no codified Moldovan rule on trans-prisoner housing, trans special units, or solitary/segregation placement is documented, and whether his planned court and European Court of Human Rights claims were filed is unverified in these sources.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Moldova: a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the Equality Council confirmed discrimination, recommending preventive measures; hate speech remained serious with no meaningful state response (echoed in the European Commission country report); election-period political hate speech rose.

Amnesty International Moldova 2025: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted (impunity for past violations); in Russian-occupied Transnistria new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

GENDERDOC-M report (2023) citing the Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022" (published January 2023): acceptance of LGBT+ people is extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance 5.7), and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022.

Attitude (2 February 2026) revisiting Moldova Pride 2024: participants of all ages and backgrounds joined the festivities — a country "slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity"; public Pride proceeds openly.

ECOM legislative analysis on SOGI and HIV in Moldova (Tallinn, 2024): identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV — access to justice, hate-crime and discrimination provisions — based on a survey of local partners, benchmarked against international standards.

PinkNews (19 May 2018): police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters trying to disrupt the annual Moldova Pride solidarity march in Chisinau (19 May) as marchers carried foam hearts; activists feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes.

PinkNews (1 March 2013): the Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February that the northern city’s "gay propaganda" ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights — local church-led bans struck down after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

sources.title: Trăind de gardă/ Deținut transgender – dublu condamnat în închisoare de către „oamenii cu epoleți”
sources.summary: Moldovan investigative outlet Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007), who served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca. He says he was held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells — including for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar') — supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the unit for detainees requiring protection) was refused. He describes staff humiliation: forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, opening his bathroom door, and calling him 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' and without any rights being violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed; Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. Outcome: de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system with prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

sources.title: Deținuți ai prejudecăților în instituțiile de stat. Persoane LGBT+, la un pas de suicid. Povestea tragică a unui locuitor al satului Dubna
sources.summary: Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

MDA.localsOnly:
The non-functional legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing.

Resident data: an equality-body study found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance score 5.7) — and marginalisation increased in 2022; in 2024 a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the equality body confirmed discrimination.

The documented custody case is resident-facing: the detainee is a national held in the national penitentiary system at Soroca, and the solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, staff conduct and administration denial described in the two investigations all fall on residents in state custody — a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.
MDA.comparisons: Moldova scores below Romania (0.67 — functional LGR, EU member longer) and above Serbia (0.64 — comparable climate but Moldova's 2022 SOGI hate-crime law and EU-candidate trajectory give it the edge) and Ukraine (0.62 — war strain).

Outcome: de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system with prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

A second report (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: a transgender man spent three years locked alone in a cell at a penitentiary, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in public institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee as of 2025.

LUX.name: Luxembourg
LUX.summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented as comparatively protective: per the Justice Minister's 2015 parliamentary answer, prison staff place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, trans-detainee situations are handled case by case, requests to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen form of address (a 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname); such cases are described as “exceptional”. No codified birth-sex placement rule, no trans special custody unit, and no solitary or administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners is documented, and the planned Uerschterhaff prison at Sanem was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation — so a visitor who ends up in custody is met by case-by-case accommodation under an explicit official warning against stigmatising or isolating LGBT detainees, not by a fixed rule.
LUX.outOfScopeNotes:
Nothing material remains unresolved. One 2018 report of the parliamentary vote was paywalled, so the vote split could not be verified from the page; and no independent incident series is documented, so the absence of recorded anti-trans violence rests on a thin cited record.

Prison axis: the placement description is a single 2015 ministerial statement — no statute, regulation or case law on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in this record, and how the case-by-case practice operates in any given prison today is unverified; the Sanem prison's sectioned design was prospective in 2015 and its operation is unverified.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): marriage and adoption; self-determination-based gender markers (no nonbinary markers); discrimination banned on sexual orientation and gender identity but not gender expression or sex characteristics; no measures on conversion practices or intersex interventions; in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, criticised by organisations for missing depathologisation and other key elements.

Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale UPR submission (April 2023) for Luxembourg: describes the organisation's services and Luxembourg's equality laws (employment, goods and services, education, health), the CET equality body and the national LGBTI action plan.

Asher Fergusson's LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index (updated June 2023): 400+ hours of research ranking all countries' laws for LGBTQ+ traveller safety, with a companion Global Transgender Rights Index - comparative data source covering Luxembourg.

Le Quotidien (June 2019, in French): 'Agressions LGBTphobes: un durcissement des sanctions attendu' - Luxembourg law lacks LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances; victims under-report; the justice minister signalled the law would evolve after ECRI's 2017 intervention.

Le Quotidien (May 2017, in French): Justice Minister Félix Braz presented a bill allowing trans and intersex people to change civil-status gender by declaration - replacing the long, costly judicial procedure; welcomed by associations.

Le Quotidien headline (July 2018) confirms the Chamber approved simplified civil-status change for trans people; body paywalled in fetched copy — vote split and procedure details unverifiable from the page itself.

AND.name: Andorra
AND.summary:
Andorra is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. The 2022 Law of the Person and Family modernised the legal framework (unified civil marriage, and legal gender recognition provisions); the Ministry of Equality now obliges all companies to maintain sexual and gender-based harassment protocols. ILGA-Europe records only three bias-motivated incidents in the most recent annual review — a tiny absolute number reflecting a small, safe, tourism-dependent country.

No traveler-facing concerns: no bathroom laws, no border issues (open border with Spain/France, though outside Schengen there are no document-gender checks), high social tolerance in practice despite a conservative Catholic history. Gaps: anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity is recent and shallower than Spain's; hate-crime law is generic rather than SOGI-specific. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
AND.outOfScopeNotes: Church influence on family law is resident-facing.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Andorra chapter: a transphobic opinion piece in El Periòdic d'Andorra (27 Sep) was removed online with a public apology after DiversAnd's request though it had already run in print; in August DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for gender-affirming protocols — puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, in some cases 14 — following the 2022 regulatory changes.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025), Andorra chapter: Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month; DiversAnd flagged incidents during June Pride celebrations and called for a formal system to register and classify bias-motivated violence so it can be recognised as hate crime; the Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during the year.

PinkNews (Sep 12, 2023): Andorra's head of government Xavier Espot Zamora, in office since 2019, came out as gay publicly saying 'I never hid it' — a societal-climate signal for a country where he remains the serving prime minister.

GayLawNet Andorra laws page: age of consent is 16 under Penal Code Article 206, with topic coverage including civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage, sodomy and trans legal status; marked 'limited information', useful as a dated legal-index pointer rather than analysis.

AND.tangentialFactors: Civil marriage was unified under the 2022 law — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a partner, not to solo travellers.
AND.localsOnly: Legal gender recognition provisions exist under the 2022 Law of the Person and Family; the anti-discrimination and hate-crime gaps are resident-facing.
AND.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Germany (0.83), below Spain (0.90 — Ley Trans, comprehensive statute), above Italy (0.76 — no LGR self-determination, political hostility).

MCO.name: Monaco
MCO.summary:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. A visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever: no bathroom laws, no border friction (a tiny tourist enclave embedded in the neighbouring country of France, entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans incidents, and street violence of any kind is rare in this heavily-policed, very low-crime destination.

The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness: no functioning legal gender recognition process and limited explicit trans protections.
MCO.outOfScopeNotes: Family-law gaps (no marriage equality, cohabitation contracts only) are resident-facing concerns kept out of the visitor score, per the record's existing split. Very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. One source notes reported discrimination is described as rare, but no independent verification of current practice exists in the record.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

MCO.localsOnly: The absence of any functioning legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing: no administrative route exists for residents to amend a registered gender.

LIE.name: Liechtenstein
LIE.summary:
Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not included in any anti-discrimination legislation, and there is no legal gender recognition law; these gaps are resident-facing, and a visitor faces no legal exposure.

No documented pattern of anti-trans violence, no bathroom law, no border friction (entry under the common border-free travel zone via its neighbours Switzerland and Austria), in a very small, very low-crime country closely integrated with those neighbours. Social attitudes are conservative but not mobilised-hostile. Marriage and joint adoption have been available since January 2025.

Very small population — the evidence base is thin, and this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. One cited feature was not retrievable at research time. VAT.name: Vatican City
VAT.summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

The custody axis completes the picture: the state operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the state serve their time in Italian prisons with costs covered by the state, so there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case in this jurisdiction; any custodial consequence for a visitor would be served in another nation's prison system, outside this record's scope.

CYP.name: Cyprus
CYP.summary:
Cyprus is a country workable for trans visitors. The legal framework is mid-transition: public incitement to hatred based on gender identity is a criminal offence (2015), and gender identity is an aggravating factor in hate crime (2017). A legal gender recognition bill (self-determination basis) was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and is pending in parliament; until it passes, legal gender recognition requires surgery under the 2002 Civil Registry Law — a resident-facing arrangement.

No traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues for an EU member, and tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to diverse visitors. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework. The divided country matters: the northern part operates under a de facto Turkish-controlled administration with a weaker protection regime and less documentation, and travelers should treat the north as closer to a riskier profile than the south, where these protections apply.
CYP.outOfScopeNotes: The north/south division of the country into two parts and the pending LGR bill are noted; LGR requirements are resident-facing. The bill's final status is pending as of the reporting dates; the training and the conversion-practices ban are noted from their reporting sources. Traveller-facing conclusions here describe the southern part where these protections apply; conditions in the northern part are less documented. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

sources.summary: UPR-info Cyprus advocacy sheet (2024): Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence/hatred on SOGI grounds; Law 31(I)/2017 makes prejudice motivation an aggravating sentencing factor; Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices; the legal gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers Sept 2022 with first parliamentary reading Nov 2022 (still pending at 2024); gender identity remains absent from equal-treatment grounds and no anti-homophobia action plan exists; prison guards received 2-day LGBTI+ training (Apr 2023) after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints to the Ombudswoman.

European Commission Network of Legal Experts country report on gender equality in Cyprus (2024, reporting period 2023): how EU equality rules are transposed into Cypriot national law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the legal framework.

Queer Cyprus Association UPR presentation (Erman Dolmacı, 4th-cycle): confirms the same three Criminal Code amendments (87(I)/2015 incitement, 31(I)/2017 aggravating factor, 39(I)/2023 conversion-practices ban), frames 'ISSUE 1' as trans and gender-diverse rights with the Sept 2022 LGR bill as the outstanding implementation step, and lists the state response to prior UPR recommendations — i.e. hate-speech law delivered, gender-identity discrimination ground and trans legislation not yet delivered.

Queer Cyprus 'Diversity of Colours' LGR booklet: documents gender-recognition practice on the divided island — the record's framework is self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping ('no psychiatric involvement'), and the northern part of Cyprus runs its own recognition process, explicitly including recognition of non-binary identities. Practical resource: Queer Cyprus runs a 7-days/week confidential psychosocial and legal support line covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues.

ILGA 32nd UPR session report (29 Jan 2019): Cyprus received 8 SOGIESC recommendations and accepted all 8; national report stated new legislation for correcting registered sex (adults and minors) was in preparation requiring only a Registrar decision, no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports; ECRI had urged gender identity as a prohibited discrimination ground; Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as 40th member (Aug 2018). Marks the reform promise the 2022 bill was meant to fulfil.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Cyprus (2020, reporting period 2019): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds in Cypriot law.

PinkNews (10 Oct 2013): Cyprus amended its penal code to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity, punishable by up to 3 years' imprisonment and/or a €5,000 fine (workplace SOGI protections added 2004). Dated, still-accurate baseline for the hate-speech offence the 2015 law extended.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.summary:
Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — the country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the country's two main cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially. The consequence axis of an arrest is thinly documented and cannot be read as a protected standard: the only placement finding is a February 2025 statement by the president of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee, made in praise of Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility (Correctional Centre 1) to the women's facility (Correctional Centre 2) — a surgery-gated practice with no statute or formal policy text cited. Nothing is documented on placement for trans prisoners who have not had surgery, and no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is on record; with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor's placement would default to birth sex absent the surgery-gated transfer — a gap that cannot be assumed safe even though the country's non-criminalising framework keeps arrest itself unlikely.
KHM.outOfScopeNotes:
LGR absence and discrimination-law gaps are resident-facing. The police-practice reports are reported but not adjudicated by any court in this record; the expert-visit findings are summarised from the hosting organisation's page and not independently re-verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

Prison axis: the placement statement is a CHRC president’s remark made in praise of the centre, not a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited; nothing is documented on placement of trans people who have not undergone surgery; no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is on record; and this is the only direct documentation of trans-prisoner placement for Cambodia found in two search rounds, so practice at other facilities is unverifiable here.

OutRight International Cambodia profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity (French protectorate 1867, independence 1953); at UPR 2019 accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage and at UPR 2024 accepted all 12 LGBTIQ recommendations incl. seven on marriage equality; legislation contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions.

Phnom Penh Post on a Cambodian Centre for Human Rights (CCHR) report: an overwhelming majority of transgender women on Cambodia's city streets face 'shocking' harassment and abuse (135+ cases documented), including a disturbing Siem Reap police practice of targeting transgender sex workers and forcing them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water.

Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) page on Cambodia's 4th-cycle UPR: Cambodia officially accepted all 12 SOGIESC/LGBT+ recommendations in 2024 - marriage equality progress, legal gender recognition for self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures; includes the civil-society joint submission (Dec 2023) and summary factsheets.

UNDP/USAID 'Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia Country Report' (2014): participatory review of the legal and social environment for LGBT persons and civil society, based on the Cambodia National LGBT Community Dialogue (Phnom Penh, Jan 2013), participant conversations, an NGO/CBO survey and a desk review of published literature.
Frommer's travel guide: 'Tips for Gay and Lesbian Travelers' in Cambodia - practical travel advice for LGBT visitors (page body is navigation; headline only).

PinkNews (20 Jul 2019) on Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) study: 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 suffered emotional abuse by a family member; 35% of under-35 participants considered suicide because of family rejection — including a 27-year-old trans man forced by his mother into rehab to 'fix his gender'.

sources.title: CHRC says transgender rights are observed in prison
sources.summary: Khmer Times (19 Feb 2025) reports Cambodian Human Rights Committee (CHRC) president Keo Remy, speaking at the handover of an ambulance to Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar prison in Phnom Penh, said Cambodia observes transgender prisoners' rights: transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from Correctional Centre 1 (the men's facility) to Correctional Centre 2 (the women's facility). The statement was made in praise of the centre, not as a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited; the article also flags that prison overcrowding has worsened because of gang-crackdown arrests. This is the only direct documentation of trans-prisoner placement practice for Cambodia found in two search rounds.

The custody findings are resident-facing: the surgery-gated transfer practice at Prey Sar and the worsened overcrowding from gang-crackdown arrests describe the national prison system — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.

The nation's two main cities have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: a human-rights organisation documents "shocking" harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially. The consequence axis of an arrest is thinly documented and cannot be read as a protected standard: the only placement finding is a February 2025 statement by the president of the national human-rights committee, made in praise of a women's correctional centre, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility to the women's facility — a surgery-gated practice with no statute or formal policy text cited. Nothing is documented on placement for trans prisoners who have not had surgery, and no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is on record; with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor's placement would default to birth sex absent the surgery-gated transfer — a gap that cannot be assumed safe even though the country's non-criminalising framework keeps arrest itself unlikely.

This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

Prison axis: the placement statement is a human-rights-committee president's remark made in praise of the centre, not a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited; nothing is documented on placement of trans people who have not undergone surgery; no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is on record; and this is the only direct documentation of trans-prisoner placement for the country found in two search rounds, so practice at other facilities is unverifiable here.

NPL.name: Nepal
NPL.summary:
Nepal is workable for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since a landmark 2007 ruling; a third-gender category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu, the capital, has an established activist scene.

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: an international observer, Human Rights Watch, documents that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside the main tourist bubbles.
NPL.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation barriers are resident-facing; citizenship-law discrimination does not affect visitors. The citizenship-document process after the rulings is not independently verified in this record; the documented failures date from the 2024 observer report and the 2024 ruling account. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

sources.summary: HRW (Feb 2024): calls on Nepal's government to urgently create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents — illustrating that despite progressive rulings, no straightforward document-change process exists (photo shows a Kathmandu trans woman holding her 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender). For this record: official-observer statement on the documentary-recognition gap.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. For this record: the landmark ruling and the pre-ruling barrier path, dated.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy. For this record: documented doctrine-versus-implementation gap.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. For this record: ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities, dated 2024.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 25, 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: argues that despite the Constitution awarding the right to self-determine name and gender markers (2007 case), 'an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law' is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community. For this record: local-activist assessment of the gap between constitutional right and statute.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.

The landmark 2007 ruling, the third-gender category by self-identification, and the harassment documented in provincial cities all fall on residents; the established activist scene (an organisation founded 2001) is resident-facing.

LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

The consequence axis makes the danger concrete: as of October 2024 the Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing — its media spokesperson/Commissioner said current facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, with separate accommodation only planned for prisons built in the future — and placement defaults to birth sex in the current male/female ward system, with a discretionary, medicalised exception route: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender ‘where possible’, while those without it undergo a doctor’s assessment of whether they ‘can be considered a transgender’ before placement, with the inmate’s preference weighed. Officials also cite the fear of people accused of sex offences ‘identifying as transgender’ to enter female housing with born-male offenders as a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. A detained trans visitor — unlikely to hold the recognition card, in a country where police already use vagrancy and personation provisions against trans people — would default to birth-sex placement under a practice with no statutory rule and no dedicated housing.
LKA.outOfScopeNotes:
Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; LGR circular limits are resident-facing.

Prison axis: the placement statements are a Prisons Department spokesperson’s remarks (October 2024), with no statutory placement rule and no written policy text; how ‘where possible’ actually operates is unquantified; separate accommodation exists only as a plan for facilities built in the future; and no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is documented for the current prison system.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Sections 365/365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); prosecutions limited but harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services are frequent; no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections; authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence - widely condemned as torture. Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation

Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

sources.summary: The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.summary:
Mongolia is a country workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and identity grounds were added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; police guidance requires officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identification documents, a favourable enforcement practice.

The realistic risk for a visitor is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside the capital's central districts, where social acceptance is low.
MNG.outOfScopeNotes: Comprehensive anti-discrimination gaps and medicalised LGR are resident-facing. The assault documentation and the training figures are from reporting sources and have not been independently re-verified in this record; the older scene account describes 2008 conditions. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

sources.summary: Outright International (last updated 12 March 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised 1993; sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination prohibited but protections fragmented (no comprehensive law); marriage equality constitutionally prohibited with no union recognition; groups can register.
thin: no usable finding

The Establishment (Aug 2018): profiles Anaraa Nyamdorj, trans man and co-founder/advisor of the LGBT Centre — came out in 2004, began transition in 2011; describes Mongolia's 2018 Pride and LGBT Centre advocacy; ground on trans life, transition access and acceptance in Ulaanbaatar.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2019): after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman, the LGBT Center trained police on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions — 500+ police officers, prosecutors and judges trained; force now has guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of ID documents.

GlobalGayz Mongolia report: no laws specifically against homosexuality though 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' provisions remain; the scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism; a 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees fear being outed.
