MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.summary:
Myanmar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Section 377 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — notably Section 30(d) of the Rangoon Police Act, allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the National Unity Government documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 Conscription Law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
MMR.outOfScopeNotes: General civil-war risks affect all travelers and are out of scope; the score reflects trans-specific persecution by the junta.

sources.summary: Outright International overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 Feb 2021 coup risks intensified — torture/sexual violence in detention, Oct 2022 Organization Registration Law (prison terms for NGO non-compliance), compulsory military service announced Feb 2024, seven LGBTQ-themed books banned 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

DVB (Jan 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; the NUG recorded 17 LGBT killed and 2 critically injured since 1 Feb 2021; 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and 68%+ fear repercussions from abusers.

Human Rights Myanmar submission (June 2024) to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; Section 377 enforcement intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

RFA (10 Jan 2025): junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; colonial-era law carries up to 10 years for gay sex; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the Feb 2021 coup.

ASEAN SOGIE Caucus (March 2025, from Queers of Burma Alternative research Jan 2025): the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement; Section 377 carries life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and 1945 Police Act s.35(c) (face covering, up to 3 months) is used specifically against transgender people.

Guardian (2 Feb 2016): Colors Rainbow's work in Yangon — trans woman Nat Nat We describes arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Washington Blade (2 Nov 2018): Aung Myo Htut (aka Addy Chen), an outspoken HIV-positive LGBTI advocate and Yangon restaurant owner, was charged under Penal Code 377 over an alleged offence against an employee — Section 377 in active use, with the community demanding fair media coverage.

HuffPost (17 Oct 2015): colonial-era criminalisation; 2013 Mandalay arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); nat kadaws (spirit mediums) are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

MMR.tangentialFactors: Section 377 criminalises same-sex intimacy — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the police-act "shadow law" is the trans-specific detention mechanism.
MMR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) only because Myanmar's persecution, while lethal, is part of generalised wartime violence rather than a codified anti-trans machine; below Uganda (0.17).
MMR.blindSummary:
Trans visitors should avoid this place entirely. The penal code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 conscription law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
MMR.blindOutOfScope: General civil-war risks affect all travelers and are out of scope; the score reflects trans-specific persecution by the junta.
blindSourceSummaries: Human-rights organisation overview (updated March 2026): a penal-code provision is used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 February 2021 coup risks intensified — torture and sexual violence in detention, an October 2022 organisation registration law carrying prison terms for non-compliance, compulsory military service announced in February 2024, and LGBTQ-themed books banned in 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

Media report (January 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; opposition figures recorded LGBT people killed and critically injured since 1 February 2021; a survey of LGBT respondents found most have no confidence in the legal system and most fear repercussions from abusers.

Civil-society submission to an international human-rights process (June 2024): killings of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled areas — a small number dead since the coup; intensified enforcement of a penal-code provision as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

Media report (10 January 2025): the junta banned LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; a historic-era legal provision carries up to 10 years for same-sex conduct; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the February 2021 coup.

Civil-society research (March 2025, based on local research from January 2025): the 2024 conscription law drives queer people into fear and displacement; the penal-code provision carries life imprisonment or a long term, and a historic-era police-act clause on face covering is used specifically against transgender people.

Media report (2 February 2016): a local trans-support organisation — a trans woman describes arrest, stripping, a beating and two weeks' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Media report (2 November 2018): an outspoken LGBTI advocate with HIV, a restaurant owner, was charged under the penal-code provision over an alleged offence against an employee — the provision in active use, with the community demanding fair media coverage.

Media report (17 October 2015): historic-era criminalisation; arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); local spirit mediums are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.
MMR.blindTangential: The law criminalising same-sex intimacy is a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the police-act “shadow law” is the trans-specific detention mechanism.

CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary:
Cuba is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's most legally transformed countries. The 2019 Constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the 2022 Family Code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — the July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme, and Havana has a visible, state-tolerated trans community.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the historical UMAP camps era is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.
CUB.outOfScopeNotes: Political repression, shortages, and detention powers affect all travelers; LGR mechanics are resident-facing.

sources.summary: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum — only the 4th national vote since 1959 — which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights; opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. Useful context for how contested (rather than state-enforced) the equality settlement is.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate; Mariela Castro (CENESEX) proposed extending it to gender identity, disability and HIV status — the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators but the report makes clear passage of the SOGI ban was the confirmed outcome. Predates the 2019 Constitution/2022 Family Code (replaced in scope, not in error).

Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: Cuba's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

CUB.tangentialFactors: The 2022 Family Code overhauled family law (including same-sex marriage) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
CUB.localsOnly: The civil-registry LGR reform, CENESEX trans-care programme, and unreliable hormone availability are resident-facing.
CUB.comparisons: Pairwise: below Argentina (0.73 — democracy, independent NGOs, stronger recourse) and above Lithuania (0.66) and Vietnam (0.63 — Cuba's constitutional GI protection and official trans programme edge it).

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary:
Ecuador is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016, and the legal framework is now among the region's strongest. The 2024 reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the identity document directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery), and in 2024-25 court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and the "internal armed conflict" against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024, with two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks; Quito and Guayaquil, the two main cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis. For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.

The consequence axis of an arrest is the record's darkest documented element. Trans women in the country's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces: the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons (an organisation working with them says there are many more), placement operates by birth sex/legal sex, and the protective 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations is used unevenly — one trans detainee was initially sent to a male pavilion with three other trans women rather than to it, and received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The sources document gender-identity discrimination, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers in custody, including the death of a trans woman during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space, a 2022 complaint over cruel and degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio, 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving and beatings targeting breast/body implants, a 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman that drew calls for an independent investigation, and reporting that rapes and torture in custody are directed at prisoners' gender identity. The leading trans-rights organisation does not push a one-size placement rule — it advocates individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, citing a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty — so a detained trans visitor would face male-space placement under an unevenly applied protective standard with documented violence.
ECU.outOfScopeNotes:
The general security emergency affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific legal/violence balance. The murder toll is a single organisation's documentation and the response assessment is that organisation's; the 2024-25 adolescent rulings are as reported and not independently re-verified here. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

Prison axis: the census count (73 trans women) and the 'prioritaria' practice are as reported by the cited investigations — how allocation to the protective pavilion is decided and how many trans women reach it is not documented, the implementation status of the 2016 protocol commitment is unverified, and no rule or case law fixing trans-prisoner placement (birth-sex vs identity) is on record beyond the documented practice itself.

sources.summary: Primicias (12 Jun 2024): President Noboa issued on 11 Jun 2024 the reglamento to the National Assembly's 12 Dec 2023 reforms of the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, streamlining civil-registry gender-marker changes — the operative procedure for legal gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Los Angeles Blade piece (Jan 2024) reports violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians increasing amid the internal armed conflict.
AP (Apr 2026): 'A transgender teen's case in Ecuador opens path for others seeking legal recognition' — Constitutional Court rulings let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage legalised in 2019 but same-sex couples barred from adoption by constitutional ban; legal gender recognition possible since 2016 (not available to under-18s); conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador: documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption - baseline context.

2008 Constitution of Ecuador (Georgetown/PDBA text): Article 11 principles bind the state to respect ethnic, national, social, generational and gender differences and sexual orientation and identity — the constitutional non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state.

PinkNews (31 May 2018): the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon (child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon); lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said refusal violated the child's rights — a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families.

sources.title: Trans Women in Ecuador's Prisons | PrisioTrans Human Rights Program
sources.summary: Silueta X (leading Ecuadorian trans-rights organisation), PrisioTrans program, documents 2011-2026: trans women in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers. Key cases: trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; 2022 complaint over cruel/inhuman/degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast/body implants; 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman drew calls for an independent investigation at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison. The program explicitly does NOT push a one-size placement rule, instead advocating individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

sources.title: Trans Women Report Being Punished for Their Identity in Ecuador Prisons (Spanish)

The story documents rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity, showing placement practice operates by birth sex/legal sex with protective 'prioritaria' placement used unevenly.

JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

The consequence axis of an arrest is directly documented. A 2018 academic study of Jamaican prisons — estimating that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities — reported that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender ‘are isolated’, that rehabilitation opportunities are ‘basically non-existent’, that homophobia/transphobia is entrenched (other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners), and that lesbians face prevalent ‘corrective rape’. The US State Department’s 2023 report confirms the state dimension: ‘prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity’, in facilities so overcrowded that Tower Street maximum-security cells held three times capacity, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. Jamaica bars legal gender registration, no specialised trans housing policy is documented, and for a detained trans visitor this is identity-targeted violence on top of an already severe, overcrowded baseline — a documented tier of its own, not merely an elevated version of a general prison risk.
JAM.outOfScopeNotes:
The buggery law is a situational/climate factor; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

Prison axis: the 300-of-1,800 Tower Street estimate and the ‘corrective rape’ prevalence claim are study-reported figures not independently re-verified here; the State Department documents severity but not the identity-targeting share of overall prison violence; no specialised trans housing policy, trans special unit, or solitary/segregation policy is documented; and with gender registration barred, no recognition framework governs accommodation decisions.

sources.summary: Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

sources.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
sources.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

sources.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
sources.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

JAM.tangentialFactors:
The buggery law (up to 10 years) is a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners and shapes police culture.

Litigation flux: the Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica proceeding before the Inter-American Commission — whose February 2024 amicus brief argued Jamaica’s continued criminalisation and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — is the state-failure pattern the prison documentation extends: the same state that failed to investigate a mob killing holds trans prisoners without a recognition framework or documented protection.
JAM.comparisons: Pairwise: above Malaysia (0.28 — adds Sharia caning statutes) and below Sri Lanka (0.33 — police-as-perpetrator but less mob-killing culture). Jamaica's mob-violence pattern plus failed investigation of the Dwayne Jones killing keeps it in High Risk.

The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an international human-rights commission case documenting the nation's failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Major tourist resort areas are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

The consequence axis of an arrest is directly documented. A 2018 academic study of the nation's prisons — estimating that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at a major correctional centre belong to sexual or gender minorities — reported that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated', that rehabilitation opportunities are 'basically non-existent', that homophobia/transphobia is entrenched (other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners), and that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. A major foreign government's 2023 report confirms the national dimension: 'prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity', in facilities so overcrowded that a maximum-security centre's cells held three times capacity, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The nation bars legal gender registration, no specialised trans housing policy is documented, and for a detained trans visitor this is identity-targeted violence on top of an already severe, overcrowded baseline — a documented tier of its own, not merely an elevated version of a general prison risk.

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

The consequence axis of an arrest is acknowledged in official terms as unsafe: the 2018 ‘Justice through a Gender Lens’ Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers states plainly that ‘in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities’. The only mechanism is a judicial officer’s sentencing recommendation that prison authorities make provisions for the inmate’s physical safety, and the Protocol’s other directives — courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress — govern court process rather than custody placement. Placement for a detained trans visitor is therefore discretionary, with no dedicated facility, special unit or statutory placement standard on record; the documented official position is that the penal system cannot safely accommodate trans prisoners.
TTO.outOfScopeNotes:
Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

Prison axis: the Protocol is a judicial-officers’ standard, not a statute — no trans-prisoner placement rule, dedicated facility, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is on record; how prison authorities actually respond to sentencing recommendations is undocumented; and the Protocol dates from November 2018 with no implementation evidence in this record.

sources.summary: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Newsday editorial (June 2024): 'Grind hate to a halt' - a spate of Grindr-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne points to gaps in the law: 'We don't have a specific hate crime category in legislation'; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

CNC3 (23 Aug 2024): the PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution (decision announced at a special convention); CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community has 'been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection'. Documents LGBTQ-rights exclusion from the 2024 constitutional-review process.

Usable as a 2012 non-enforcement baseline; predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so dated for current-law purposes.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 Jun 2016): PM Keith Rowley told Parliament (17 Jun 2016) the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws; cites Newsday. Documents the reform-refusal gap in official rhetoric as of 2016.

GHA.name: Ghana
GHA.summary:
Ghana is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected. That reintroduction materialised in late May 2026, when parliament passed a new Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to three years’ imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, longer terms for promotion/advocacy, and a ‘duty to report’ prohibited acts to police — passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required and widely expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.

The consequence axis of an arrest is the direct state pathway this bill creates: if ratified, identity alone becomes an imprisonable offence for the population that any prison-placement practice would apply to. Neither the 2026 reporting nor any source in this record contains a provision on how such prisoners would be housed, and no Ghanaian prison placement rule, trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is publicly documented. In a state that criminalises identity and lacks legal gender recognition, with documented mob violence, an undocumented placement practice cannot be assumed safe: a detained trans visitor would be held under a system with no documented housing standard and no documented recourse.
GHA.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

Prison axis: the May 2026 bill’s ratification status is unresolved in the sources — parliament passed it on 29-30 May 2026 and President Mahama had not yet accepted as of the reporting, which expected his signature — and must be rechecked; neither the 2024 nor the 2026 text, as reported, contains any provision on how trans prisoners would be housed; and no Ghanaian prison placement rule, trans special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record.

sources.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
sources.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison sentences of three to 10 years - up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer for promotion/advocacy. Community groups (e.g. One Love Sisters Ghana) report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.summary:
Morocco is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years), and Cairo 52 documents that trans people face de-facto criminalisation under Article 498 morality provisions — arrests based on gender-expression discrepancies and forced outing. The 2026 Cairo 52 report “A Web of Violence” describes a legal-medical-social system of erasure for trans people, including a de facto prohibition on transition care.

Visitor-relevant cases exist: in 2024, Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh, accused by police of being transgender, and alleges she was forced to show her genitals — she spent a month in jail. In 2019, Marrakesh police filmed and humiliated a cross-dressing man after a traffic accident, leaking the video online. There is no LGR framework and police have wide discretion; tourist areas (Marrakesh, Agadir) are more tolerant in practice but the legal exposure is constant.

The Gutierrez case demonstrates that even a cisgender visitor suspected of being trans can face genital inspection and jail.
MAR.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; the 2024 Gutierrez arrest was officially for filming a policeman — the trans-suspicion genital inspection is her allegation, disputed by Morocco.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 report 'A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco' (Jan 2026, by Hamzawya and Nora Noralla): based on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans - documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility; Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens; Article 489 weaponised to arrest trans people based on gender expression; no legal gender recognition pathway.

Cairo 52 country review of Morocco: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under Article 498 (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.
Hindustan Times (Nov 2024): an Instagram model alleges Moroccan police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions - reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

El País (Jan 2019): Moroccan police subjected a Marrakesh cross-dresser to online humiliation - after a minor traffic accident, Chafiq was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum in Europe. Homosexuality is punishable in Morocco.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 489 criminalises 'indecent acts' between persons of the same sex (6 months to 3 years) with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; 170 people charged with same-sex relations in 2018; HRW documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; no legal gender recognition; public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment; authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Morocco's Article 489 criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.
ILGA 'State-Sponsored Homophobia' (May 2008, Daniel Ottosson): world survey of laws prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults - country-by-country legal survey including Morocco.
Washington Blade (Sept 2014): the UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution - international context for human-rights scrutiny of countries including Morocco.

LGBTI organisation world survey (May 2008): world survey of laws prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults — country-by-country legal survey including this country.

Media report (September 2014): an international human-rights body adopted the sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity resolution — international context for human-rights scrutiny of countries including this one.

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised, but Cairo 52 documents that it is effectively criminalised through Penal Code Articles 333, 338, and 333 bis (indecency provisions), and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these articles. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years under Article 338. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.
DZA.outOfScopeNotes: Indecency-law application to trans people is documented in aggregate, not per-case; tourism volume is very low.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 country page (Algeria): NGOs document arrests within the LGBT+ community with little information on the trans identity of those arrested; no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare — arts. 274/264 could be used against providers (de facto criminalisation); no legal gender-recognition route, so civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked.

UK Home Office CPIN 'Algeria: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression' (26 Jul 2026, covering since May 2025): same-sex activity prohibited under Penal Code 1966 ('acts of homosexuality', Human Dignity Trust updated June 2026); internal relocation viable for gay males but lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties; refusals rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded — the current asylum-authority baseline.

Snopes fact-check (5 Aug 2024): Rating TRUE — Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and being transgender; published while debunking the false Imane Khelif 'trans boxer' rumour, confirming the ban is real even though the rumour about the athlete was false.

US State Dept 2023 Country Reports (Algeria): law criminalised undefined 'homosexual acts' with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment plus fines; prison authorities separated vulnerable persons but LGBTQI+ detainees had no specific legal protections; civil society noted compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons.

ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia 2008: Algeria — male/male and female/female relations illegal under Penal Code (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966): 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. Dated but the same Penal Code 1966 that the 2026 CPIN confirms is still in force.

Human Rights Watch (15 Oct 2020): after a 24 Jul 2020 raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, police arrested 44 people (9 women, 35 men, mostly university students) over an alleged 'gay wedding'; on 3 Sep 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and 42 to suspended terms, using decorations and 'gay appearance' as evidence.

BBC/Arab Barometer (23 Jun 2019, 25,000 respondents across 10 countries + Palestinian territories): Algeria was the exception where fewer than 50% accepted a woman head of state; region-wide, 'not religious' identification rose from 8% to 13% since 2013 — social-conservatism context datum for the record.

TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.summary:
Tunisia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.
TUN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.

sources.summary: Amnesty International (11 Feb 2025): at least 84 people — mainly gay men and trans women — arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef between 26 Sep 2024 and 31 Jan 2025 on 'public indecency'/morality charges; a 31 Oct 2024 mass conviction drew prison terms up to 4.5 years, upheld on appeal 5 Feb 2025 (four released after reduction). Quantified 2024-25 crackdown evidence.

Cairo 52 country page: Penal Code Article 230 criminalises same-sex conduct with up to 3 years' imprisonment; records enforcement (e.g. Oct 2021 arrest of two transgender women under morality/debauchery provisions) and gaps in legal gender recognition. Primary-law summary for visitor risk.

Intersection Association (Nov 2024): transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings — systemic identity refusal from detention onward, described as continuous suffering and discrimination inside the prison system. Direct trans-specific custodial-risk evidence.

Cairo 52 (30 Jan 2024): reports the Tunis Court of First Instance's Apr 2023 refusal of legal gender recognition to a transgender man; the court weighed contradictory lower-court judgements (incl. case No. 12304/2018) and found no consistent precedent, leaving recognition unsettled below the Court of Cassation. Shows LGR is court-by-court and often denied.

Human Rights Watch (29 Mar 2016): documents at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months, all convicted under Penal Code art. 230 (up to 3 years); interviewed detainees reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police. Core enforcement-abuse evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 Sep 2017): Tunisia pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases, but kept the anti-gay law itself; Kapitalis warns the pledge does not decriminalise anything. Shows reform-by-commitment without legal change.

TUN.tangentialFactors: Article 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the 2024-25 arrest wave explicitly included trans women on gender-identity grounds.
TUN.comparisons: Pairwise: below Egypt (0.22) and Algeria (0.22) on the strength of the current documented arrest wave explicitly including trans women; above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute and lynching culture Tunisia lacks). Tunisia's trajectory is among the world's worst right now.

CMR.name: Cameroon
CMR.summary:
Cameroon is dangerous for trans visitors. The Shakiro case is the defining documentation: in February 2021, trans women Shakiro and Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing, convicted of “attempted homosexuality,” “indecent dressing” and ID irregularities, and sentenced to five years. They described five months of “hell” in Douala's central prison, initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; Shakiro later received asylum in Belgium. Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years), and Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates.

Police and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and there is no legal gender recognition or protection of any kind. The Shakiro conviction shows that visible trans expression in a public place is itself treated as a prosecutable offence.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation in public risks arrest on indecency/ID grounds; prison conditions are severe.
CMR.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; the Shakiro case demonstrates direct application to gender expression.

sources.summary: BBC (12 May 2021): Douala court jailed trans woman Shakiro (YouTuber) and friend Patricia for five years under 'attempted homosexuality' plus 200,000 CFA francs ($370) each — the maximum statutory term — with appeal filed; detained since February 2021. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu called it a political decision with no proof of acts. Notes Cameroon's 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, one of 31 African countries criminalising, with beatings of gay/trans people common in public.

Wikipedia biography of Shakiro (b. 29 July 1997, Douala): Cameroonian trans activist who gained Facebook/YouTube following discussing trans life; arrested and charged with 'attempted homosexuality' in 2021, sentenced to five years, subsequently fled Cameroon and claimed asylum abroad. Serves as biographical corroboration of the 2021 case and its outcome (exile), tracking the human-rights profile of the criminalisation cases.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Cameroon: documents discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prisons, and arbitrary arrests - the criminalisation context (Article 347).

Human Rights Watch (11 May 2022): documented a 2022 uptick of violence against LGBTI people — since 9 March, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least 6 and detained 11 people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity; gendarmes beat two in detention. Frames the pattern: the criminalisation law lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence, per HRW senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi.

CNN (9 Jan 2013): Cameroon appeals court acquitted Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, jailed five years in November 2011 solely because they wore women's clothes and ordered Baileys — the original judge had cited dress, speech and the drink as proof they were gay. Conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts (lawyer Alice Nkom, All Out petition; Amnesty welcomed the acquittal). Establishes the pattern: arrests on effeminacy/appearance grounds under colonial-era sodomy law with six-month-to-five-year sentences.

CMR.tangentialFactors: Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years) — the vehicle for the Shakiro convictions and a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
CMR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — adds SSMPA mob-lynching culture at scale) and below Egypt (0.22).

TZA.name: Tanzania
TZA.summary:
Tanzania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since the Magufuli-era crackdowns (arrests, forced anal examinations documented by HRW in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case of Mauzinde is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest in Rahaleo, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack the UN Human Rights Office called “horrendous.”

OONI documented extensive targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites correlating with the escalating crackdown, and Amnesty's 2024 regional report notes Tanzanian pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. Zanzibar has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; Zanzibar is worse than the mainland.
TZA.outOfScopeNotes: Life-imprisonment statute is same-sex (climate/situational); the Mauzinde attack is trans-specific.

sources.summary: JURIST (9 Jun 2024): UN Human Rights Office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo — abducted by 12 men, found beaten in a forest with her ears cut — calling for 'bold action to combat discrimination against #LGBTIQ+ people'; the UN flagged possible violations of ICCPR Art. 20 and Tanzania's Constitution Art. 13 equality guarantees.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Tanzania's criminalisation of same-sex activity (life imprisonment possible).

OONI report 'Tanzania: Surge in online LGBTIQ censorship' (2024, PDF): documents the blocking of LGBTIQ websites and other targeted blocks in Tanzania based on OONI measurement data — including LGBTIQ social networks and rights sites — evidencing state-directed online filtering that constrains LGBT access to information.

Amnesty International report (Jan 2024, AFR 01/75/33/2024, 'We Are Facing Extinction'): documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people in Tanzania, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment — national-level findings.

Interview (Rainer Ebert, 4 Sep 2020) with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists: documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy; includes definitions of sexual orientation, gender identity and trans woman terms.

Zanzibar Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 (full text, PDF): enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives; defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute under 12; under-18 and marriage distinctions) and penalties including imprisonment for three years — Zanzibar-specific criminal law applying to the semi-autonomous islands alongside mainland law.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania: the three most widespread problems were security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice; also 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' and societal violence against persons with albinism.

TZA.tangentialFactors: Same-sex activity criminalised with up to life imprisonment — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
TZA.comparisons: Pairwise: below Tunisia (0.19 — active arrest wave but no life-imprisonment statute) and above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute, though Tanzania's mutilation attack and life-imprisonment law put it in the same tier).

ETH.name: Ethiopia
ETH.summary:
Ethiopia is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. The 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner than Cameroon's or Tunisia's — Ethiopia's LGBTQ+ community (self-identified as “zega”) is deeply underground, and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation + no LGR catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection place it clearly on the dangerous side of the scale. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the UPR reporting.
ETH.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation captures trans people via birth-sex legal status — a direct, not situational, mechanism.

sources.summary: Stakeholder submission to Ethiopia's UPR (47th session): same-sex activity criminalised, leaving LGBTQ+ people at serious risk of harm and systematic exclusion; discrimination, violence, lack of police protection and stigma in services; no legal gender change - trans men are legally women and trans women legally men, so trans people in different-gender relationships can fall foul of the same-sex conduct law.

Stakeholder UPR report by The Advocates for Human Rights and House of Guramayle (April 2024) on SOGIE in Ethiopia: documents discrimination, violence, and lack of protection; notes transgender people are particularly at risk given the criminalisation framework.

F&M Global Barometers country profile, time series 2011-2024 (all years scored 'no' on every protection axis): no legal gender recognition (neither surgical nor psychiatric pathway exists), no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no freedom from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity/expression, LGBTI organisations cannot register, Pride events not allowed and participants unprotected, no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protections including gender identity. National LGBTI organisations exist despite the ban on registration.
US State Department 2008 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): documents the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma - baseline country-of-origin information.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): documents arrests of opposition figures, CSO-law restrictions on civil society, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia: documents the anti-terrorism prosecutions, CSO-law restrictions, torture, harsh prisons - general context with the LGBT section noting criminalisation.

Lund University master's thesis (2009) by Daniel Iddo Balcha: 'Homosexuality in Ethiopia' - analyses the construction of homosexuality in relation to gender and feminism; male homosexuality criminalised (up to 3 years); media and elite create homophobia in discourse; the church effectively campaigns hatred; female homosexuality simply overlooked; attitudes shifting under globalisation.

sources.title: Ethiopia — Outright International country overview
sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code outlaws same-sex conduct between men and between women — rarely enforced but underpinning pervasive anti-LGBTIQ stigma, harassment and violence; in August 2023 security forces cracked down on 'homosexuality' while non-state actors drove an online incitement wave ending in physical attacks; Christian and Muslim groups campaign for harsher penalties (Orthodox Church declared its stance June 2024). Charities & Societies Proclamation Art 69 blocks registration of LGBTI groups as 'contrary to public morality'. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal nationwide, no legal gender recognition, LGBTI orgs cannot register.

sources.title: US State Dept 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices — Ethiopia

High levels of societal discrimination nationwide in education, employment and healthcare; being outed risks physical violence and ostracism. Authoritative annual baseline for state and social risk to a trans visitor.

ETH.tangentialFactors: Same-sex criminalisation (up to 1 year, more under aggravation) — because there is no LGR, a trans person's relationships are legally same-sex; a direct mechanism, not merely climate.
ETH.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Ghana (0.24 — Ghana's near-passed bill signals worse trajectory; Ethiopia's steady-state is worse today), above Tanzania (0.18) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts, visible community, and a 2023 Supreme Court NGO-registration win).

A government 2010 human-rights report: documents the anti-terrorism prosecutions, civil-society-law restrictions, torture, harsh prisons — general context with the LGBT section noting criminalisation.

A university thesis (2009): analyses the construction of homosexuality in relation to gender; male homosexuality criminalised (up to 3 years); media and elites create homophobia in discourse; a religious institution effectively campaigns hatred; female homosexuality simply overlooked; attitudes shifting under globalisation.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): a 2004 criminal-code article outlaws same-sex conduct between men and between women — rarely enforced but underpinning pervasive anti-LGBTIQ stigma, harassment and violence; in August 2023 security forces cracked down on 'homosexuality' while non-government actors drove an online incitement wave ending in physical attacks; religious groups campaign for harsher penalties. A charities law blocks registration of LGBTI groups as 'contrary to public morality'. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal nationwide, no legal gender recognition, LGBTI organisations cannot register.

A government 2023 human-rights report: criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct drives near-total concealment of identity — individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+; activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, with harassment/violence increasing toward end of 2023. High levels of societal discrimination nationwide in education, employment and healthcare; being outed risks physical violence and ostracism. Authoritative annual baseline for government and social risk to a trans visitor.
ETH.blindTangential: Same-sex criminalisation (up to 1 year, more under aggravation) — because there is no legal gender recognition, a trans person's relationships are legally same-sex; a direct mechanism, not merely climate.

LBN.name: Lebanon
LBN.summary:
Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence.

For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.
LBN.outOfScopeNotes: LGR case law and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing; Art 521/534 are the traveler-relevant statutes.

EUAA Country Focus Lebanon sec. 7.5 (fetched 2026-09-29): dedicated section on LGBTIQ persons including activists in the asylum country-of-origin report — treats LGBTIQ claims as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and source methodology.

HRW (8 Apr 2022, Nora Noralla): regional dispatch 'Tough Territory for Transgender People' — Egypt, Lebanon and Tunisia should ensure access to legal gender recognition; documents trans people's exposure to policing and documentation barriers in Lebanon alongside neighbours.

Manara Magazine (Mar 2022, Nora Noralla): maps MENA case law on legal gender recognition — the Lebanese judiciary has a long history of reviewing trans plaintiffs' name/marker changes governed by the civil registry code of 1951, with an 1887-era... [Lebanese Civil Decision 1987] precedent and heavy roles for medical and religious authorities; compares Lebanon with Egypt, Kuwait and UAE reasoning.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026), at-a-glance: same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country; legal gender recognition not possible (overview page cached truncated at ~5KB; article-level detail on Art. 534 not retrievable in cache).

HRW (18 May 2018): security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride — nine days of LGBT-identity activities — in a crackdown HRW called a violation of freedom of assembly and a step backward for LGBT rights.

The Daily Beast (15 May 2018): profile of Georges Azzi, who co-founded Helem in 2004 (the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world) and later led the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile regional countries.

HRW (2 Feb 2017): 'Another Judge Questions Legal Basis of Prosecuting Homosexivity Under Lebanese Law' — a ruling pushed Lebanon closer to decriminalising same-sex conduct, following the 2009 precedent that consensual same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence.

JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.summary:
Jordan demands real caution from trans visitors — the safest of the Levantine Arab states by a clear margin, but on a deteriorating trajectory. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1951, and courts have granted legal gender recognition in individual cases (the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling — though justified by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex). There is no statute criminalising gender expression itself.

The deterioration is documented: Cairo 52 reports a notable rise in targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, using Ottoman/British-era morality laws; Jordanian security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activities; the 2023 cybercrime law (“inciting immorality”) gives authorities a digital tool against LGBT expression; and gender-affirming surgery is criminalised for trans people (Article 8, Medical and Health Liability Law) while permitted for intersex people. In 2021 security forces arrested 14 people at a private party.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression per se, but morality-law discretion, shuttered community infrastructure, and family-society hostility make outing dangerous.
JOR.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: whether morality-law and cybercrime enforcement targets visitors in practice or is applied mainly to residents, and how border screening treats transgender travellers given the absence of a general legal-recognition pathway for them. Unverified: the current sources record no documented incidents involving trans visitors specifically; the documented deterioration trajectory runs through 2024.

sources.summary: CAIRO 52 Jordan country profile: new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave; intersex people can change legal gender markers but transgender people cannot, and gender-affirming healthcare is penalised for providers under medical-liability law.

OutRight International Jordan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised — Jordan abolished the colonial-era ban in 1951; no clear legal pathway for trans people to change gender markers (allowed 'in some cases'); gender-affirming surgery permitted for intersex people but criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018.

HRW World Report 2024 Jordan chapter (11 Jan 2024): authorities limited civic space in 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online; peaceful dissidents and journalists arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws, with intrusive digital surveillance — the environment shaping online expression for visitors and locals alike.

CAIRO 52 analysis of Case No. 2092/2014 (Jordan): Jordanian legislation criminalises sex reassignment with penalties up to 10 years' imprisonment (except intersex cases); the plaintiff (born 1977) sought name and gender change from male to female in official records after undergoing hormone therapy and surgery in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically.

HRW (6 Jun 2024): in Egypt, Jordan and Kuwait, same-sex relations are not explicitly criminalised in some, yet authorities 'legally' harass LGBT people via public-morality and debauchery laws — alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation, so decriminalisation on paper does not equal safety.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - despite state-sponsored repression and stigma, LGBT people are speaking out, building alliances and regional movements; includes an annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA (Jordan among them).

HRW (4 Dec 2023): Jordanian authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality; officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation and social-media users posted their photos with messages inciting violence — two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation.

JOR.localsOnly:
The criminalisation of gender-affirming surgery (Article 8, the medical liability law) and the case-by-case recognition rulings are resident-facing.

Transgender residents lack a general legal-recognition pathway — recognition comes only through individual court cases — and cannot access sex-reassignment procedures domestically; the 2014 case involved a plaintiff who underwent such procedures abroad.

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.summary:
Iraq is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it now has one of the world's most explicitly anti-trans statutes, in force since 1 July 2024. Amendments to the 1988 anti-prostitution law criminalise same-sex relationships (10–15 years), “biological sex change based on personal desire and inclination” (criminalising transition itself), and men who “intentionally act like women” (1–3 years) — a direct statutory criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Promoting homosexuality carries a minimum 7-year sentence. President Rashid signed the law on 29 June 2024.

Behind the statute stands a documented milieu of lethal violence: militia-led campaigns against men perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming (HRW's “They Want Us Exterminated” documented mutilated bodies dumped as warnings), with impunity. Most LGBT Iraqis hide their identity entirely. The Kurdistan Region has not passed the federal law but shares the social climate and has no protections.

For a visitor: being visibly trans is a statutory offence; discovery risks 1–3 years, with severe custodial and militia risk beyond the legal penalty.
IRQ.outOfScopeNotes: The 1988-law amendments apply in federal Iraq; the suspended KRI parliament has not adopted them, but no protection exists there either.

sources.summary: HRW (20 May 2024): Iraq's parliament passed (27 Apr 2024) an anti-LGBT amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution — same-sex relations punishable by 10-15 years' prison, 1-3 years for undergoing/performing gender-affirming procedures; HRW calls for repeal.

BBC: the new law criminalises same-sex relationships with 10-15 years' jail, 1-3 years for transgender people, plus penalties for 'promoting homosexuality' — framed by supporters as upholding religious values, condemned by rights groups.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry (May 2024) documents Iraq's new law prohibiting prostitution, homosexuality and gender-change procedures.

ILGA Asia briefing (15 Jan 2025): on 28 Apr 2024 Iraq amended the 1988 prostitution law to explicitly criminalise consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression; signed by the President 29 Jun 2024 — the operative legal baseline.

UK Home Office CPIN Iraq: Sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v3.0, July 2025): assessment of risk from state and hybrid actors and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Iraq: documents sectarian violence, torture, impunity, and 'societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity' - official acknowledgment of the dangers facing LGBT Iraqis.
CNN (27 Oct 2023): prominent Iraqi TikToker fatally shot in Baghdad amid a crackdown on the LGBTQ community — targeted killing of a visible figure as the anti-LGBT climate hardened.

BBC investigation: dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people killed in recent years in post-occupation Iraq while authorities turn a blind eye — the UN says state neglect makes Iraq a perpetrator; documented culture of abuse and impunity for anti-LGBT violence.

VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary:
Venezuela demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

The capital, Caracas, has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.
VEN.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: whether arbitrary detention and the wider repression wave would touch a trans visitor in practice, since the documented persecution is tied to the political crisis rather than trans-specific enforcement; general humanitarian and repression context affects all travellers, and the assessment reflects the trans-specific protection vacuum. Unverified: the current sources record no documented incidents specifically involving trans visitors.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (10 Sep 2024): LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after the disputed July 2024 election; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 Sep 2024 -- persecution of LGBTQ people tied to the political crisis, dated.

EUAA asylum country-focus (reference period through 2025): dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of conditions in Venezuela used for international protection decisions -- the EU asylum agency's factual baseline on how LGBTIQ+ people are treated.
NOTE: The AFS/Vance Center LGBTQ guide on Venezuela (Oct 2024) (image-based PDF; no text extractable).

Sydney Morning Herald (8 Aug 2015): Tamara Adrian, Venezuela's first transgender candidate, ran for the National Assembly -- landmark trans political candidacy under Venezuela's gender-recognition law context.

Cronica Uno poll (2-3 Mar 2023): a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% know the LGBTIQ+ term (13% do not); 36% think gay/lesbian/bisexuality is innate -- dated public-opinion data.

Blog record (31 Jan 2014): an equal-marriage bill was set to be presented to Venezuela's National Assembly that week (per Aporrea) -- legislative push for same-sex marriage, historic milestone (no later enactment recorded).

El Mundo (13 Dec 2015): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla -- Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian -- a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell -- state persecution of an openly gay politician.

The degraded healthcare, including HRT access, is resident-facing, and the post-2024 persecution wave primarily affects resident activists and communities.

Resident-facing political facts: a 2023 poll recorded a majority of the public supporting equal rights for the LGBTIQ+ population, with most respondents familiar with the term; a transgender candidate ran for the national legislature in 2015; and an openly gay parliamentarian was declared a prisoner of conscience in 2015.
