BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary:
Bolivia is workable for trans visitors — on paper a legal pioneer within this region. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (an administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. The constitution also names gender identity.

Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside the two largest cities (La Paz and Santa Cruz); and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.
BOL.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: whether the anti-discrimination guarantees are effectively enforced for visitors outside the largest cities, where limited protection is documented. Unverified: the current sources record no documented pattern of police targeting of trans visitors specifically; the survey exclusion data describes residents' daily lives rather than visitor incidents.

sources.summary: Comparative Politics article (April 2024) 'Activists, Parties, and the Expansion of Trans Rights in Bolivia': Bolivia prohibits gender-identity discrimination and passed a ground-breaking gender identity law (2016, allowing name/marker change) despite low voter support; trans activists leveraged access to ruling-party legislators; contradictory heteronormative laws passed alongside because both organised religion and LGBT activists were party constituents.

PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary:
Paraguay demands real caution from trans visitors — the most conservative country in its region. There is no legal gender recognition (ten lawsuits on trans name recognition remain pending, unresolved), no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. AP documents that many LGBTQ+ people feel compelled to leave their hometowns due to discrimination, harassment, and gender-based violence; trans women face particular social rejection. Amnesty reports persistent structural discrimination and high gender-based violence.

Nothing criminalises being trans, the capital, Asunción, has a small organised community, and there is no documented police targeting pattern — the risk is social hostility and a total protection vacuum rather than state persecution. Tourist traffic is low and there are no documented trans-visitor incidents.
PRY.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: the pending gender-recognition lawsuits have produced no final rulings, a communication before the international human-rights committee remains pending, and the discrimination-law absence is resident-facing so its direct application to visitors is untested. Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources — tourist traffic is low, and recorded hostility is social rather than institutional persecution.

Documented pace of recognition litigation.

PinkNews (20 Oct 2017): political climate report - ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes said he would 'shoot himself in the testicles' if his son married another man (later apologised to those offended); frames the report's account of a push to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'. Elite-level anti-LGBT rhetoric.

Tico Times (10 Jan 2018): on the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage - notes Bolivia, Paraguay and Peru recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions, i.e. the ruling binds Paraguay (OAS party) though local law lagged; ~300 Costa Ricans celebrated at the court. Inter-American framework applying to Paraguay.

Adoption-law reality check.

Ultima Hora: post-IACtHR ruling analysis says people in Paraguay must overcome difficulties adapting the country's laws to extend the right to marriage to everyone - the domestic-law gap the inter-American opinion leaves for Paraguay to close.

GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group such as Lambda, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is documented and dangerous: Human Rights Watch (7 October 2020) records that Guatemalan authorities facilitate anti-trans violence by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence including sexual assault — activist Bárbara Herrarte (Redmmutrans) described her time in a men's prison: 'Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him.' Placement operated by birth sex in the men's prison system as of 2020, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no special trans unit, and no trans-specific solitary/segregation practice on record; in a country with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor faces men's-prison placement with documented sexual-assault risk and no documented custody rule or court ruling anchoring a remedy.
GTM.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: how the general violence level in communities outside the tourist areas applies to visitors is unquantified — general gang violence affects all travellers, and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from it.

Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources, and the femicide-law exclusion is resident-facing though it signals institutional stance.

Prison axis: the birth-sex placement finding rests on a single Human Rights Watch documentation (7 October 2020); no Guatemalan law, regulation, court ruling or custody policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented — in a country without legal gender recognition, that absence cannot be read as a protected standard.

HND.name: Honduras
HND.summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the region, outside the two largest countries.

The consequence axis of an arrest is one of the region's most dangerous documented elements: Honduras places transgender women in the men's prison system — birth-sex placement with no placement-by-gender-identity policy, documented in 2017 and independently confirmed in 2020. At the national penitentiary (Tamara), LGBTI prisoners were concentrated in the “La Isla” module beside the mentally-ill unit, where trans women were forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women, and denied conjugal visits; at Marcala, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after the torture-prevention centre intervened was she isolated from the men and her belongings returned. Human Rights Watch states the practice “can lead to physical and sexual abuse,” and documents a Honduran judge's account of a trans woman raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards — prosecutors were informed and did not investigate (“There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons”). A detained trans visitor therefore faces male-facility placement with documented sexual-violence risk and official inaction, matching the record's already severe street-level warning.
HND.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: how the documented gang and security-force violence applies to short-stay visitors in tourist contexts is not quantified in the current sources — gang violence affects everyone. Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources; the state-responsibility finding covers an individual case and signals institutional accountability rather than a visitor-specific enforcement pattern. Prison axis: no Honduran statute, regulation or department policy fixing trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented — the placement practice rests on the 2017 and 2020 documentation; “La Isla” is a de facto concentration module rather than a codified special unit; and whether the documented practices persist as of the research date is unverified.

SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented and grim: since the state of exception began (March 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in the mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. The only documented custody case (2024 investigative reporting): a trans woman arrested in San Salvador in April 2022 was held at police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported, while the second trans woman remained imprisoned. The state-of-exception risk mechanism is therefore not hypothetical in custody: it is where the regime's arbitrary power meets identity-based mistreatment, with no special custody provision documented and release dependent on judicial review.
SLV.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: whether the exceptional security regime is applied to trans visitors in practice — its trans-specific application is a risk mechanism, not a documented pattern, and the regime affects all travellers. Unverified: the sources document no trans-visitor incidents, and the historic danger figures describe residents' experience before the recent crackdown. Prison axis: the custody documentation is a single 2024 investigation of one case — no Salvadoran statute, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) appears in this record, no special custody provision is documented for prisoners captured in the raids, and how widespread the documented mistreatment is across the mass-detention population is unverified.

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented as a policy-practice gap: since June 2017 the Justice Ministry has announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility — relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, with a census of self-identified trans prisoners ordered and an exclusive module for trans people under consideration. The practice side diverged: a June 2019 investigation found a trans woman serving a ~6-year sentence at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility, where the prison offered only two options — 'you're a man or a woman here' — and she recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape at La Reforma (Alajuela) that a custodian witnessed; the Justice Ministry then counted 23 transgender people in the national system. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a formal identity-based choice policy whose documented practice still placed trans women in men's facilities in 2019, with violence and custodial inaction.
CRI.outOfScopeNotes:
ID sex-marker limits and Church influence are resident-facing/climate.

Prison axis: no Costa Rican data on trans special units or solitary/segregation practice is documented — the exclusive module was 'under consideration' in 2017 and whether it was ever built is unverifiable from these sources; how the 2017 choice policy operates today is likewise unverified, with the 2019 men's-facility placement the only documented practice point.

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery — a resident-facing barrier. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and in March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled same-sex marriage is not a constitutional right, signaling judicial conservatism. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

No traveler-facing restrictions exist: no bathroom laws, no border friction, no documented police targeting pattern. Social hostility is moderate — machista culture persists, and trans women face documented employment exclusion — but violent targeting is far below Northern Triangle levels.
PAN.outOfScopeNotes: Surgery requirement for LGR and marriage ruling are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Outright International current Panama overview: amendment of the general anti-discrimination law to include SOGI grounds was blocked by the National Assembly in 2024 (claiming implicit coverage), no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes, intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited; at the 2025 UN UPR multiple states urged explicit anti-discrimination protections, gender-recognition reform and stronger violence safeguards — legal reforms remain stalled and Panama lags much of Latin America.

Equaldex data for Panama: homosexuality legal, marriage banned, gender change legal but requires surgery, no nonbinary recognition, no hate-crime protections, no employment/housing discrimination protections, blood donation banned (indefinite deferral), conversion therapy not banned. Only 12% approve of same-sex marriage (AmericasBarometer 2023, ranked #18 of 22).

Washington Blade (16 Feb 2018): Supreme Court Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega withdrew his October 2017 draft ruling against marriage rights — the draft had held the family code's same-sex marriage bars not unconstitutional while suggesting the Assembly consider civil unions; the Panama government signalled it would comply with the landmark 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision.

BBC features (14 Aug 2018): in Panama's Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing 'third gender' community (Omeggid) is accepted as completely normal, with powerful matriarchal figures elevating women's status — cultural context for how gender diversity is received in this part of the country.

Outright International current Panama overview (fetched page resolves to the country overview): anti-discrimination amendment blocked by the National Assembly in 2024, no hate-crime recognition, unregulated intersex infant surgery, 2025 UPR calls for SOGI protections and gender-recognition reform, reforms stalled.

Washington Blade (22 Oct 2017): La Estrella reported Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega's draft ruling finding the family-code sections barring same-sex marriage 'not unconstitutional' while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions ('equality must be constitutionally guaranteed via the law'); the two marriage lawsuits (a UK-marriage recognition suit and a direct family-code challenge) were combined after summer 2017 oral arguments, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition.

PAN.tangentialFactors: The 2008 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2023 marriage ruling is a climate signal.
PAN.localsOnly: The surgery-required LGR process is resident-facing; the documented employment exclusion affects residents.
PAN.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Bolivia (0.63 — different profiles: Bolivia has self-declaration LGR, Panama has lower social hostility and better infrastructure) and Vietnam (0.63), below Costa Rica (0.72 — the regional outlier), above Cambodia (0.61).

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary:
The Dominican Republic demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, and the 2024 Constitutional Court review of the remaining sodomy-law articles (210/260, which applied to police and armed-forces members) has resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations — though the existence of these articles revealed the institutional culture. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering SOGI (Brazil, a foreign government, formally recommended one at the 2024 UPR review), and documented violence against trans women is high, particularly affecting the most marginalised.

Tourist zones (Punta Cana, Puerto Plata) are heavily insulated resort enclaves with international norms; Santo Domingo, the capital, has a visible community and annual Pride caravan. Outside those bubbles, machista culture, police harassment of trans women (especially sex workers), and anti-Haitian (xenophobic) dynamics that compound for dark-skinned trans people are documented.
DOM.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: how the resort-versus-non-resort risk divide applies to trans visitors in practice is unquantified — tourist zones are heavily insulated, but the documented risk to trans women outside them is high for residents and untested for visitors. Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources, and the accepted review recommendations have no documented domestic implementation.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical. For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets; the current sources report no marriage or partner-travel friction.

The consequence axis of an arrest is among the most protective documented: since Bill C-16 (2017) banned discrimination based on gender identity, transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, and transgender prisoners imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery; the documented Synthia Kavanagh litigation — a transgender prisoner's court proceedings over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution — shows placement and care are litigable in Canadian courts. The caveats are documented practice gaps: a 2022 CTV report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault; a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; and no special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail is on record beyond the federal identity-based placement rule. For the rare visitor who ends up in custody, the documented standard is identity-based placement with functioning judicial recourse — the abuse allegations are the practice gap to weigh.
CAN.outOfScopeNotes:
Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals; the current sources do not address marriage or partner-travel questions for a visitor in any detail.

Prison axis: no special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail is on record beyond the federal identity-based placement rule; the CTV abuse allegations are reported allegations rather than adjudicated findings; and the Kavanagh case's dates and final outcome are not given in the source, so its precedential weight is unverifiable.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court’s landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW, another state, passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented at state level in Queensland: under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 (fully in force 2023) and its August 2023 inspection standards, transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender — identity-based placement — but staff still hold discretion at admission, and only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process; the 2009 Corrective Services procedure this oversight replaced was assessed as largely ineffective. Placement practice in the other states is not detailed in the current sources.
AUS.outOfScopeNotes:
State-level legal gender recognition patchwork and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing; the current sources do not assess marriage or partner-travel questions beyond the 2017 marriage-equality baseline, and border-document screening practice for visitors is not detailed.

Unverifiable in the current sources: three of the seven listed sources were not retrievable at research time (access denied; page removed; assembly bill text), including the 2024 discrimination ruling report and a state bill text; the remaining assessment of organised campaigns rests on the research brief alone.

Prison axis: the placement finding is Queensland-only and rests on a single Wikipedia section; no data in these sources documents trans-prisoner housing in the other states, special units, or solitary/segregation practice, and how the surgery exclusion is applied in practice is not documented.

Policy evolution behind the placement standard: the 2009 Queensland Corrective Services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective (Jenny Samiec, Queensland Law Student Review 2009), and oversight shifted to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 — institutional history rather than a visitor-facing risk.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.summary:
New Zealand is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant for the street climate: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit (the visiting campaigner); the national survey (Counting Ourselves) found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats).

For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.
NZL.outOfScopeNotes:
Counting Ourselves (resident-survey) data describes residents; healthcare gaps are resident-facing; marriage and partner-travel questions are not covered by the current sources (equal marriage has been legal in this nation since 2013, per the historical materials).

Unresolved: whether the documented 42% hate-incident increase translates into visitor-facing encounter rates; the community-archive source is context material with no risk finding for this record.

For this record: a usable local community/archive resource base (context, not risk).

ALB.name: Albania
ALB.summary:
Albania is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; a National LGBTI Action Plan (2021–2027) is in force (implementation is admittedly flawed); and the UN Independent Expert on SOGI conducted a full country visit in July 2024 — a sign of government openness unusual for the region. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, no bathroom laws, no documented police targeting; the realistic risk is social hostility outside Tirana and along more conservative rural areas. EU candidate status is driving slow alignment.
ALB.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and action-plan implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: End-of-mission statement of the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity after the country visit to Albania, 1-12 July 2024: assesses good practices and challenges and offers recommendations to the State — the international-review baseline for Albanian SOGI conditions.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) Albania chapter: discrimination complaints filed over the film 'Strange World' screenings were mediated, with the Commissioner ruling in favour in one case; Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people; groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

UN report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 (17 Jun 2025) by Independent Expert Graeme Reid on the Albania visit of 1-12 Jul 2024: evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.

PinkNews (Feb 5, 2010): Albania passed an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation but without same-sex marriage; homosexuality had carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for gay marriage in July 2009, framing the law as EU-integration driven.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda' — a record of parliamentary hostility toward LGBT education work under the Berisha-led opposition.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): MP Nard Ndoka's Facebook post branding the government 'LGBT' and accusing it of pushing LGBT values in schools, illustrating political anti-LGBT messaging in the same week as the schools campaign row.

Balkan Insight (Oct 27, 2011): Albania's Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community.

ALB.tangentialFactors: No SOGI hate-crime statute, and discrimination in key areas drew European Parliament concern — relevant mainly to visitors who experience or witness bias incidents.
ALB.localsOnly: There is no legal gender recognition (Albania rejected a self-ID recommendation at its UPR) — a resident-facing gap that does not affect a foreign passport holder.
ALB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Serbia (0.64 — comparable climate; Albania's action plan vs Serbia's larger community infrastructure) and below Moldova (0.65 — SOGI hate-crime law) and Montenegro (0.66 — partnership law).

MKD.name: North Macedonia
MKD.summary:
North Macedonia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised, and the capital, Skopje, hosts both Pride and an organised Trans March for Visibility (TransFormA, March 2024) — public trans organising that proceeds without serious incident. Anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity (2019 amendments). There are no same-sex or equal marriage rights (the 2014 marriage-definition motion, defining marriage as a union of one man and one woman) — a consideration for partners travelling as a couple — and the Law on Civil Registry’s legal gender recognition chapter was withdrawn.

Counterweights: hate speech and hate crimes remain common with no effective justice-system response (European Commission), social-media death threats are routine, and the legal gender recognition absence is documented.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; small but functioning community; standard regional street-hostility caution; no marriage recognition for same-sex visiting couples and no local document-change pathway; border and document-screening practice is not covered in the current sources.
MKD.outOfScopeNotes:
Justice-system non-response and legal-gender-recognition absence are resident-facing/climate signals; the sources do not address visitor document screening or border treatment of trans travellers.

Unverified: whether the 2014 marriage-definition motion is current law (the sources only record its submission), and whether reported community events continue to proceed without serious incident.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia: hate speech remained serious with countless reports and no meaningful state response (European Commission country report concurs); in September the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with SOGI aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code; ECRI called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Global Voices (30 March 2024): TransFormA’s March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility — "we march bravely" — while noting a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

ILGA-Europe/ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia chapter with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia: top priority is Legal Gender Recognition — the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the LGR chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review.
US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for North Macedonia: official assessment including the SOGI section - anti-discrimination law, societal violence and discrimination against LGBT persons.

Washington Blade (13 October 2023): economic analysis with Serbian and North Macedonian LGBTI groups quantifying how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms the economies of Serbia and North Macedonia — discrimination cast as a measurable drag on growth and jobs, without country-specific figures in the piece.

Balkan Insight (February 2012): ILGA-Europe’s Rainbow Europe Index ranked Macedonia worst in the Balkans at −2 on the 17-to−7 scale — the only Balkan country in the "red zone" of gross human-rights violations and discrimination.

Balkan Insight (July 2014): the government submitted a constitutional motion defining marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman — ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption — as an early act of the re-elected Gruevski government, needing two-thirds of MPs with the conservative DPA expected to supply the extra votes.

MNE.name: Montenegro
MNE.summary:
Montenegro is workable for trans visitors — the Western Balkans' most advanced legal framework. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and SOGI-inclusive hate-crime provisions; Podgorica Pride proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by ILGA-Europe: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (European Commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution in the north.
MNE.outOfScopeNotes: LGR inconsistency and prosecution-practice gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Montenegro: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a groundbreaking study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with €45,000; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.

Human Dignity Trust global legal history (updated 18 June 2026): Montenegro appears among the 1977 European decriminalisations (Croatia/Slovenia/Montenegro cohort); reference source for MNE's decriminalisation date rather than MNE-specific analysis.

GlobalGayz (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; small gay scene with deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination and harassment when visible; the first Podgorica Pride was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people in the capital. Dated but concrete on social climate.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Pride marched through Podgorica — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; Queer Montenegro's Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both state protection and organised hostility.

PinkNews (2 Aug 2019): MPs blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — ERA's Western Balkans office: LGBT people 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted.

CDM (Dec 2018): the Government adopted the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

MNE.tangentialFactors: The 2020 same-sex partnership law — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
MNE.localsOnly: No LGR law (administrative practice inconsistent) — resident-facing; the misdemeanour-overuse practice affects resident victims.
MNE.comparisons: After the 2026-08 audit: the audit found Montenegro’s framework (partnership law + SOGI hate-crime provisions + protected Pride) objectively stronger than Hungary’s (propaganda law in force + LGR ban + German court’s extradition-refusal finding). MNE raised to 0.67, effectively tied with ROU; HUN sits at 0.68 by its own anchors; MNE at 0.67 reflects slightly thinner implementation.

BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; the capital Sarajevo’s Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress.

Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report (the annual monitor): negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially in one internal region, Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in the hostile internal region (Republika Srpska) and rural areas. Marriage recognition is restricted to opposite-sex couples in the entities — relevant to same-sex partners travelling together; the border and document position for visitors is not detailed in the current sources.
BIH.outOfScopeNotes:

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament (the elected national assembly) passed the law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region’s harshest legislative package. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia’s best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in the capital (Tbilisi); mourners and the news agency AP drew a direct line between the law’s rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking local rights groups and LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases before the regional human-rights court, still unimplemented). Georgia’s visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

For a visitor: being visibly trans in Georgia now carries both statutory risk (assembly/information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors; border and document-screening practice is not covered by the current sources.
GEO.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2024 law’s healthcare and legal-gender-recognition provisions are resident-facing; its assembly/information provisions can reach visitors. The current sources do not detail border/document screening for visitors or whether the statutory assembly and information provisions have been enforced against individual travellers.

Unverified: the practical enforcement rate of the 2024 provisions on the street, and the current status of the unimplemented court rulings; the 2012 legal-barriers item predates the 2024 law.

sources.summary: BBC (Sep 2024): trans model and influencer Kesaria Abramidze was killed just one day after the Georgian parliament passed the anti-LGBTI law; German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Georgia's anti-LGBTQ+ measures raise fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation' — after the stabbing death of trans actress-model Kesaria Abramidze, Russia-style 'gay propaganda' laws stoke fear.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Georgia: the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as 'foreign agents' face fines/bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

WISG et al. report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers (5 Aug 2024) on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions in Georgia: recommends urgent action — effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.

IWPR Global Voices (May 2012): 'Georgian Laws Discriminate on Transgender Rights' - legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity doesn't match official paperwork - trans-specific legal barriers in Georgia.

OC Media (Jun 2019): Georgia's Interior Ministry declared Tbilisi Pride 'impossible' in the planned city-centre locations 'due to safety risks' (programme 18–23 June); organisers reported a week of pressure from an 'unidentified government official' to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it — the country's first-ever pride.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.summary:
Armenia demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Armenia has no anti-LGBT legislation of the restrictive type seen in neighbouring countries — and an administrative practice for legal gender recognition exists (medicalised). Pink Armenia’s 2024 annual report documents ongoing violations including inhuman/degrading treatment, and hate speech is routine in public discourse; the 2018 failed anti-discrimination bill means there is still no SOGI-specific (sexual orientation and gender identity) protection statute. The capital, Yerevan, has a small organised community (Pink Armenia and Right Side — a national rights organisation and a trans-led local group), but visibility carries real risk.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; social hostility significant outside central areas of the capital (Yerevan); police response unreliable; border and document-screening practice is not covered in the current sources.
ARM.outOfScopeNotes:
Protection-statute absence and legal-gender-recognition medicalisation are resident-facing. The current sources do not describe border/document-screening practice for visitors, and the practical enforcement of “ambiguous” hate-crime protections is unquantified.

Unverified: the current administrative status of the medicalised recognition path, and whether it could apply to a visitor; the 2009 mission and 2012 report are dated context.

sources.summary: Pink Human Rights Defender NGO annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024. Documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech - including a chapter on pressure around a transgender individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Equaldex comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia: Armenia decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections 'ambiguous' since 2022; no SOGI discrimination protections; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low (5/100).

ILGA-Europe/COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in Armenia.

Unzipped: Gay Armenia blog (May 2012): neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan - Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via CCTV - documents anti-LGBT hate violence in Armenia.

The Guardian (April 2019): Armenia's first registered trans woman, Lilit Martirosyan, received death threats (including MPs calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination - documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.summary:
Azerbaijan is dangerous for trans visitors. The documented pattern is grim: a trans woman was tortured and murdered in the capital, Baku, in July 2023; a second trans woman’s murder in March 2024 was met with a police response lacking comprehensive investigation; several other trans people were physically assaulted, including by police themselves; and two trans women were detained for “hooliganism” for making noise. Government-affiliated media air targeted discriminatory hate speech.

Nothing formally criminalises gender expression, but police are perpetrators rather than protectors, and the state is one of the world’s more closed authoritarian systems — there is no recourse and no community infrastructure that can operate openly. An April 2024 ECtHR ruling (the regional rights-court) found violations in Azerbaijan’s treatment of LGBTI applicants.

For a visitor: no statute bars entry or expression, but discovery risks police abuse with no remedy, and the murder-impunity pattern is documented; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources.
AZE.outOfScopeNotes:
Economic exclusion data is resident-facing; the police-perpetrator pattern is traveler-relevant. The current sources do not detail border/document-screening practice for visitors, and the specific identity-document impossibility is a resident administrative matter.

Unverified: whether foreign visitors are at the same risk of police attention as residents, and the current enforcement trajectory of the 2024 ruling; the 2017-era reports are dated context.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents the March murder of a trans woman in Baku met with an inadequate police investigation; state-affiliated Real TV airing discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding trans healthcare access; a family forcibly transporting an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out; and an April ECtHR ruling on the September 2017 police arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, which Azerbaijan acknowledged in 2019.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents a July police raid on a private birthday party where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of outing; QueeRadar monitoring found 77% of 428 analysed media pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people; and an activist being told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe.

OC Media feature by Ali Malikov on trans people in Azerbaijan: discrimination has direct economic impacts - trans people are rejected from jobs and housing, pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. Profiles 'Durdana', 29, arrested, denied housing and employment, and dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

HRW (Oct 2017): Azerbaijan's anti-gay crackdown — police raids in Baku (Sept 2017) detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges with beatings documented; HRW called for investigation and release.

Gender & Development Social Union shadow report to CEDAW (44th session) on discrimination and violence against lesbian, bisexual and transgender people in Azerbaijan: documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia/transphobia in official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women; the organisation serves 200+ LBT people.

The Guardian (Sept 2017): outcry as Azerbaijan police launch crackdown on the LGBT community - at least 60 people imprisoned or fined after raids in the capital; part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games.

KAZ.summary:
Kazakhstan demands real caution from trans visitors — Central Asia's most liveable country for trans people, a relative statement within its region. Nothing is criminalised: no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory. Legal gender recognition exists but is heavily medicalised (psychiatric boards, surgery requirements applied in practice). An international monitoring body recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real incidents, yet documented and reported, which itself signals a functioning civil society (Feminita, ECOM).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; low visibility keeps visitor exposure small; the main cities are navigable.
KAZ.outOfScopeNotes: The propaganda petition remains under official review as of the 2024 reports; whether it ripens into a statute is unresolved. The police-are-unhelpful description rests on behavioural reporting that could not be independently verified. The ECOM regional report is abstract-level, with country data held in a linked report body.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering Jan–Dec 2023 (Kazakhstan): documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

OSCE/ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting 2024 summary for Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since the 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

HRW (10 Jul 2024): in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information said it was reviewing a 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!' petition (Union of Parents) that met the threshold for government consideration; HRW warns the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide — a live, dated legislative threat.

ECOM regional report library page (2024): ECOM has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017; the analysis identifies health-right barriers across the EECA region as a whole and in individual countries (incl. Kazakhstan), plus informal behavioural practices missed by policy analysis — abstract-level, country data is in the linked report body.

HRW (24 Sep 2019): Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

KAZ.localsOnly: The heavily medicalised legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing: psychiatric boards and surgery requirements are applied in practice to residents, not to visitors.
KAZ.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Peru (0.48) and just below the USA/Mexico (0.50) — Kazakhstan has no institutional hostility machinery but a far weaker protection floor — and above Armenia (0.46) and Turkey (0.47).

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.summary:
Uzbekistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — and Human Dignity Trust notes transgender people may be targeted under it, since there is no legal gender recognition and trans people are legally their birth sex. There is substantial evidence of recent enforcement: frequent arrests, and extortion by threat of arrest, with police as the most common perpetrators of anti-LGBT violence; torture goes unpunished (HRW). Because of criminalisation, victims cannot report violence to authorities.

ECOM's 2024 national report documents continuing rights violations, and the Justice Ministry denies registration to independent human-rights groups — no community infrastructure can operate openly. There is no documented trans-visitor case, but the legal mechanism (birth-sex status + Art 120) means a trans visitor discovered in a same-sex-appearing relationship faces direct prosecution risk, and discovery itself invites extortion.
UZB.outOfScopeNotes: Art 120 formally applies to male same-sex conduct; its application to trans people is via birth-sex legal status — a direct mechanism, not merely climate.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Uzbekistan's criminalisation of same-sex activity (Article 120 of the criminal code, up to 3 years).

HRW World Report 2024 (events of 2023): same-sex conduct between men remains criminalised (up to 3 years); police target gay/bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment; forced 'forced examinations' amount to torture per WHO; impunity for police ill-treatment persists.

ECOM national report (2024) on violations of the rights of LGBT people in Uzbekistan: legislation, anti-discrimination legislation, criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, right to health and right to work.

UK Home Office COI note (Jul 2024): consensual same-sex conduct between men criminalised under Article 120 of the 1994 Criminal Code, up to 3 years; documented Article 120 cases 2009-2023; police intimidation/violence/exploitation of gay men and trans people routine; LGBTI orgs cannot register, operate unofficially; rural taboo drives discrimination.

US State Dept 2021 HRR: Section 6 documents legal and societal abuses -- torture/ill-treatment and arbitrary detention concerns in custody, plus social stigma and violence affecting LGBT people under the criminalised framework.

US State Dept 2023 HRR: LGBTQI+ people arrested then released or threatened with arrest unless paying bribes; police coerced LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison; websites and bloggers self-censored on LGBTQI+ issues; societal harassment continued.

HRW (23 Mar 2021): Article 120 punishes consensual sex between males up to 3 years; gay/bisexual men face discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from state and non-state actors with almost no protections; HRW urges decriminalisation (Uzbekistan then on UN rights council).

UZB.tangentialFactors: Article 120 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; extortion-by-threat-of-arrest targets discovered trans people.
UZB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Egypt (0.22 — Egypt's entrapment machinery is more systematic; Uzbekistan's extortion pattern is comparable) and Algeria (0.22), below Morocco (0.25) and above Tunisia (0.19).

NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.summary: Nicaragua is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans — sodomy was decriminalised in 2008 — but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGBTIQ+ community in 2024 alone and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years, and arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents. Since 2018 virtually all independent civil society has been shut down or exiled, so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse for a visitor facing harm.
NIC.outOfScopeNotes: The violence and murder totals are NGO-counted resident tallies; how far visitors appear in them is unresolved. Generalised repression is regime-wide, so detention risk is not trans-specific; conversely the trans-murder count is trans-specific and cannot be generalised to visitors.

sources.summary: thin: no usable finding

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report on Nicaragua: documents a police/parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among significant violations. For this record: official US assessment that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International (May 2019): the post-April-2018 protest crackdown left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the IACHR; journalist Miguel Mora describes being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay, illustrating the intersection of political repression and homophobia. For this record: documented violence context and homophobia within the repression, with the casualty figures.

PinkNews (Nov 2007): Nicaragua's new penal code, effective March 2008, repealed the 1992 sodomy law (1-3 years' imprisonment), whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work. For this record: dated decriminalisation — same-sex conduct not criminalised since 2008.

NIC.localsOnly: The documented violence falls on residents: 108 cases of violence against the LGBTIQ+ community in 2024 and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years. The civil-society shutdown affects resident organisations and the residents who depended on them.
NIC.comparisons: Pairwise: level with El Salvador (0.41 — different profiles: NIC has state-suppression of all NGOs plus trans murders; SLV has gang-violence collapse plus arbitrary-detention state), above Guatemala (0.40) and below Trinidad & Tobago (0.42).

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary:
Guyana is dangerous for trans visitors — one of only five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising same-sex conduct (buggery carries life imprisonment on paper, though rarely enforced). The IACHR heard evidence in November 2024 of severe violence against trans women: 69 cases of violence against trans women documented 2018–2022, in a country of under a million people. Police fail to investigate anti-LGBT violence; there is no anti-discrimination legislation (the UN Human Rights Committee called for it in April 2024) and no legal gender recognition.

Cross-dressing was decriminalised after a 2018 CCJ ruling (McEwan v AG), removing the most direct trans-expression statute, but the climate and investigative failure keep risk high. Georgetown has a small organised community (SASOD).
GUY.outOfScopeNotes: Buggery statutes are rarely enforced (climate/situational); the CCJ struck cross-dressing laws in 2018.

sources.summary: Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Guyana one of five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct — ss.352-354 Criminal Law Act (gross indecency; attempted buggery; buggery with life imprisonment), rarely enforced but fuels stigma. Five of six parties in the 2025 election, incl. ruling party, backed decriminalisation. Cross-dressing law (s.153(1)(xlvii)) struck 2018 (McEwan); no legal gender recognition; 2022 poll: 72% acceptance, 13pp less hostility vs 2013.

Stabroek News (16 Nov 2024): at the IACHR's 191st session (OAS HQ, Washington), a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum — 'Impact of Gender-Based Violence on Migrant Women, Sex Workers, and Transgender Women in Guyana' — heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action (record's cited figure: 69 documented cases of violence against trans women 2018-2022).

BBC (26 Mar 2017): trans woman Petronella Trotman stabbed in Georgetown Jan 2017, then told by magistrate Dylon Bess to 'dress like a man' and refused courtroom entry on 2 Mar — case dismissed. Turns on the 1893 Summary Jurisdiction Act cross-dressing offence (124 years old, 'improper purpose' open to magistrate interpretation). Documents both street violence and justice-system failure for trans Guyanese.

Stabroek News (13 Nov 2018): Caribbean Court of Justice allowed the appeal of Quincy McEwan, Angel Clarke, Peaches Fraser et al. and struck s.153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act as unconstitutionally vague and contrary to freedom of expression. Backdrop: 2009 arrests of trans women under the 1893 act with three nights' detention; challenge filed 2010 with SASOD — removed the direct anti-cross-dressing offence.

PinkNews (26 Mar 2017): corroborates the Trotman attack (stabbed with scissors/neck wound, glass bottles) and the courtroom exclusion; SASOD's Joel Simpson calls magistrate Bess's conduct a 'dereliction of duty' while arguing Parliament, not courts, must repeal the 1893 law. Unique value: named LGBT-organisation response demanding legislative repeal.

News Room Guyana (16 May 2019): SASOD's Joel Simpson documents police using residual Summary Jurisdiction clauses to extort LGBT people — men in 'compromising positions' threatened with arrest to extract bribes; same-sex couples harassed at seawalls/parks; formal complainants face secondary discrimination at stations and give 'watered down' accounts. Post-CCJ, loitering/vagrancy clauses remain usable against LGBT (mostly sex-worker) populations.

GUY.tangentialFactors: Buggery (life imprisonment on paper, rarely enforced) remains a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2018 CCJ ruling struck cross-dressing laws.
GUY.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Sri Lanka (0.33 — both criminalisation-plus-police-failure profiles), above Jamaica (0.31 — Jamaica's mob-killing culture is worse), below Lebanon (0.36).

SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.summary:
Suriname is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's 'any other status' clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination, and the penal code has carried sexual-orientation discrimination and hate-speech provisions since March 2015. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but the capital's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in the capital; low tourist infrastructure generally.
SUR.outOfScopeNotes: The absence of any documented trans-murder pattern is an absence-of-evidence finding, not proof of safety. Interior protection levels and the real-world operation of the 2022 labour act are unverified. Community harassment reports are anecdotal rather than systematically counted.

sources.summary: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: same-sex relations legal for men and women nationwide; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations CAN register. Constitution Article 8.2's 'any other status' clause is read by the government as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity despite no explicit statutory protection.

Civil-society report of July 2024 (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform): Constitution Article 8 covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869. The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname: documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality, corruption, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities'.

Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (115th session) from LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata: despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization. It records that in March 2015 Penal Code Articles 175, 175a and 176 were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

Human Rights Committee review of Suriname, July 2024: the State asserted its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while experts pressed on implementing the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity. The Committee welcomed abolition of the death penalty in the Penal Code (2015) and Military Code (2021).

UN UPR pre-session summary of March 2016 from the Suriname LGBT Platform: since the 2011 UPR the State revised the penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions. The platform also reports it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.

SUR.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition — a resident-facing gap. The 2022 Equal Treatment Labour Act adds employment protections for workers, and the harassment reports concern residents' daily street experience; the community also reports continued daily discrimination despite the constitutional reading.
SUR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Ecuador (0.57 — far less violence) and below India (0.58, tie).

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.summary:
Kyrgyzstan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has been legal since 1998 and there is no expression statute, but legal gender recognition has been removed, police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and an active anti-LGBT political campaign is running in the country — in 2023-2024 two discriminatory laws targeted the LGBTI community and restricted LGBTI organisations, with homophobic and transphobic legislator rhetoric accompanying them.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal, a police extortion culture, and the political campaign make being outed risky.
KGZ.outOfScopeNotes: The record says there is no expression statute, but source reporting ties the capital's LGBT-club closures to a ban on 'LGBT propaganda' — the two cannot be reconciled from the material here. Whether the 2023-2024 discriminatory laws are actively enforced is not documented. One monitoring body dates LGR removal to 2021 while the civil-status amendment blocking birth-certificate changes dates to 2020 — the discrepancy is unresolved.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (Kyrgyzstan): anti-LGBT legislative pushes accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from MPs; since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition (Law on Civil Acts amendments); ECOM data shows high stigma and discrimination, particularly from law enforcement.

TGEU Trans Rights Index Map 2024: Kyrgyzstan (2021) joined Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia in removing the right to legal gender recognition; for Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan the 'bare minimum' of not banning recognition is all they score — the regional floor on trans legal status.

OutRight International Kyrgyzstan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex activity decriminalised 1998 with age of consent equal at 16; no same-sex marriage or civil unions and a 2016 constitutional amendment explicitly bans same-sex marriage; the provision allowing trans people to change legal gender markers was removed by a 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation in the country shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids, registry practices, and zero recourse make discovery dangerous.
TJK.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the on-paper medicalised registration route is ever granted in practice is unverified. Registry practices are maintained informally, so their current status is opaque. The 2022 anti-discrimination law is on the books but assessed as failing to address discrimination — a gap between statute and practice.

sources.summary: IPHR report 'Rights for All?' (Feb 2024): consensual same-sex relations decriminalised since 1998, yet authorities introduced a police register of LGBTIQ people in 2016; 2022/2023 police raids brought forced HIV-testing and arbitrary criminal charges; ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police documented; the 2022 anti-discrimination law fails to address discrimination — the systematic-risk evidence for a visitor.

Outright International overview (updated Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal throughout the country since independence, no SOGI non-discrimination protection; in 2024 ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people with police arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion; a 2017 government registry of 'proven' LGBT persons flagged — legality without safety.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services incl. HIV prevention/treatment and HRT across the EECA region, with a Tajikistan country coordinator contributing — maps what gender-affirming/HIV care is actually reachable in-country and includes guidance for trans migrants.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): police lure LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database, harvest social-media contacts and extort money (10+ cases in Sughd); forced/sham marriages used against LGBT people with police inaction; the 2022 anti-discrimination law only partially aligns with UN standards — quantified police-entrapment risk.

ECOM legislative analysis (2020): comparative analysis identifying legal barriers and gaps for gay men, MSM and trans people in Tajikistan, built from a questionnaire completed by local partners — documents where the written law protects but practice does not.

HRW World Report 2017, Tajikistan chapter: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 — opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned, and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule — the repressive state context surrounding LGBT life.

Global Voices (Jan 20, 2013): despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier (1998) there is very little tolerance; those who disclose orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police, and the community remains one of the most closed in society — social-climate evidence predating the 2016 registry.

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary:
Turkmenistan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, Turkmenistan is one of the world's most closed states: the state exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (ILGA-Europe). Amnesty has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a state that monitors communications pervasively.
TKM.outOfScopeNotes: Absence of documentation is itself evidence of severity: data collection is impossible because it is unsafe.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the April 2022 Criminal Code not only kept the 'sodomy' provisions but increased both the severity and scope of punishments; torture and inhumane treatment remain present throughout the country with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them — the current penal-risk read.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Turkmenistan: lists among significant human-rights issues the existence of laws criminalizing consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, alongside officials in security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity — official assessment of law plus enforcement climate.

EHPV mid-term UPR stakeholder submission (2020): LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; identifies article 135 of the Criminal Code criminalising consensual same-sex acts between adult men as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination, and notes increasing flight abroad.

ECOM legislative analysis, 'Legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan' (Tallinn, 2019, 11pp, with Turkmen.news): maps the legal landscape and barriers for LGBT people and PLHIV — deliberately compiled so NGOs, community activists and government can use it when planning advocacy; the standing legal-baseline reference for the country.

Columbia Law School (May 1, 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured US asylum (DHS) for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions — believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan; documents persecution grounds cited by people fleeing the country.

Goldberg Kohn (Sept 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

TKM.tangentialFactors: Article 135 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 2 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
TKM.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Qatar (0.12 — different profiles: TKM's opacity prevents even documenting abuse; QAT's abuse is documented), below Uzbekistan (0.22 — UZB has enforcement data and some civil society) and Russia (0.12, tie).
