SYR.name: Syria
SYR.summary:
Syria is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise “sexual acts against nature” and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024), the situation has worsened: the Guardians of Equality Movement documented “waves of violence” against Syrian transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both non-state armed groups and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.
SYR.outOfScopeNotes: General conflict risk affects all; the 2025 trans-women violence waves are trans-specific.

sources.summary: GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025 on LGBTQIA individuals in Syria after the fall: working through an on-the-ground reporter network, the organisation investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.
thin: no usable finding

Country overview updated 12 March 2026: Syria's legal landscape remains highly restrictive - Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa including Syria, with tallies that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 in Iraq, 3 in Libya). Activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the UN Security Council.

Syria Direct feature of 11 October 2020 (Will Christou, Alicia Medina): LGBT Syrians describe life at home and abroad - in Damascus homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old (Amira al-Tabbaa) describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

Newsweek, 2015: two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council - a closed session co-sponsored by the US and Chile - about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews, 23 June 2010: Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop - most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs, per gaymiddleeast.com.

SYR.tangentialFactors: Articles 520/517 criminalise “sexual acts against nature” — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SYR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Saudi Arabia (0.05 — SYR's chaos vs SAU's systematic state machinery) and below Iraq (0.08 — IRQ now has a codified anti-trans statute; SYR has codified indecency + active violence waves).

LBY.name: Libya
LBY.summary:
Libya is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises “illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” (up to 5 years), and Cairo 52 documents de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition through these provisions — compounded by recent religious rulings declaring the very term “gender” haram, making anyone using it in media or institutions susceptible to prosecution. Militias control territory and operate detention sites where torture is systematic; there is no functioning central judiciary, no LGR, and no protection of any kind.

For a visitor: detention by any of several militia authorities is the modal bad outcome, with no consular reach in much of the country.
LBY.outOfScopeNotes: Militia fragmentation means enforcement varies by territory; the trans-specific mechanism is documented de-facto criminalisation.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 country review: Libya has de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process (social, medical, surgical), enforced through 'indecent acts' and 'illicit intercourse' provisions; recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not legal for men or women; 'indecent acts' provisions carry up to 5 years' imprisonment; no legal protections against SOGI discrimination; same-sex relationships not legally recognised; legal gender recognition unavailable (official identity documents cannot be changed); LGBTI organisations cannot register.

The Guardian, Brian Whitaker guide (21 Jun 2016): Libya is among regional states where homosexuality carries imprisonment as the penalty (specific terms vary by country); where no specific law exists, other laws are used — the guide assesses the catastrophic effect of these regimes on gay people's lives.

HRW (8 Jun 2015): documents Islamic State's killing of men accused of homosexuality in territory it controlled, including Derna, Libya — a young man there was targeted by local Islamists for effeminate dress and 'contemporary' clothes (case named from Nov 2014).

D+C (Jun 2015): Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in Derna in April 2015; the piece reports information in Derna flows only through the mosque and concludes the situation for homosexuals in Libya is getting worse as militias control territory.
HuffPost (26 Nov 2012): 12 men accused of being gay faced torture and threatened death at the hands of a Libyan militia — early post-revolutionary vigilante violence against suspected gay men.

LBY.tangentialFactors: “Illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” provisions (up to 5 years) capture same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity alike.
LBY.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Oman (0.09 — OMN has an explicit enforced statute; LBY has de-facto criminalisation plus militia detention risk), below Iraq (0.08, comparable) and above Syria (0.06).

YEM.name: Yemen
YEM.summary:
Yemen is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The legal framework criminalises same-sex conduct (up to death under some interpretations of the Penal Code; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise), but Cairo 52 emphasises the operative mechanism: the erosion of the rule of law and the power of militias has facilitated a surge in attacks targeting transgender individuals — de facto criminalisation operating outside any judicial system. Houthi-controlled areas impose their own moral-policing regime; the south has its own militia authorities.

For a visitor: no safe authority to appeal to anywhere in the country.
YEM.outOfScopeNotes: War risk affects all; the documented surge in trans-targeted attacks is trans-specific.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 country review of Yemen: erosion of the rule of law plus humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands (vigilante risk); critically, the penal provisions apply ONLY in government-controlled regions — other areas sit under different factions in the ongoing conflict, so legal exposure varies by territory.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018, MENA): Yemen is one of 14 covered countries where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited; the report could identify NO activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work (a documented safety gap), and notes 'breach of modesty' laws used against expression.

HRW World Report 2026, Yemen chapter (events of 2025): its Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section states Yemen's penal code prohibits same-sex relations — Article 264 punishes anal sex with 100 lashes and one year in prison if participants are not married, with the article prescribing differently if married — alongside world's-worst humanitarian crisis (19.5M needing aid) and Houthi/government factional control affecting where law applies.

Amnesty International (Feb 2024): two Huthi-run courts in Yemen sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct — the Dhamar criminal court (23 Jan) sentenced nine to death (seven by stoning, two by crucifixion) with 23 more given 6 months-10 years for 'homosexuality'/'spreading immorality', and an Ibb court (1 Feb) handed further death sentences; Amnesty demanded an immediate halt.

GayLawNet Yemen laws page: consensual same-sex sex is unlawful under Penal Code 1994 Article 264 — homosexuality between men defined as anal penetration; unmarried men punishable with 100 lashes (and up to one year's imprisonment per the statute); the canonical statute citation for Yemen's criminalisation.

IPS (16 Aug 2013) 'No Place for Gays in Yemen': Sana'a social climate — a gay man describes hiding (hood over long hair) as 'still problematic'; conservative society has no place for them while the law sees homosexuality as punishable by death; illustrates discretionary-social enforcement layered on the statutory penalty.

YEM.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to death under some interpretations; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise) — a catastrophic exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
YEM.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Syria (0.06 — both are active-conflict states where trans people are targeted extra-judicially), above Afghanistan (0.02 — AFG's Taliban system is more totalising and systematic) and below Iraq (0.08).

blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring organisation's review of this nation: erosion of the rule of law plus humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands (vigilante risk); critically, the penal provisions apply ONLY in government-controlled regions — other areas sit under different factions in the ongoing conflict, so legal exposure varies by region.

A human-rights organisation's report (16 April 2018, regional): this nation is one of 14 covered nations where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited; the report could identify NO activists in this nation willing to speak about their work (a documented safety gap), and notes 'breach of modesty' laws used against expression.

A human-rights organisation's world report 2026 chapter on this nation (events of 2025): its sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity section states this nation's penal code prohibits same-sex relations — Article 264 punishes anal sex with 100 lashes and one year in prison if participants are not married, with the article prescribing differently if married — alongside a world's-worst humanitarian crisis (tens of millions needing aid) and factional control between an armed movement and the government affecting where law applies.

An international human-rights organisation (February 2024): two courts run by an armed movement in this nation sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct — one court (23 January) sentenced nine to death (seven by stoning, two by crucifixion) with 23 more given 6 months to 10 years for 'homosexuality'/'spreading immorality', and another court (1 February) handed further death sentences; the organisation demanded an immediate halt.

A legal-reference website's laws page for this nation: consensual same-sex sex is unlawful under Penal Code 1994 Article 264 — homosexuality between men defined as anal penetration; unmarried men punishable with 100 lashes (and up to one year's imprisonment per the statute); the canonical statute citation for this nation's criminalisation.

A news outlet (16 August 2013): the capital's social climate — a gay man describes hiding (hood over long hair) as 'still problematic'; conservative society has no place for them while the law sees homosexuality as punishable by death; illustrates discretionary-social enforcement layered on the statutory penalty.
YEM.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to death under some interpretations; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise) — a catastrophic exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary:
Bhutan is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression.

Tourism is tightly regulated (daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 2021, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections; LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Legal gender recognition is unavailable — earlier administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Discrimination and stigma persist, especially in health-care access.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service (Nov 2024): trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report violence — police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male ('both parties are men'), families pressure victims to accept it as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. Practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

UNFPA Bhutan report 'Fostering Awareness' (31 Mar 2025, 37pp): the 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General's Office and Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.

Erasing 76 Crimes (10 Jun 2019): Bhutan's lower house voted 43-1 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213-214 'unnatural sex' provisions (1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); upper-house ratification still pending at that point. Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

Erasing 76 Crimes (11 Mar 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 Feb 2021 — after the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation (global criminalising-state tally fell 72 to 71). Freshness pass (2026-09-27) confirms this stands with no post-2021 reversal.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow': the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page (from c.2014) produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population; profiles admins and Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform kira — a first in Bhutanese society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

The Daily Beast (28 Oct 2015): Bhutan's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility — 'growing up gay in Bhutan was a very alienating experience', no shared language for gay or trans identities, lesbianism under-recognised. Karma Dupchen, one of the most public LGBT figures, founded the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page in 2013.

BTN.tangentialFactors: The 2021 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
BTN.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition — resident-facing; the 4x assault likelihood and violence/discrimination reports describe residents' experience.
BTN.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nepal (0.64 — Nepal has stronger jurisprudence but Bhutan lower reported violence) and below Romania (0.67).

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary: Laos demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans in this country, which has a socially visible tradition of trans-feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation — the one-party system restricts all civil society — and no documented recourse. The tourist cities are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque system) more than violent.
LAO.outOfScopeNotes: Civil-society restrictions affect all, not visitors specifically; no trans-specific enforcement mechanism is documented anywhere in the record. One diplomatic source page could not be fully retrieved, so its detail rests on its summary.

sources.summary: thin: no usable finding
thin: no usable finding

Human Dignity Trust history: Laos (with Cambodia) achieved independence from France in the 1950s and modelled its penal code on the French system — it has never formally criminalised same-sex conduct, distinguishing it from neighbours that retained colonial sodomy offences.

GlobalGayz first-person account (2000, Richard Ammon): during a week in Vientiane the writer met a small circle of lesbians and gay men whose lives centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks — the country's LGBT scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional.

Al Jazeera in-depth (Oct 2018): government crackdown on social media — influential Facebook users ('net idols') face retribution for posts, and 'Proud to be us Laos', the country's only LGBT advocacy group, is quoted; indicates online LGBT expression operates under tightening state attention.

EEAS page (title-verified; body behind JavaScript wall): the EU celebrated International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane — diplomatic visibility for LGBT rights; no further detail retrievable.

LAO.comparisons: Pairwise: below Cambodia (0.61 — functioning NGOs, UPR engagement) and Vietnam (0.63), above China (0.53) and Myanmar (0.15).

TLS.name: Timor-Leste
TLS.summary:
Timor-Leste is workable for trans visitors — a country where same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's equality provisions have been read inclusively, and the capital hosts an annual Pride march with government participation, remarkable for a young, Catholic-majority nation. There is no legal gender recognition and services are thin, but no pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence is documented, and the small community operates openly.

For a visitor: no documented risk pattern; the constraint is thin services and the absence of legal gender recognition rather than active hostility.
TLS.outOfScopeNotes: The absence of a documented police-targeting or anti-trans-violence pattern is an absence-of-evidence finding, not proof of safety. Service thinness is unquantified. Participation and endorsement claims rest on news reporting. The Catholic-majority character is a social qualifier, not a legal fact.

sources.summary: Australian Volunteers Program Pride Guide, Timor-Leste: country snapshot for volunteers — same-sex sexual acts decriminalised in 1975; the UN Human Rights Council joint statement on SOGI was adopted in 2011; Timor-Leste voted in favour of the 2013 UN resolution on vulnerability/disability... sets out the legal and policy context for living openly as a volunteer.

New Naratif (June 2018): Timor-Leste's first-ever Pride parade in 2017 drew international attention and a televised endorsement from the Prime Minister, while the report also captures day-to-day rejection (the organiser's family messages) — social-climate depth beyond the headline acceptance.

VOA (July 2018): East Timor held its second annual LGBT pride parade in Dili on July 20, cementing a regional leadership role while neighbours Indonesia and Malaysia turn hostile — the open-environment evidence for visitors.

Star Observer (July 2019): an estimated 3,000 people joined the 'Marsa Diversidade' Pride March in Dili on July 12 — six times the turnout of the 2017 first parade; President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the event ('I am a President for all people'). Quantified growth of visible acceptance.

TLS.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Panama (0.63) and Bolivia (0.63), above Cambodia (0.61) and below Moldova (0.65).

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and PNG has extreme levels of gender-based violence generally — among the world's highest documented rates. Port Moresby and Lae are dangerous cities for everyone; tribal-justice dynamics and police brutality affect marginalised people severely. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and sorcery-accusation violence shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in the Pacific.
PNG.outOfScopeNotes: General security conditions affect all travelers severely; criminalisation is the trans-relevant mechanism.

sources.summary: ADB publication landing page: 'Assessment of the Legal Status of Sexual and Gender Minorities in 17 Countries in Asia and the Pacific' (content dated 17 May 2024) lists Papua New Guinea among its 17 assessed countries, with keywords including decriminalization and SOGIESC inclusion; the fetched landing page itself carries no PNG-specific finding (full report required).

HRW commentary (27 Jan 2009): PNG violence-accountability climate — a mob stripped, beat with hot iron rods and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded 50+ sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008 with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations (linked to HIV deaths) used to hide murders and mitigate sentences; police routinely take no action.

ABC News (8 Oct 2014): Hanuabada village on Port Moresby's outskirts is a safe haven for PNG's gay and transgender community — residents live openly, transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation, while in Port Moresby gay/trans people are commonly raped or beaten, sometimes by police (documentary maker Vlad Sokhin, who found the village while travelling).

The Guardian (13 Jan 2017) on HRW's annual world-report assessment of PNG: the government of Peter O'Neill has failed to protect women and children and to respond to corruption and police violence — 'police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse'.

Guardian Nigeria (reprint): describes Hanuabada ('big village', built over the sea) as a pocket of tolerance where the gay community is accepted — set against PNG where sex between men is illegal and stigma/violence widespread (a 24-year-old gay man recounts being pelted with stones and bottles); campaigners say attitudes shift with exposure to the LGBT community.

PNG.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
PNG.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Cameroon (0.21 — both pair criminalisation with extreme ambient violence), above Nigeria (0.19) and below Egypt (0.22).

There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and violence driven by accusations of harmful spiritual practices shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

BWA.name: Botswana
BWA.summary:
Botswana is workable for trans visitors — Africa's strongest judicial record after South Africa. The High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2019 (Letsweletse Motshidiemang v AG, upheld 2021); the Court of Appeal ordered the government to register LEGABIBO; and trans people have won document-change cases (ND v Attorney General, 2017). Draft 2024 constitutional changes even contemplate intersex rights. Implementation lags the rulings (SALC documents unsatisfactory compliance), social conservatism persists, and there is no general LGR statute — but the courts are a genuine protection, unique in the region.

For a visitor: decriminalised, functioning courts, moderate social hostility.
BWA.outOfScopeNotes: LGR requires litigation per-case; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: SALC, Digashu & Mmolai-Chalmers (20 May 2024): Botswana's precedent wins — 2016 Court of Appeal ordered registration of LEGABIBO (freedom of association, expression, assembly), a 2017 High Court ordered the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male (dignity and humanity), and the 2021 Court of Appeal decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct — yet implementation across Botswana and Namibia 'has not been satisfactory so far'.

Alta Advisory (18 Jun 2024): Botswana's draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities; in June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep 'intersex' and 'same-sex' distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process, but the intersex provision signals momentum toward broader LGBTQI+ protection.

UN UPR outcome, 43rd session (May 2023): Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendations to repeal Penal Code Section 167 (same-sex conduct between women) and to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition — 'a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced' (para 570); abortion-decriminalisation recommendation also declined.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana: general human-rights assessment (violence against women, prison conditions, San discrimination) - the LGBT section documents the then-criminalised status and societal discrimination.

LEGABIBO official site: Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health/HIV work (e.g., World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong), with Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources — a functioning, legally registered community infrastructure (registration won in the 2016 Court of Appeal order).

The Independent (19 Dec 2017): Botswana's High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time — Tshepo Ricki Kgositau won a female identity card after a four-year legal battle (gender confirmation surgery December 2016), dedicating the victory to 'every single trans diverse person in Botswana'. A landmark for legal gender recognition in the country.

Human Rights Watch (24 Jan 2018): previewed the coming Botswana constitutional challenge to the colonial-era 'carnal knowledge' law (hearing set for March 2018) as one of the year's key LGBT court fronts alongside India and Kenya. replaced: colonial sodomy laws struck down 11 Jun 2019 (upheld on appeal 29 Nov 2021); trans legal-gender right confirmed 2017-22.

BWA.tangentialFactors: The 2019 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
BWA.localsOnly: Document-change rights exist only via per-case litigation (ND v AG 2017); there is no general LGR statute — resident-facing; implementation gaps documented by SALC.
BWA.comparisons: Pairwise: just below South Africa (0.66 — SA has constitutional protection and fuller infrastructure; BWA's recent jurisprudence is comparable but its implementation record is weaker) and above Serbia (0.64).

NAM.name: Namibia
NAM.summary:
Namibia demands real caution from trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 Digashu recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 High Court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (SALC). Windhoek has a small organised community (Equal Namibia); police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
NAM.outOfScopeNotes: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Washington Blade op-ed (22 May 2024) by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre: Namibia's Supreme Court in May 2023 ordered the government to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the Immigration Act, but compliance has failed — immigration officials tell litigant Digashu himself that the ruling covers only case couples (he receives a visitor's visa on every exit), and gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than 'all persons'. A hostile parliamentary marriage-bill response and misleading media amplified the non-implementation. Documents the enforcement gap between pro-equality rulings and administrative practice.

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - regional framework document; Namibia's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Namibia' (2017): constitutional analysis - Article 10 omits gender identity/sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the UN Human Rights Committee; section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per the Legal Assistance Centre (2015).

Mambaonline (28 May 2018): Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May (IDAHOT) at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. ORN director Friedel Dausab: 'It is a first.' The article notes the colonial-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence in 1990, and recalls 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations urging SOGI non-discrimination legislation.

Mambaonline (12 December 2018): dozens marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund on 8 December for LGBTI+ Pride — described as the 'biggest pride event' to date in Namibia. Dated evidence of a visible, tolerated public community presence.

Daily Maverick (26 June 2014): a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original. Documents organised political hostility to LGBT rights in the record's political environment.

NAM.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct technically remains criminalised under the common law (unenforced) — a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 legislative backlash signals trajectory.
NAM.localsOnly: The earlier document-change court wins are per-case resident litigation; implementation gaps documented by SALC are resident-facing.
NAM.comparisons: Pairwise: below Botswana (0.65 — BWA decriminalised; NAM retains the common-law crime and legislative backlash) and above Brazil (0.55, tie).
NAM.blindSummary:
This nation demands real caution from trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 high court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (by a regional legal organisation). The capital has a small organised community; police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
NAM.blindOutOfScope: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: An op-ed (22 May 2024) by two lawyers of a regional legal organisation: the supreme court in May 2023 ordered the government to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the immigration act, but compliance has failed — immigration officials tell the litigant himself that the ruling covers only case couples (he receives a visitor's visa on every exit), and gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than all persons. A hostile parliamentary marriage-bill response and misleading media amplified the non-implementation. Documents the enforcement gap between pro-equality rulings and administrative practice.

A regional development programme report (December 2024): regional framework document; this nation's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

A regional legal organisation's report (2017): constitutional analysis — the constitution's equality article omits gender identity or sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the international human-rights committee; section 7B of the births, marriages and deaths registration act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per a legal assistance centre.

A news outlet (28 May 2018): an LGBTI organisation opened this nation's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre on 17 May — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. The organisation's director said: 'It is a first.' The article notes the historic-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence, and recalls 2016 international human-rights committee recommendations urging non-discrimination legislation.

A news outlet (12 December 2018): dozens marched in two cities on 8 December for LGBTI+ Pride — described as the 'biggest pride event' to date in this nation. Dated evidence of a visible, tolerated public community presence.

A news outlet (26 June 2014): a local version of a neighbouring nation's political movement was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the original. Documents organised political hostility to LGBT rights in this nation's political environment.

NAM.blindTangential: Male same-sex conduct technically remains criminalised under the common law (unenforced) — a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 legislative backlash signals trajectory.

MUS.name: Mauritius
MUS.summary:
Mauritius is workable for trans visitors — the Indian Ocean's most liveable jurisdiction. The Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct; the Equal Opportunities Act covers discrimination; and in 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan competed as the first trans woman in Miss Universe Mauritius — a public milestone met with national discussion rather than violence. There is no legal gender recognition law (a barrier highlighted by AfricLaw), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.
MUS.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and recognition gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct — advances noted for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with 'less evident' progress for trans or intersex people. No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised; Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned; legal gender recognition not possible and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Pride held since 2005 with counter-protesters; during the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

AfricLaw (23 August 2024, Lakshita Kanhiya): analyses the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan — the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 — against the country's legal obstacles: the Civil Status Act of 1981 and Central Population Database as the framework denying recognition, plus pervasive stigmatisation, with activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G. Concludes legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone.

US State Department 2016 Country Report — Mauritius: Section 250 sodomy statute almost never reached same-sex couples in court (sodomy references overwhelmingly arose in heterosexual divorce cases as an aggravating factor); documents societal discrimination, with LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing. Dated pre-2023 baseline for the record.

Young Queer Alliance policy brief (July 2021): 'Administrative recognition of Trans People in Mauritius' - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law.

MUS.tangentialFactors: The 2023 decriminalisation ruling removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
MUS.localsOnly: No LGR law — resident-facing gap highlighted by AfricLaw.
MUS.comparisons: Pairwise: below Seychelles-region comparators and level with Latvia (0.69)/Israel (0.69) — above Hungary (0.68).
MUS.blindSummary:

There is no legal gender recognition law (a gap highlighted by a regional legal-aid organisation), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.
MUS.blindOutOfScope: The absence of legal gender recognition and related documentation gaps are resident-facing.

MUS.blindTangential: The 2023 decriminalisation ruling removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

SYC.name: Seychelles
SYC.summary: Seychelles is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent archipelago with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
SYC.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the tiny population.

sources.summary: Cornell Law gender-justice page: under the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) Section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences. The Constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Art 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Art 27).

PinkNews, 18 May 2016: Seychelles repealed colonial-era Penal Code Section 151, which had allowed up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex sex - framed as the popular holiday destination 'opening its arms to LGBT people'.

Travel guide: notes the 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts as a significant victory for the islands, while advising both local residents and tourists to stay vigilant and informed about the current legal and social landscape - practical visitor guidance for the destination.

Erasing 76 Crimes, 27 September 2024: a newly revised law calls for increased prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward victims' sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability - per the Human Dignity Trust, after South Africa Seychelles is only the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation. Before 2016 the penal code punished male same-sex intimacy with up to 14 years.

SYC.tangentialFactors: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
SYC.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Poland/Croatia/Costa Rica (0.72 — different profiles; Seychelles lacks their legal infrastructure but has lower hostility), above Mauritius (0.70 — MUS has the Equal Opportunities Act and 2023 decriminalisation ruling; SYC edges it on ambient safety) and below Chile (0.74).

SEN.name: Senegal
SEN.summary:
Senegal is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “unnatural acts” (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 for “false news” after accusing the Prime Minister of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — Dakar's scene is deeply underground.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.
SEN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; mob violence is documented climate.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity (Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, up to 5 years' imprisonment). (only the opening was retrievable)

76crimes (16 Jul 2024): anti-LGBT forces in Senegal are pushing for 15-year prison sentences for gay sex, up from the current maximum of five years — a debate running since 2020, with abuses against LGBT+ people commonplace in the West African nation.

BBC News: two men were jailed in Senegal for criticising opposition leader Ousmane Sonko — months and fined 100,000 CFA francs ($165, £130) each. They had been angered that Mr Sonko had allowed a visiting French politician to express his support for same-sex marriages. Homosexual acts are banned in the mainly Muslim West African country and are punishable by up to five years in prison. The political activist and the preacher were arrested two weeks ago after posting a video attacking Mr Sonko for giving a platform t

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Senegal: documents preelectoral violence, torture, and 'violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons' among major human-rights problems.

76crimes (24 Sep 2018): four LGBT people — two women and two men — were detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature' amid a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, triggered after videos circulated.

Metro (Nov 2023): a man's body was dug up and burned in the street in Senegal after it was revealed he was gay — exhumed and set on fire in the street after locals are said to have found out he was gay, in a case that has shocked the West African country. Four men have been arrested in connection with the incident, though images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathering around the fire. The 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, had been buried in Léona Niassene cemetery i

SEN.tangentialFactors: “Unnatural acts” criminalised (up to 5 years, both sexes) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SEN.comparisons: Pairwise: below Malaysia (0.28 — comparable criminalisation-plus-mob climate) and above Pakistan (0.26) and Côte d'Ivoire (0.34 — CIV decriminalised but has the 2024 hunt-down violence wave; SEN has statutory criminalisation but no equivalent mob-hunt wave; net SEN slightly worse).

CIV.name: Côte d'Ivoire
CIV.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: the only prison-axis source in this record — Human Rights Watch's Côte d'Ivoire country page — contains no document, case or report on transgender prisoners, nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary/segregation practice in Ivorian prisons. In a state with no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection and an inadequate police response to organised targeting, an undocumented placement practice cannot be read as a protected one: a detained trans visitor would be held in a prison system with no documented housing standard and no documented recourse.
CIV.outOfScopeNotes:
The main late-2024 reporting on the hunt wave was not retrievable at research time — the news article returns a hard error — so the wave's details rest on the source summary and corroborating official reporting. A freshness flag notes that 2023-era reports cited criminalisation language; the current source text no longer contains it and whether such provisions persist is unresolved and needs rechecking.

Prison axis: the only prison-axis source is thin — Human Rights Watch's Côte d'Ivoire country page has no usable finding on where trans detainees are housed ('LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link, and no HRW publication is listed on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice in Ivorian prisons) — and with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, that absence cannot be read as a signal of any protected placement standard.

US State Department 2023 report, Côte d'Ivoire: same-sex conduct not criminalised, but LGBTQI+ persons faced violence — three community deaths reported in the year; police responses to non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim; a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire: post-electoral-crisis context (3,000 deaths, sexual violence, displacement) - general human-rights baseline with limited LGBT-specific content.

Critical African Studies (2015), Thomann & Corey-Boulet, 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis': travestis (born anatomically male, living as women) face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and have been underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them; examines isolation after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

MLI.name: Mali
MLI.summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.
MLI.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 penal code application to trans expression is via indecency provisions; drafting vagueness noted by HDT.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (6 November 2024): Mali’s new penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with harsh penalties; previously legal but vague "public indecency" provisions (Article 225) were used against LGBT people and gender-nonconforming expressions, and the new law bans the undefined "promotion" of homosexuality, greatly expanding who can be prosecuted.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Mali's new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Conversation (15 January 2025), interview with anthropologist Christophe Broqua: Mali’s new penal code — announced October 2024, in force 13 December 2024 — criminalises homosexuality and any citizen seen to encourage it, a sharp escalation under the military junta alongside clampdowns on opposition and media.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Mali: official assessment - same-sex conduct not criminalised but significant societal stigma; violence and instability from armed groups.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Mali: documents gender inequality, FGM, corruption, and 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' among other human-rights problems.

BFA.name: Burkina Faso
BFA.summary:
Burkina Faso is dangerous for trans visitors. In July 2024 the military junta approved a revised Personal and Family Code criminalising homosexuality — Burkina Faso had never previously outlawed it. The junta (Traoré) has clamped down on opposition and media, promised elections have not been held, and much of the country faces jihadist insurgency. Enforcement details of the new law remain unclear (HDT notes drafting uncertainty), but the direction and the absence of any institutional recourse are unambiguous.

For a visitor: new criminalisation under a junta, plus severe general security conditions.
BFA.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 family-code criminalisation is new; enforcement practice not yet documented.

sources.summary: BBC (11 July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta announced a ban on homosexual acts — homosexuality had never before been outlawed in the socially conservative West African state; part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage/family law. the ban entered into force as criminal-code law on 1 Sep 2025. For this record: the decisive policy-reversal date, later confirmed in force.

Africanews (11 Jul 2024, updated 13 Aug 2024): the junta's council approved a decree for a new Personal and Family Code (CPF) that 'enshrines the ban on homosexuality', per a presidency statement, joining the ~22 of 54 African states disallowing same-sex relations. entered into force 1 Sep 2025. For this record: legislative vehicle and date for the criminalisation.

Human Rights Watch (3 Sep 2025): the Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the law on 1 September 2025 making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence — two to five years' imprisonment plus fines — enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space. For this record: the operative criminalisation date and penalties; core current-state evidence.

LGBTQ Nation (Sep 2025): the junta unanimously passed the law; Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala states prison 'between two and five years as well as fines' for perpetrators of 'homosexual or similar practices', and that foreigners will be DEPORTED under the law; junta rule since Sep 2022. For this record: penalties plus explicit deportation exposure for foreign nationals — directly visitor-relevant.

BFA.tangentialFactors: The 2024 family-code criminalisation targets homosexuality — trans people are captured via birth-sex legal status and the law's broad drafting.
BFA.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Egypt/Algeria/Uzbekistan (0.22), above Mali (0.20 — MLI's code is harsher and more explicitly enforced) and below Ghana (0.24).

MOZ.name: Mozambique
MOZ.summary:
Mozambique demands real caution from trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside Maputo is significant, and the Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the north.
MOZ.outOfScopeNotes: Cabo Delgado insurgency is a general risk; LGR absence is resident-facing.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the 2015 penal code; no legal gender recognition procedure exists; societal attitudes broadly neutral but LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and employment/education barriers; the 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations then disappointed. Freshness confirmed: the new 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection that had existed.

GlobalGayz archive (2006-2011): dated milestones — first newspaper article arguing gay rights (Agencia de Informacao, 7 July 2006), Maputo men petitioning parliament, the LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, refugee deaths en route to South Africa; documents early organising under the colonial-era law.
Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2016) from Afrobarometer: Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant — 56% would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour (vs Uganda/Burkina Faso/Niger at 5%).

Global Voices (28 Nov 2017): after a decade of blocked applications (since 2008), the Constitutional Council — supreme court equivalent — ruled Lambda Mozambique's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration of the country's only LGBT organisation.

Guardian (30 June 2015): Mozambique's new penal code erased the colonial 'vices against nature' provision; Lambda (not yet officially registered at the time) pivoted to anti-discrimination lobbying; Lambda's Carina Capitine: the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination.

RWA.name: Rwanda
RWA.summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations).

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman — a partner-travel consideration for a trans visitor.
RWA.outOfScopeNotes: Sweep detentions are documented against trans persons specifically (2025 HRF submission). No source in this record covers visa or border document screening for trans visitors, and implementation practice of the 2024 NGO law is unverified. The 2016 presidential statement is dated and may not reflect current policy.

AGO.name: Angola
AGO.summary:
Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

If a trans visitor is arrested, the consequence axis is largely undocumented: the 2024 shadow report — the only prison-axis source in this record — contains no data on where trans prisoners are housed in Angola (nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice). Its closest custody finding is the June 2024 case of a transgender woman in Viana (Luanda) attacked by police because of her gender identity, physically injured, arbitrarily detained and subjected to degrading treatment (under investigation by the judicial military police of the Provincial Command of Luanda; police custody, no prison-placement information). In a legal system with no gender recognition and under-investigated violence, an undocumented placement practice cannot be assumed safe: what is on record is police violence against a trans person in custody.
AGO.outOfScopeNotes:
Statutory protections vs implementation gap documented by Angolan CSOs.

Prison axis: no Angolan rule, case or practice is documented on trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement finding, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice; the June 2024 case ended in police custody rather than prison placement, and what happens to trans people held after charge is unrecorded in these sources.

sources.summary: Shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter, submitted for the African Commission's 81st session (Oct-Nov 2024, Banjul) by Angolan organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA, Diversidade Masculina and others) with ILGA/Synergia support: documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people in Angola.

Submission by Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights pre-session (74th, review of Angola): foregrounds the Angolan context for lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people ahead of the state's review — a formal international-review channel raising discrimination and health-access issues.

Southern Africa Litigation Centre chapter 'Transgender Rights in Angola': maps constitutional protection gaps — Article 23 does not list gender or sexual orientation as prohibited discrimination grounds — and locates identity, privacy, liberty, torture-protection and expression rights across Title II articles of the Angolan Constitution.

VICE continental overview (Oct 28, 2019): Angola singled out as having gone furthest among African reforms — not only removing the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision but also criminalising discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services; contrasts legislative drafting strategies across the continent.

BBC profile (Apr 12, 2012): kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, becomes a mainstream star at 25 in what the article describes as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour — evidence of visible trans presence alongside formal criminalisation at that time.

PinkNews (Feb 11, 2021): Angola's decriminalisation took effect on this date — the law adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era ban describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and made discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds punishable by prison.

AGO.tangentialFactors:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised and sexual-orientation discrimination prohibited — of direct concern mainly to trans visitors who have relationships or are perceived as same-sex-active while travelling.

Legal context: the 2020 Penal Code that decriminalised same-sex conduct also criminalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment — a statutory sanction the same 2024 report documents as failing to stop persistent discrimination in health, education and employment.
AGO.localsOnly:
Trans people have no legal gender recognition; the implementation gap (health, education, employment discrimination, under-investigated violence) falls on residents.

The June 2024 Viana incident is a residents' case: a transgender woman attacked by police because of her gender identity, physically injured, arbitrarily detained by Esquadra 43 and subjected to degrading treatment, with the case under investigation by the judicial military police of the Provincial Command of Luanda — police custody with no prison-placement information produced.
AGO.comparisons: Pairwise: above Mozambique (0.56 — AGO's statutory package is stronger) and below India (0.58). For a visitor: no legal exposure and formal anti-discrimination law; social hostility moderate-high outside Luanda.

COD.name: DR Congo
COD.summary:
DR Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised — but the reality on the ground is severe insecurity: mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented, police extortion is routine, parts of the country are an active conflict zone (M23), and LGBT organisations (Savie asbl in Bukavu) report systematic violations in their 2024 universal periodic review submission. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure; Kinshasa's small scene is underground.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but outing risks mob violence with no effective protection anywhere in the country. Public same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code, rarely invoked), and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned, so a trans visitor's partner has no recognition.
COD.outOfScopeNotes: Conflict conditions in the east are general; mob justice against LGBT people is documented in universal periodic review submissions. No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors. The Article 176 indecency provision is rarely invoked but its contemporary charging practice is verified only through the 2025 freshness confirmation that it is still occasionally used.

sources.summary: Stakeholder submission to the DRC's 5th-cycle UPR (March 2024) by Savie asbl NGO and others: the DRC does not criminalise same-sex relations but neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights; public displays of same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code: 'anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions...').

Human Rights Watch (4 Dec 2017): 120+ interviews (incl. nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials, 21 M23 fighters) document security forces recruiting ex-M23 fighters from Uganda/Rwanda in Oct–Dec 2016 and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi — background on state violence and impunity in the security environment; no LGBT-specific content.

GayOut travel guide for DR Congo: rates the country 'High Risk for LGBTQ+' - no explicit national criminalisation but Article 176 ('indecent acts') and local ordinances applied to LGBTQ people; armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity; state authority collapse means legal protections are theoretical.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror) on LGBTQ rights in the DRC: same-sex activity legal for both sexes (never outlawed, even under Belgian rule), equal age of consent; but no gender-identity recognition, no relationship recognition (same-sex marriage banned constitutionally since 2006), limited protections; church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral; public same-sex affection can trigger prosecution under indecency provisions.

Queer In The World (updated 3 Dec 2023; covers both Congos): DRC-specific parts — homosexuality legal but LGBT expression censored with imprisonment exposure; violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people reported involving police, security forces and army; no legal gender change for trans people; advises visitors discretion and low profile.

ZMB.name: Zambia
ZMB.summary:
Zambia is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) with documented recent enforcement: Amnesty International's November 2024 campaign highlights Madalitso Zulu, serving a 15-year sentence with hard labour; Amnesty's 2024 regional report documents rising hostility in Zambia. There is no legal gender recognition, religious leaders lead anti-LGBT mobilisation, and police are perpetrators more than protectors.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest; the documented serving-sentence case shows courts impose maximum terms.
ZMB.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; trans people are captured via birth-sex status and indecency provisions.

sources.summary: Amnesty International campaign story (26 Nov 2024) 'Madalitso's story': a Zambian medical professional —36, three years behind bars by Nov 2024 — imprisoned for consensual same-sex conduct; his medical expertise lost to a health system short of workers; frames individual persecution of LGBTI people in Zambia.

US State Dept 2021 Country Report, Zambia: government continued to reject recognition/protection of LGBTQI+ rights; police perpetrated violence and verbal/physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation; LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of law; advocacy groups report police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals (fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha / $30-$900); discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued.

HRW report 'Dignity Debased' (12 Jul 2016): documents forced anal examinations in at least eight countries including ZAMBIA — less frequent there than Egypt/Tunisia but prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal exams as court evidence in sodomy cases (incl. a mass trial of ~20 men); recommends worldwide ban; such exams are treated by victims as painful, degrading sexual violence.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Zambia: no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons; when police detain LGBTQI+ members they often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release; no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, but President Hichilema's 30 May statement opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults; societal violence and employment/housing/education/health discrimination continued.

ZWE.name: Zimbabwe
ZWE.summary:
Zimbabwe is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2006 Criminal Law Act criminalises sodomy (up to 1 year — a lighter formal penalty than neighbours, though indecency provisions add exposure), and Amnesty's 2024 report documents shrinking civic space threatening LGBT organising (GALZ operates under pressure; its offices have been raided historically). There is no legal gender recognition, political rhetoric is hostile, and mob violence is documented — but prosecution under the sodomy law is rarer than in Zambia, and a small organised community persists openly enough to litigate.

For a visitor: statutory exposure exists but enforcement is sporadic; social hostility is the main risk.
ZWE.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; enforcement pattern is sporadic.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women (sodomy and 'acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent'). (only the opening was retrievable)

Amnesty International report, 9 January 2024, index AFR 01/7533/2024: 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries'. The cached copy is only the title/index page: it fixes the report's date, scope and thesis but contains no Zimbabwe-specific passages, so it cannot carry incident-level claims — treat it as the report's existence record, not its evidence.

New Zimbabwe, 9 July 2018: the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender/non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty ('nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups'), issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor: formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Mabvurira et al., 'The politics of sexual identities in Zimbabwe: A Social Work perspective?' (Int'l Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012): homosexuals live secluded lives due to prejudice; argues homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins', tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe; social workers should promote social justice for the gay community.
Taylor & Francis (Journal of Homosexuality): academic article on homosexuality in Zimbabwe (page body is navigation; headline only).

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe) official site: voluntary membership organisation established 1990, now 4,000+ community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups, 4 resource centres. Services include legal support (explicitly including for 'sodomy' arrests), counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. For the record: documented local support infrastructure — legal aid and counselling reachable despite criminalisation, useful for an LGBTI traveller needing assistance.

MWI.name: Malawi
MWI.summary: Malawi is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) AND Human Dignity Trust lists Malawi as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. A moratorium on prosecutions has held since 2014, but in June 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the ban — a case brought partly by a local trans woman and her Dutch partner — and religious leaders led nationwide anti-LGBT marches in 2023. Discrimination and violence are regular despite the moratorium.
MWI.outOfScopeNotes: Prosecution moratorium is informal and revocable; the 2024 ruling keeps the statute fully alive.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch dispatch (11 July 2024): Malawi's Constitutional Court on 28 June 2024 rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 — a three-member panel dismissed the application brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. The sections carry up to 14 years' imprisonment; faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament; HRW called it a 'dark day' and warned of heightened arbitrary-arrest and violence risks.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Malawi: documents the July 2011 protest killings (20 dead), harsh prisons, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons'.

Human Rights Watch (26 October 2018), releasing the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre plus lawyers, activists and officials: police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people, sometimes assaulting them, and medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds (a trans man beaten then refused treatment; nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests). Men face up to 14 years and women five years under sections 153/156; the 2012 justice-minister moratorium on arrests was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after religious leaders' litigation, leaving its legality contested. People whose gender expression differs from expectations are 'most likely to be targeted'.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 December 2015): two men arrested in Malawi on 7 December on homosexuality charges suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion and humiliation by community police — forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photos distributed on social media. CEDEP's Gift Trapence contrasts the arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services. Documents the arrest-and-abuse pattern under the penal code.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 April 2018): police arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, in Mzuzu for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 ('indecent practices between males') rather than section 153 — apparently to circumvent the six-year moratorium on anti-gay arrests while both laws faced a constitutional challenge. Police spokespersons confirmed the custody. Evidence of law-enforcement attempts to elude the moratorium.

MWI.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years, moratorium since 2014) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the moratorium is informal and revocable.
MWI.comparisons: Pairwise: above Zambia (0.24 — ZMB has an active 15-year serving case; MWI's moratorium holds) and below Zimbabwe (0.27, comparable). The gender-expression criminalisation listing is what places MWI in the mid-0.2s rather than higher.

SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.summary:
Sudan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 152 of the Penal Code criminalises gender nonconformity directly; sodomy carries life imprisonment (capital/corporal punishment removed in 2020 reforms); and Cairo 52 documents state violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings. Since April 2023 the country has been in a catastrophic civil war (SAF vs RSF) with documented mass atrocities — the conflict intensifies every risk and eliminates any recourse. There is no LGR and no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity plus one of the world's worst active conflicts.
SDN.outOfScopeNotes: War conditions affect all; Art 152 is trans-specific.

Gender-nonconformity framing for visitor risk.

Rainbow Sudan — Sudan's community magazine: runs sections on LGBTI rights in Sudan (history and analysis), a profile of Sudan and LGBTI organisations, i.e. documents an organised local community presence. Landing/index page: thin for current findings.

SSD.name: South Sudan

The 2008 Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years), and Human Dignity Trust lists South Sudan as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. The country has barely emerged from civil war, state institutions are vestigial outside Juba, communal violence is endemic, and there is no documented LGBT community infrastructure whatsoever — no organisation can operate openly. No trans-specific case is documented because documentation itself is nearly impossible.

For a visitor: statutory risk plus a near-total absence of protective institutions.

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.summary:
Somalia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: Al-Shabaab controls significant territory and applies its interpretation of sharia, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in Somalia.
SOM.outOfScopeNotes: Fragmented authority means enforcement varies; Al-Shabaab areas apply capital punishment.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Somalia: criminalizes 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex', 3 months' to 3 years' imprisonment, no official reports of enforcement available; under local interpretations of sharia, homosexuality is punishable by death; no known state-conducted executions of that sort reported. Impunity generally remained the norm.

[report excerpt] — non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.

ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.summary: Eritrea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 310(1) of the 2015 Penal Code criminalises “homosexual conduct” (up to 7 years), there are no anti-discrimination protections of any kind, and Eritrea is among the world's most closed states — indefinite national service, mass arbitrary detention, no independent media, no civil society, and no way to document conditions. Eritrea has rejected every SOGI recommendation at every UPR cycle. Nothing is known about trans people in Eritrea because nothing can be known — the absence of data reflects total informational control.
ERI.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation absence reflects totalitarian informational control.

sources.summary: Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Article 310(1) of the penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' with up to 7 years' imprisonment — inherited from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code and retained with an enhanced sentence in the first post-independence penal code (adopted 2015).

No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.
