HTI.name: Haiti
HTI.summary:
Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the national government has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of the capital (Port-au-Prince), the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary.

The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal. A 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity, particularly in the capital; freshness confirms trans people remain exposed to vagrancy-law fines with zero protection or hate-crime coverage.
HTI.outOfScopeNotes: Collapse of national governance is general; mob violence against LGBT people is documented but not quantified. The status of the 2017 senate action at the other legislative chamber is unverified in the sources. No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (25 Nov 2019): Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, Haiti's national LGBTQ advocacy organization, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince; poisoning reports were unconfirmed by the Blade. ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. The piece cites the US State Department's 2018 report that attitudes in Haiti 'remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince' — a direct climate warning for visibly trans visitors.

HRW World Report 2018 (Haiti chapter): LGBT persons continued to face high levels of discrimination. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs (a good-conduct certificate employers and universities require) on grounds of homosexuality; in August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy with up to 3 years' prison and a ~US$8,000 fine for parties. Both awaited a Chamber of Deputies vote as of November 2017 — status must be verified before relying on them.

FJI.name: Fiji
FJI.summary: Fiji is workable for trans visitors — the Pacific islands' leader. Same-sex relations decriminalised in 2010; the 2013 Constitution bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity AND expression — reportedly the only constitution in the world with that explicit pairing. Counterweights: no gender-marker change mechanism, and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network documents high rates of violence and harassment against trans people. Suva has an organised community (Haus of Khameleon, Rainbow Pride Foundation).
FJI.outOfScopeNotes: Constitutional protection vs documented street violence gap.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex conduct decriminalised 2010 (Crimes Act); Fiji among the first countries to ban SOGI discrimination constitutionally — SO protection in the 1997 Constitution, reinstated and expanded to gender identity and expression in the 2013 Constitution; workplace SO protections since 2007; health professionals barred from trying to change sexual orientation. Traditional third-gender vaka sa lewa lewa recognised culturally but no legal gender recognition route; no same-sex marriage/civil unions (Marriage Act 2002: one man, one woman); intersex bodily autonomy unprotected. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal per overview flag, LGR No, orgs cannot register.

Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Fiji' (2023): the 2013 Constitution's discrimination protection on gender identity and expression is described as unique worldwide, yet legislative/policy frameworks permit NO gender-marker change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities — headline constitutional protection with zero implementation for trans people, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.

Human Rights Watch (11 Apr 2005): two men (one an Australian tourist) received two-year prison sentences under colonial-era Penal Code Art 175 (up to 14 years) for consensual sex; HRW urged charges dropped and release, citing Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on SO discrimination (Fiji one of first two countries worldwide, with South Africa); the judge called the acts 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Documents the enforcement era before the 2006 no-arrest policy and 2010 decriminalisation.

PinkNews (10 Jul 2006): the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex will no longer be arrested — the practical end of enforcement two years before the Crimes Act 2010 decriminalisation; NZ AIDS Foundation (Exec Dir Rachael Le Mesurier) linked criminalisation to undergrounding of sex and HIV spread.

GlobalGayz country page (pre-2013, undated): Fiji timeline — 1997 second country in the world to enshrine SO non-discrimination; 2006 no-arrest policy confirmed; 2007 state of emergency ousted PM; 2009 Constitution abolished; 1 Feb 2010 full decriminalisation under Crimes Act 2010; Marriage Act 2002 bars same-sex marriage; ~322-island archipelago. Legacy-era overview — its claim that SOGI discrimination was not banned predates the 2013 Constitution.

Sydney Morning Herald (14 Apr 2005): PM Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in 'the conservative Christian nation', days after an Australian tourist and a Fijian man received two-year sentences — the political/religious climate context behind the sodomy-law enforcement that HRW protested.

WSM.name: Samoa
WSM.summary:
Samoa is workable for trans visitors — anchored by one of the world's most institutionalized third-gender traditions. Fa'afafine (and fa'atama) are culturally embedded: recognized as heirs to customary land and eligible for matai (chiefly) titles within fa'a Sāmoa, organized nationally through the Samoa Fa'afafine Association (a formal UN UPR stakeholder since 1987), and visible through a famous pageant culture. Samoa repealed its colonial-era “female impersonation” crime in 2013, so no law touches gender expression itself.

The remaining negatives are modest for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition (both resident-facing); documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine (APTN peer-led study — primarily resident/domestic contexts); isolated police-harassment reports (2 respondents, no convictions); and village fono councils that enforce conservative dress and behaviour norms. The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for a fraction of visitors, not a trans-universal one.
WSM.outOfScopeNotes: Fa’afafine cultural embedding is informal protection; criminalisation unenforced.

sources.summary: APTN (9 May 2024): Nadi, Fiji convening gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua, PNG — documents the Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum (fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga, fakafifine in Niue, etc.) as living community infrastructure Samoa participates in.

Samoa Fa'afafine Association (SFA) stakeholder report for Samoa's UPR (39th session, 2021): 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa' - describes the culturally unique third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.

Schmidt, 'Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa' (Intersections, Aug 2001): fa'afafine = 'in the manner of a woman'; academic analysis argues fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality/transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone — background for how visitors may encounter the term.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fa'afafine of Samoa (with American Samoa and Tokelau) among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

It sits level with Greece — its lack of EU-style institutional recourse (a resident-weighted factor) is the only axis where European comparators hold an edge, and Estonia (0.77) keeps a 0.02 edge on that basis alone.

TON.name: Tonga
TON.summary: Tonga demands real caution from trans visitors. The Criminal Offences Act criminalises sodomy (10 years, plus corporal punishment on paper — unenforced in recent years) and also criminalises males “impersonating a female” while soliciting — a direct trans-expression statute on the books. Against that: Tonga has a visible leiti (trans-feminine) community with the famous Miss Galaxy pageant (documented by the Washington Post in 2024), family and church networks that are devout but not systematically violent, and no documented recent prosecutions.
TON.outOfScopeNotes: The male-impersonation statute is on the books but unenforced.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (timeout); the underlying Washington Post piece (Aug 2024) covers Tonga's trans pageant and LGBT rights.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Tonga: domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption were the most prevalent problems; no reports of government abuses; the LGBT section notes the criminalisation of sodomy but rare enforcement.

Washington Blade (Feb 2018): Cyclone Gita 'tore off' part of the roof of Tonga's LGBTI drop-in center and shelter on Tongatapu (Nuku'alofa) with winds over 120 mph, damaging bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans — documents the fragility of the country's only community shelter infrastructure.

KIR.name: Kiribati
KIR.summary: Kiribati is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; tiny, isolated, church-dominated society with no visible community infrastructure.

sources.summary: 76crimes reprint of 2015 US State Department report, Kiribati section: consensual sex between men illegal, 5–14 years' imprisonment depending on offence, no prosecutions reported; constitution bars discrimination by race/national origin/colour (observed) with land ownership restricted to I-Kiribati; gender discrimination prohibited only in employment and poorly enforced; no SOGI non-discrimination law and no reported societal discrimination or violence.

University of Hawai'i at Manoa research guide 'Gender Identity and Sexual Identity in the Pacific and Hawai'i': resources on sexual and gender diversity across the Pacific, documenting identity expressions defined as homosexual/transgender only in Western vocabulary — including the Pinapinaaine/Binabinaaine role of Tuvalu and Kiribati (Besnier 2014, 'Gender on the edge', p. 327).

76crimes (7 Aug 2015): at the 21st-session UPR, France, Slovenia and Chile urged tiny island nation Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality — the Kiribati delegation made no response, but said it is considering Uruguay's advice to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation.

76crimes (21 Nov 2016): the UN General Assembly rejected the amendment to defund the SOGI Independent Expert mandate, 84–77; the article notes Sri Lanka and Kiribati as two countries that at the time still had anti-homosexuality laws — dated criminal-law status evidence for Kiribati.

VUT.name: Vanuatu
VUT.summary:
Vanuatu demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised) with no legal gender recognition; there is a small VPride community in Port Vila, and kastom and church conservatism — but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

Direct risk signals for visitors: in November 2024 the government moved to develop a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion, framed as contrary to constitutional and Christian values, and the Marriage Act was amended to define marriage as the union of a male and a female, so same-sex marriages cannot be registered — a partner-travel consideration.
VUT.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data: only three usable sources, no freshness re-check of the 2024 policy developments, and no source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors. The drafted policy's scope, timeline and enforcement are unverified.

sources.summary: Sista (Oct 2016): VPride Foundation and Vanuatu Women's Centre's first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop (SPC-funded) established that same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes; USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case and near-invisible LGBTI court presence; VPride (est. 2014) faced church/official/chief opposition at founding.

NRU.name: Nauru
NRU.summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.summary: US Mission Geneva (Mar 2011): publishes the full text of the Joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation & gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries — Nauru is among the signatories (with Fiji, Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others). For this record: dated evidence of Nauru's diplomatic position supporting SOGI rights.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, far below top-ranked Germany/Spain at 4.88 and below most Pacific neighbours. For this record: a comparative-index placement for Nauru.

The Guardian (29 May 2016), headline-level (article body did not survive retrieval — nav shell only): 'Nauru decriminalises homosexuality and suicide' — the 1899 Queensland-derived criminal code provisions repealed, replacing them including attempted-suicide provisions. For this record: the dated decriminalisation event.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru country page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for LBTI people; Nauru supported the 2011 UN HRC Joint Statement, and its last CEDAW state report (2016) contained no LBTI-specific information. For this record: the current legal-status snapshot for trans/intersex people specifically.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nauru (Wikipedia) — Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014 gender-identity non-discrimination clause
sources.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Nauru article documents the only detention-related gender-identity provision found for Nauru: the Nauru Regional Processing Centre (RPC) Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, ban discrimination against any person based on sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within the RPC immigration-detention facility. This covers immigration detention, not Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and concerns non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex vs identity, special units, or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, nor any trans-prisoner case or ruling.

BEN.name: Benin
BEN.summary: Benin is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but 76crimes documents that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace; the Hirondelles Club provides safe housing for LGBT youth fleeing family violence. No LGR, no anti-discrimination law; community organises underground.
BEN.outOfScopeNotes: Lynching pattern is documented climate, not statute.

sources.summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (9 Apr 2024): the Hirondelles Club at Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth in Benin since about 2020 — a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; the report's framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. For this record: the current statutory baseline — legal but entirely unshielded, no recognition pathway.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. For this record: official US assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. For this record: regional religious-institution hostility including Benin — dated 2015, treat as context not current-state evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile (fetched this session): Togo criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine — the core exposure fact for a visitor.

AAEC Togo + Synergia alternative report to the UN Human Rights Committee (June 2021): the Togolese association works on HIV within MSM-TG populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016-2020, documents LGBT rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa, and provides legal/judicial support to victims — evidence of an active civil-society documentation and assistance channel.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Togo: the law prohibits 'acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex' (widely understood as same-sex conduct) and also the 'promotion of same-sex conduct', reaching advocacy and gender identity expression; the law was enforced, and violence/threats targeting LGBTTQI persons were listed among significant human-rights issues — official current-law + enforcement read.

Washington Blade (Aug 31, 2015): interviews with LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria (conducted 14-31 March 2015) include a Togo section — the author returned to Lomé, visited the site of a 2008 attack on him, and reports the capital's police are 'particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists', a rare on-the-ground note naming TOURIST exposure.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Togo: documents security-force torture, impunity, and 'official and societal discrimination... against members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for Togo: significant issues include cruel treatment, harsh prisons, arbitrary detention, criminal libel enforcement, and 'crimes involving violence or threats of violence targeting lesbian, gay, bisexual...' persons.

NER.name: Niger
NER.summary:
Niger is dangerous for trans visitors — and newly criminalising: in March 2025 the junta's Charter of Refoundation explicitly outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the first time (Article 25). Junta rule, jihadist insurgency, no recourse.

The criminalisation is now codified: a February 2026 revision of the penal code criminalises 'indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts' (penal code article 390; 5–10 years' imprisonment and fines), same-sex marriage (article 391; 10–20 years), and LGBTQIA+ associations (article 392); article 390 also covers anyone who 'artificially change[s their] sex at birth'. The drafting is broad and confused enough that asexuality has been read as included among sanctionable conducts, per reporting on the law. Junta-state enforcement followed: from July 2026 the junta began arresting LGBTQIA+ people under the new provisions, with dozens of arrests reported within days.
NER.outOfScopeNotes: March 2025 criminalisation is brand new; enforcement undocumented.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the July 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276 (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

BBC News (December 2022): Niger's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships.

The Guardian (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, imprisoned across Niger following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026. Campaigners describe a 'witch-hunt' in a 'toxic' climate, and sources fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses.

Agence Nigérienne de Presse (1 Jun 2026): 'Niger criminalises LGBTQIA+ practice in the country' — official state-press coverage of the criminalisation provisions adopted in the 2026 penal code revision.

The law is decried as violating intersex and LGBTQIA+ human rights.

TCD.name: Chad
TCD.summary:
Chad is dangerous for trans visitors — a high-risk verdict reached on thin data, not in spite of it. Consensual same-sex conduct between adults has been criminalised since 2017 as a misdemeanour carrying up to two years' imprisonment, so a trans visitor stands under formal criminal exposure — including one travelling with a partner. There is no legal gender recognition, no recourse, no protective or community infrastructure documented, and the state operates under junta-adjacent governance.

Enforcement of the criminalisation is not documented in either direction. That gap denotes an unknown, not safety: in a state that criminalises, denies recognition, offers no recourse and no documented protective or community infrastructure, the structural signals resolve toward danger, and the law remains usable against a visibly trans visitor at any time — arrest, prosecution and imprisonment of up to two years are live possibilities.
TCD.outOfScopeNotes: Very thin data: enforcement of the 2017 criminalisation in either direction is undocumented; no community or protective infrastructure is documented since criminalisation; the resident-side record rests on the pre-criminalisation baseline.

sources.summary: US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Chad: criminalisation section states the law criminalised consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment — official current-law baseline for visitor exposure; report also covers societal abuses.

US State Dept 2010 Human Rights Report, Chad (pre-criminalisation baseline): law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts' with no evidence it was used against LGBT persons that year; no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, most persons discreet due to social strictures — documents the pre-2017 legal climate.
US State Department 2006 Human Rights Report for Chad: documents the Deby regime's abuses - extrajudicial killings, torture, MINURCAT withdrawal - general context.

HuffPost/GroundTruth Project analysis: while further criminalisation attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda, they succeeded in Chad and Nigeria — situates Chad's criminalisation drive within the broader wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy, relevant context for how the law's trajectory developed.

GAB.name: Gabon
GAB.summary: Gabon demands real caution — and on a surprising positive trajectory: after briefly criminalising same-sex intimacy in 2019, it decriminalised in 2020, and in November 2024 voters ratified a new constitution that rejected calls to criminalise homosexuality. No LGR; social conservatism; but the constitutional debate is now public and the pro-criminalisation side lost.
GAB.outOfScopeNotes: 2020 decriminalisation + 2024 constitution are formal; social climate lags.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminalised same-sex intimacy in 2019 (max 6 months + US$8,561 fine), repealed in 2020 after Senate approval — reversal sharply divided public opinion; Nov-2024 constitution (military regime since Aug-2023) codifies privacy (Art.18) but retains Art.16 marriage definition; no legal gender recognition, LGBTI groups cannot register; same-sex relations legal for men and women per its country page (with caveat that criminalisation remains 'No' nationwide only since the 2020 repeal).

Erasing 76 Crimes (25 Nov 2024): Gabon's new constitution was ratified by referendum 16 Nov 2024 (over 90% yes, ~55% turnout) and rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality, adding LGBT+-protective privacy provisions — but codifies a marriage definition excluding same-sex couples. Context: Aug-2023 military coup ended 56 years of Bongo-family rule.

US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for Gabon: official assessment covering the year the new penal code criminalised same-sex conduct - documents the legal change and societal discrimination.

LGBTQ Nation (13 Dec 2019): Gabon criminalised same-sex relations by law passed quietly in July 2019 — up to 6 months + 5m CFA francs (~US$8,500); two men already arrested and released only after paying police bribes; Gabon inherited no colonial-era sodomy law (independence 1960). Enforcement precedent: arrests occurred within months of enactment — later reversed by the 2020 repeal.
Washington Blade (July 2020): Gabon formally decriminalised homosexuality - the National Assembly overturned the 2019 ban, restoring the pre-2019 status where same-sex conduct was not criminal.

Gabon Review (29 Oct 2019, French): Law 042/2018 of 5 Jul 2019 (new penal code) criminalises same-sex relations without naming 'homosexuality' — Art.402 files 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' (sexual assaults/attacks on morals); earlier Dec-2013 police arrest of two alleged 'gay marriers' released. Primary-source detail on the criminalisation year (2019) later reversed in 2020.

GAB.tangentialFactors: The 2020 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 constitution rejected criminalisation.
GAB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with USA/Mexico (0.50), above Côte d'Ivoire (0.34) — a stark intra-regional contrast — and below Paraguay (0.52).

COG.name: Republic of the Congo
COG.summary:
The Republic of the Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised) — but the 2024 official assessment (EUAA COI) documented societal discrimination, police harassment (including bribes extracted under an ambiguous 'acts against nature' provision) and the absence of protection; there is no legal gender recognition, and only a small underground community.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure to a criminalisation regime, but the ambiguous under-21 'shameless act / acts against nature' provision has been used to justify discrimination and, in police practice, to extract bribes; no arrests or prosecutions under it were reported in 2022 or 2023.
COG.outOfScopeNotes: The official assessment documents the harassment pattern; it is qualitative and does not quantify incidence. No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors, and no source documents legal gender recognition practice. The age-of-consent provision's application to trans persons specifically is unreported.

sources.summary: EUAA COI Query Response Q29 (May 2024) on the Republic of the Congo: systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by state and society, and availability of state protection for LGBTQI+ people. Key findings: no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults; Penal Code Article 331 (per ILGA) sets age of consent at 21 for same-sex vs 18 for different-sex acts; the under-21 'shameless act / against nature' provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct is 'ambiguous', and sources say it is used to justify discrimination.

US State Department 2022 human rights report (Republic of the Congo), SOGI section: no law specifically prohibits consensual same-sex conduct between adults; a provision punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under age 21 (6 months–3 years plus fine), scope ambiguous and not invoked for prosecutions. Police at times cite the provision to extract bribes from gay men; local NGOs reported violence, psychological/physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government and nonstate actors.

US State Department 2023 human rights report (Republic of the Congo): no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguous under-21 provision during 2023; police continued using the 'act against nature' law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men; NGOs reported continuing psychological/physical harassment and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by both government actors and nonstate actors, with no anti-discrimination protections in law.

COG.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Lebanon/Kyrgyzstan (0.36), below Gabon (0.50) and above Côte d'Ivoire (0.34).

BDI.name: Burundi
BDI.summary: Burundi is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Same-sex conduct has been criminalised since 2009 (2 years), and the head of state himself has called for mob violence: in December 2023, President Ndayishimiye said LGBT people should be “taken to a stadium and stoned” because “that's what they deserve” — condemned by HRW as stoking fear; the Iteka League called it a call to lynching. There is no LGR, no community infrastructure (the oldest rights group works from exile), and arbitrary detention is routine.
BDI.outOfScopeNotes: Presidential incitement is documented by HRW (Jan 2024).

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (Jan 2024): 'Burundi President Stokes Fear Among LGBT People' — President Ndayishimiye's call to 'stone' homosexuals; HRW urges the ruling party to renounce persecution.

SOS Médias Burundi (Jan 2024): after President Évariste Ndayishimiye called for 'homosexuals to be stoned', LGBTQ Burundians reported terror; the Iteka League (in exile) called the remarks 'a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people'. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the remarks as 'a real license to kill (us)'. Same-sex relations are criminalised in Burundi.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents the country's crisis (extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, media shutdowns) and includes the section on acts of violence and discrimination against LGBT persons - same-sex conduct criminalised since 2009, with arrests and harassment documented.
US State Department 2009 Human Rights Report for Burundi (archived): covers the year the penal code criminalised same-sex conduct; documents discrimination against gays and lesbians.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Burundi: lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among common human-rights abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Burundi: documents torture, extrajudicial executions, prolonged pretrial detention, and discrimination against LGBT persons under the criminalised framework.

CAF.name: Central African Republic
CAF.summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors.

For a visitor: nothing protects, and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned (defined as a union between one man and one woman); a trans visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition, and public affection can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.
CAF.outOfScopeNotes: No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors, and the exact charging practice under the public-morals provisions is unreported.

sources.summary: ILGA World 'Our Identities Under Arrest' (2023) - global report on laws criminalising LGBT people; the fetched copy contained no extractable text at research time (image-based PDF).

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Central African Republic: no legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons; marriage constitutionally defined as a 'union between one man and one woman' with same-sex marriage banned; legal gender recognition not permitted; LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military; criminalisation of same-sex activity in public pushed the community underground, and there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic: documents extrajudicial killings, torture, rape by security forces and Seleka rebels, harsh prison conditions - general human-rights context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Erasing 76 Crimes / ILGA overview (20 May 2019): in the Central African Republic same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, but Article 85 of the criminal code criminalises 'attacks on public morals' — public same-sex acts carry harsher penalties than other moral offences. SOGI issues remain taboo and seen as 'imported from Europe'/'contrary to African values'; CAR received two UPR recommendations (SOGI non-discrimination, improving the situation of sexual minorities).

UN OHCHR summary of stakeholders' submissions for the CAR's UPR (45th session, Jan 2024): covers international obligations, national human-rights framework, institutional infrastructure - includes SOGI-related stakeholder recommendations.

CAF.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Malawi (0.26), above Zambia (0.24), below Senegal (0.27).

MDG.name: Madagascar
MDG.summary:
Madagascar's trans visitors get legality without protection. Same-sex conduct between adults is legal from age 21 under the Penal Code, but the age of consent is unequal: same-sex acts involving someone under 21 remain offences, with Penal Code Article 331 attaching an indecent-assault band of five to ten years' imprisonment. There is no anti-discrimination law, no legal gender recognition, and no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, so a trans traveller — alone or with a partner — holds no local status and no named protection.

Practical safety is the dominant concern: LGBT people must hide their lives to keep jobs and live in peace, and there is no visible community outside the capital, Antananarivo. No police targeting pattern is documented, and the government has rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech, so no protection is in prospect.
MDG.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data; legal but closeted profile. No source addresses border-screening, document handling, or passport-marker practice for trans visitors, and no police targeting pattern is documented either way — the absence of a documented pattern is not proof of safety. The legal baseline rests on a 2020 decriminalisation overview, a December 2023 guide, and a 2011 human-rights report describing a post-coup period.

sources.summary: France 24 'Focus' report (Aug 2024): 'LGBT people in Madagascar forced to hide their sexuality' — although homosexuality is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable; many hide to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Madagascar: documents the post-coup regime, unlawful killings, and 'societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

BBC News Pidgin overview of decriminalisation in Africa (July 2020): Madagascar entry — same-sex activity legal only from age 21 under the Penal Code (under-21 same-sex acts remain offences); no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions; regional context as ~22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise.

Queer In The World Madagascar guide (updated 3 December 2023): same-sex activity legal for over-21s but LGBT people face discrimination and lack civic rights such as marriage and adoption; the legal framework is limited in progress compared with other countries.

Erasing 76 Crimes (17 July 2025): in Madagascar’s fourth UPR (January 2025, 235 recommendations) the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent; six Malagasy organisations (Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers’ Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage, Madagascar LGBT+) protested that "Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence."

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Madagascar resources: Penal Code Article 331 sets a different age of consent for same-sex acts (indecent-assault band of five to ten years’ imprisonment); documents general societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ people plus state-protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations.

DJI.name: Djibouti
DJI.summary: Djibouti is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions (Arts 353/354) make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no community infrastructure; authoritarian state with US/French bases but no rights space.

Wikipedia overview (current): legality of same-sex conduct is ambiguous — no law says either way, but authorities can prosecute public same-sex conduct under 'good morals' provisions, so it is treated as de facto illegal; discrimination protection exists in employment only; no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Djibouti SOGIESC section: law does not explicitly criminalise consensual LGBTQI+ conduct, but status and conduct are taboo; a societal pattern of discrimination with no official violence cases citable — complaints can be filed with police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH); no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination; pervasive social and religious intolerance makes people fear family and community shunning on disclosure.

MRT.name: Mauritania
MRT.summary: Mauritania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. The 1983 Penal Code criminalises “acts against nature” with death by stoning (de facto moratorium on executions, but the statute is live); and Cairo 52 documents that gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through debauchery, heresy, and Islamic-morality provisions — trans people can be apprehended solely for their gender expression. There is no LGR, no healthcare, no community, and sharia courts operate alongside the civil system.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report (Mauritania): consensual same-sex conduct criminalised but penalties not enforced; reports of violence and threats against LGBT people; civil society objected to scant indictments and officials sometimes acted with impunity.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Jan 2026, from Outright): the Penal Code keeps a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men; the government confirmed a de facto death-penalty moratorium in 2021; arrests and detentions under the provisions continue in recent years; low visibility drives stigma; since 2008 the country has served as refuge for Senegulese LGBTIQ people.

Liberals Mauritania (organisation website, c)2026): openly campaigns from within Mauritania on freethinker and LGBT-adjacent causes — titles include 'When the Law Deprives Rights and Freedoms' and 'The First Trans Woman to Speak Out in Mauritania's Media' — evidence of a minimal but real public advocacy space.

GNB.name: Guinea-Bissau
GNB.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal — one of few nations in the region never to criminalise it: a 1993 penal code decree omits same-sex offences and a 2014 domestic-violence law protects victims regardless of sexual orientation. No legal gender recognition, no trans framework and no partnership recognition exist, and there is no anti-discrimination protection, so no document or screening pathway for trans travelers is documented.

Enforcement and practical safety dominate: chronic instability (a 2012 coup), a weak national apparatus, documented impunity for security-force abuse (arbitrary killings, torture), documented social hostility and stigma, some violence cases in 2018, no visible LGBT scene, and a poor 34/100 ('Caution') travel-safety score, with no mob-lynching pattern reported for a neighbouring nation.
GNB.outOfScopeNotes: Passport marker and border-screening treatment for trans travelers is not documented in any source; with no legal gender recognition, no procedure for aligning identity documents is identified. Security reporting dates to 2011–2012, secondary overview pages are derived from an open encyclopaedia, and sources focus on LGB matters rather than trans-specific experiences, so trans-specific local data remains unverifiable.

SWZ.name: Eswatini
SWZ.summary: Eswatini is dangerous for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility.

LSO.name: Lesotho
LSO.summary: Lesotho demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (sodomy common-law crime struck down in 2012); the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by state and non-state actors (2024 UPR submission); no LGR; small organised community inside South Africa's geographic envelope.

CPV.name: Cabo Verde
CPV.summary: Cabo Verde is workable — Africa's most tolerant jurisdiction alongside South Africa's legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; Praia and Mindelo host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. No explicit GI protections and no LGR statute (administrative practice unclear), but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

MDV.name: Maldives
MDV.summary:
Maldives is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the Penal Code and sharia framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming Maldivians face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 HRC shadow report documents ICCPR violations). BUT: the tourist resort islands operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted on a resort; the risk concentrates in Malé and local islands.

A resort-only visit is lower-risk than the score suggests; any local-island contact raises it.
MDV.outOfScopeNotes: Resort islands are de-facto insulated; the score reflects the national legal framework and local-island exposure.

Erasing 76 Crimes (1 September 2015): police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men (aged 56 and 27) on 29 August for homosexual activity in their private home; the 2014 Penal Code extended criminalisation beyond Muslims to everyone, with death-penalty provisions theoretically in reach; Rainbow Warriors warned tourists could face similar threats.

PRK.name: North Korea
PRK.summary: North Korea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely: same-sex conduct is not named in the Criminal Code, but Article 193 prohibits “decadent culture,” and broad obscene-activities provisions give the authorities unlimited discretion, and reported incidents of criminalisation and even execution for homosexuality exist. Gender identity does not exist in public life, visitors travel under constant escort and surveillance in the world's most totalitarian system, and any nonconforming presentation or discovered digital material risks detention, with no recorded protection or recognition of gender identity to offset that exposure.

PSE.name: Palestinian Territories
PSE.summary:
Trans visitors face grave danger here, with a hard internal split: in the West Bank, same-sex conduct is not criminalised (Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual-private-sex offences, carried into the 1960 penal code applied there), but there are no protections, family/clan hostility is severe, and the Palestinian Authority has not legislated or signed key treaties. In the other part, Gaza, a 1936 British Mandate code technically allows up to 10 years for consensual same-sex acts, Hamas has executed people for alleged homosexuality, and the area is in a catastrophic war.

Trans identities are nowhere explicitly criminalised, but public-morality provisions can catch trans people, gender-affirming healthcare is essentially destroyed or unavailable, police action against a queer organisation drew rights-group condemnation, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are reported.
PSE.outOfScopeNotes: The two parts — West Bank and Gaza — are scored as one de jure unit, yet Gaza is far worse in practice because of the war and Hamas, the group controlling the area. No source covers border screening, document handling or passport-marker practice for trans visitors, and no marriage or partner-travel recognition fact for trans visitors is recorded anywhere in the sources. Reported Hamas executions for alleged homosexuality and the police clampdown are documented claims, not independently verified elsewhere.

XKX.name: Kosovo
XKX.summary: Kosovo is workable for trans visitors — the Balkans' strongest legal framework on paper. GIB.name: Gibraltar
GIB.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Gibraltar; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Gibraltar legislates its own civil and criminal law as a self-governing territory on the Iberian peninsula's southern tip. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993 with an equal age of consent since 2012; discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment date from 2007; civil partnerships followed in 2014, and same-sex marriage was enacted unanimously in December 2016 after a 2015 public consultation returned overwhelming support (3,490 replies from a 24,117-person electorate).

For a transgender visitor the standing gap is legal gender: no route exists to change legal gender, and there was no specific hate-crime provision denigrating a person for sexual orientation until, in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice said it would 'urgently' consider one after a wave of online homophobia during Pride month drew a rare public rebuke from the head of government. Governance of the territory is subject to regular scrutiny by the UK parliament's overseas-territories committee, which has pressed accountability standards across the portfolio.
GIB.outOfScopeNotes:
A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where flagged in the summary. Whether the hate-crime provision the Ministry for Justice said in July 2021 it would 'urgently' consider has since been enacted is unresolved in this record; no enforcement data for the 2007 discrimination protections appears in the sources.

One 2016 news report framed the December 2015 consultation as leaving locals polarized while the consultation result showed overwhelming support.

BMU.name: Bermuda
BMU.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Bermuda decriminalised private adult same-sex conduct in 1994 (House of Assembly, 22-16) and in 2013 outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act — the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality — and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the traditional-marriage definition, so partnerships, not marriage, are the available status for same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the more telling fact is the protection gap: there is no legal recognition of transgender people, and therefore no gender-identity-specific discrimination protection at all. Church influence is significant in local politics — when a prominent entertainer's gay-charity cruise sought to dock in 2007 the premier's colourful defence was needed against religious objections — and the tourism economy that the island depends on has repeatedly had to be pointed at inclusivity.
BMU.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary. No source covers border screening or identity-document practice for transgender visitors, so that element of the visitor picture is unverifiable; nothing in the record documents how the 2013 discrimination ban is enforced in practice.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Social climate: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre' — organised religious hostility to visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections — a debate that split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

CYM.name: Cayman Islands
CYM.summary:
Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature refused, albeit with an unequal age of consent surviving the reform. In 2020 the Court of Appeal held that a same-sex couple's overseas marriage must be recognised, and in July 2021 roughly 600 people — including the premier, the governor and other ministers — joined the islands' first Pride parade, one of the broadest official turnouts a community there has seen.

The sharp turn came in 2022: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect and, in March of that year, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it. Same-sex couples therefore have no marriage or civil-partnership status, the country that administers defence and foreign affairs declined to force the issue, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself.
CYM.outOfScopeNotes: A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted. No source documents border-screening practice, documents handling, arrest patterns, or the operational enforcement of the unequal age of consent, and nothing on the record distinguishes protections or risks specific to trans travelers as opposed to same-sex couples. The practical working of the recognition-for-immigration-effects line at ports of entry is unverified.

VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
VGB.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to British Virgin Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Same-sex intimacy in the British Virgin Islands was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the United Kingdom's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act — a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed. Family status remains contested rather than settled: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the UK, who were seeking recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success.

Visitors encounter a tolerant-but-quiet society: travel surveys rate these twin islands among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, with most local hostility 'silent and invisible' and most visitors hardly noticing either way. Discretion, not danger, is the operative norm.

A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted.

No source in this record addresses border-screening or document practice for trans visitors, and no source documents legal gender recognition or trans-specific statutes — the assessment rests on the same-sex record and the general social climate. The marriage case's final resolution is unrecorded: the 2022 appeal refusal concerned case-management orders, and no ruling on the validity of a marriage performed abroad appears in the current sources.

AIA.name: Anguilla
AIA.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Anguilla; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'

A queer family travelling openly in 2023 described the experience as uneventful on a 35-square-mile island. The practical visitor picture is quiet neutrality — nothing protects you much, and little opposes you at all.

MSR.name: Montserrat
MSR.summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Montserrat: its prohibitions were swept away in January 2001 by the same Order in Council that overrode the region's reluctant legislatures. What public LGBT life existed was effectively extinguished twice by disaster: the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions that buried the southern half of the island and depopulated it, leaving a scatter of survivors in the north and a gay presence described as 'decimated', only partially recovered.

Local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable,' and the territory appeared resigned to following London's order. Visitors today find a tiny, dispersed, private society where neither hostility nor community is much visible.

Whether the scene has recovered since the disasters is not measurable from the available sources. TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
TCA.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Turks and Caicos Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Turks and Caicos decriminalised same-sex activity in 2001 through the UK-imposed Caribbean reform, and its constitution now bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The live frontier has been recognition rather than criminal law: the Court of Appeal ordered a residence permit for the same-sex spouse lawfully married abroad, holding that 'spouse' in the immigration ordinance must include same-sex spouses and declaring violations of the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees — while declining to touch the constitution's male-female marriage definition, which it treated as controlling.

the United Kingdom's passport guidance maintains a standing profile of the territory's rules on marriage, civil partnerships, adoption and gender recognition. Socially, a resident's account described 'virtually nothing' documented about gay life — in a territory where around two-thirds of inhabitants are themselves not native-born — so visitor experience runs on privacy and the resort economy rather than any visible scene.

The 2025 passport-office profile establishes the document framework but no source verifies that local border practice matches it; whether a trans traveler's documents are accepted at entry without friction is unverified. The appellate ruling has no later confirmation recorded in this record. The 'virtually nothing' social read rests on a single 2009 resident account, no newer survey data exists here, and no trans-specific incident data is recorded.

FLK.name: Falkland Islands
FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, legislate locally: same-sex activity has been legal since 1989, the age of consent has been equal since 2005, and same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017 — approved 7-1 after a public consultation showing 90 per cent support for marriage and 94 per cent for partnerships, with adoption following the same year and the first Pride held in Stanley that April. The Constitution Order 2008 bans sexual-orientation discrimination (Article 16).

UK law does not automatically apply here. The Equality Act 2010, the UK's 2025 single-sex-services code and the April 2025 Supreme Court 'For Women Scotland' ruling govern Great Britain, not the Islands, and no Order in Council extends them; the Islands' own ordinances govern instead. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 criminalises stirring up hatred on grounds of sexual orientation, and the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014 treats sexual orientation as an aggravating factor.

Trans-specific law is narrow. The UK Gender Recognition Act 2004 does not itself extend to the Islands, but the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014 treats the holder of a UK gender recognition certificate as their acquired gender at law; there is no local self-identification process and no non-binary recognition, so a trans visitor without a UK certificate is treated at law as their birth-registered sex. No gender-identity anti-discrimination protection exists — the constitutional ban names sexual orientation only.

Social picture: a tiny, remote island community. The 'open, tolerant and respectful' characterisation rests on a single local official's statement; no attitude-survey data and no trans-specific incidents are recorded. The remote dependency administered from Stanley (South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands) did not follow on marriage equality.
FLK.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: border-screening and document practice for trans travellers at entry is not sourced; the Wikipedia source carries a 'failed verification' flag on the claim that the Gender Recognition Act 2004 does not extend to the Islands, though the 2014 ordinance presupposes that reading.

PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
PCN.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Pitcairn Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Pitcairn's roughly fifty inhabitants govern family law themselves, and on paper they have adopted the most complete equality package in this group of territories: activity legal since 2001, a 2010 constitution that bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and a 2015 Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance — marriage defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, orientation or gender identity, foreign civil partnerships recognised, and adoption open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

IMN.name: Isle of Man
IMN.summary:

Isle of Man: a self-legislating Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea whose parliament, Tynwald, works through its own bills on these questions. The House of Keys in 2005 proactively adopted a clause protecting employees from dismissal over sexual orientation, framing it in human-rights terms; the chief minister publicly committed to marriage equality in 2015, at a time when this parliament and Northern Ireland's assembly were the only British legislatures refusing it; the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill passed its final legislative stages in April 2016 and the first civil partnership was converted to marriage that July, preserving the couple's 2015 wedding date.

Current reference material confirms the settled picture: civil partnerships from 2011, marriage since 2016, and a legal gender-recognition right in force since 2009 alongside 'gender reassignment' protections in island equality law. The metropole's single-sex code and its statutory guidance are not documented as extending to the island.

GUF.name: French Guiana
GUF.summary:
French Guiana stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

Full French framework applies as an overseas department: same-sex marriage (2013), anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, simplified administrative gender-marker change since 2017, and hate-crime sentence provisions — nothing criminalises being trans, and Pride is held in the main city with a small but visible community.

The friction a trans visitor meets is practical rather than legal. Specialised gender-affirming healthcare is thin and remoteness pushes residents into metropolitan France for care; local reporting describes conservative community norms and cultural taboos that discourage visibility and reporting. The sharpest documented state machinery is custodial: the national watchdog on places of detention found persistent, serious violations against transgender prisoners, and investigative reporting details how trans women incarcerated by legal-gender assignment fall through procedural cracks — practice that applies in the territory as in the hexagon. A current-status review adds locally elevated violent crime against a backdrop of a visible, tourism-oriented economy: ordinary-visitor caution is warranted, trans-specific state action is not documented.

GLP.name: Guadeloupe
GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

The full French framework applies: same-sex marriage, gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and simplified legal gender recognition — no legal penalty attaches to trans existence, and the territory's institutional life is now visible: its first dedicated LGBT+ centre opened in the main city in April 2024 under a programme establishing one in each overseas department, and local associations run twice-weekly community space, joint social programming, gay-friendly events on a dependency island, and outreach toward the tourism sector.

The documented cautions are social and custodial. A 2023 local mapping of anti-LGBT violence exists, and community organisers describe a gap between Caribbean-French LGBT life as seen from the metropole and everyday reality on the islands, where religious and communal pressure keeps many invisible outside festive settings. As elsewhere under the framework, the prison system is the weakest documented institution: the national detention watchdog found serious persistent violations of transgender prisoners' rights. For visitors: legal protection complete, community present but small, discretion still the norm.

MTQ.name: Martinique
MTQ.summary:

Nothing criminalises being trans, and case law and state protection capacity track the metropolitan norm.

Community infrastructure is real but modest: the island's lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans network organises private parties and garden socials and provides information and meeting services, supported by gay-friendly allies — there is no large commercial scene in the capital. The trans-relevant state mechanism documented across the framework is custodial: the national detention-places watchdog's findings of serious persistent violations against transgender prisoners apply to the island's prisons as to the metropole.

L1132-1 (2008); gender-identity discrimination prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with 'sexual identity' replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. MYT.name: Mayotte
MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

On paper the fullest of regional frameworks: French civil and criminal law applies — same-sex marriage (a genuine rarity in this part of the world), gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and legal gender change by simplified procedure following the national reforms. No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship.

The gap between book and life is the documented story. A 2023 report on a binational couple describes a 'long and complicated' path even to marry on this predominantly Muslim island; a legal-access directory shows no openly LGBT-friendly lawyer resident in the department (metropolitan counsel take cases); and the framework's prison findings — the state detention watchdog's report of serious violations against transgender prisoners — apply to the local jails. Social environment is conservative in a way the audited sources show through practice, not statute. For visitors, legal protection exists and enforcement of rights is slow; visibility invites social pressure more than police action.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Extends to local jails as French establishments.

Same-sex marriage is legal here — a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world — since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

PYF.name: French Polynesia
PYF.summary:
Full France metropolitan law does not extend to French Polynesia unchanged; the territory legislates locally on many matters, with France responsible for documents and justice.

French equality law applies in full — gender-identity anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions since 2017, a conversion-practice ban since 2022, and legal gender recognition without medical prerequisites — and it lands on genuinely entrenched indigenous ground: the mahuu third-gender role predates colonisation, rae-rae identities are visible in daily life across the archipelago, the territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023 with government and church participation, and travel literature calls the openness cultural rather than legal.

The undertow is real but social, not statutory: the rights overview records varying stigma, employment discrimination, and episodic transphobic violence that has pushed some rae-rae into sex work, while healthcare depth thins sharply outside the main island. For a visitor the combination is among the region's strongest — law, culture, and visibility aligned — with the standard framework caveat that the state's prison-system findings apply here too, and small-island anonymity cuts both ways.

WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna
WLF.summary:
The French civil and criminal framework applies: gender-identity anti-discrimination protection since 2012 and judicial gender-marker change under the 2016-17 reforms without surgery or diagnosis requirements; same-sex relations are lawful; non-binary recognition does not exist. No law criminalises trans presence.

Exposure here is shaped by scale and mores rather than statutes. The rights overview describes an isolated community of roughly eleven thousand where Catholic and Polynesian social norms create practical barriers to visibility, a traditional third-gender presence (fakafafine) coexists with stigma, there are no local gender specialists — residents travel out for any care — and anonymity in village life is close to zero. No hostile state action is documented; the only state-level adverse mechanism in evidence is the framework's own prison findings (the national detention watchdog's report). Visitors should expect personal identifiability, warm discretion, and effectively absent local institutional support.

This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

Under the metropolitan civil law that governs this collectivity: same-sex marriage since 2013, gender-identity anti-discrimination protections, surgery-free legal gender change, gender-affirming care available for decades, and the state's 2023 conversion-practice ban — no legal restriction touches trans or same-sex visitors, and a rights-rating page scores the territory among the region's strongest frameworks with the caveat that non-binary recognition is absent and healthcare capacity is tiny.

Visitor-facing evidence is unusually direct: verified 2026 destination guides describe a discreet luxury culture — full legal protections, 'a cosmopolitan crowd that genuinely doesn't care', no organised scene but complete safety for same-sex couples — and the rights overview reports the island attracts trans residents from less accepting neighbours. A current-status review tempers that surface: local acceptance runs lower than the visitor economy implies, though no legal regression exists. The only documented adverse mechanism remains the framework-wide prison findings. Read: protected and comfortable, shallow community depth, care requires travel.
BLM.outOfScopeNotes: Collectivity of France; local deviations noted in the summary. The framework-wide prison findings concern detention conditions and are unresolved for visitor-facing practice; whether local acceptance figures track the visitor-economy picture is not independently measured.

BLM detainees fall under this French system.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: based on ~40 referrals since 2010, it finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

Dossier on BLM trans rights: the French framework applies — legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Travel guide: 'full equality' under French law on ~8 square miles and ~10,000 residents; luxury-yacht economy long welcoming to gay couples with zero visible scene — discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10 (9 positive rights, 1 red flag): legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access; no government LGBT+ travel advice (FCDO shows no warnings); no trans-specific visitor tips yet submitted.

Luxury-operator guide: low crime, open and accepting culture with no Pride-specific events, staff trained for diverse guests; visitors are high-end and discreet — no LGBTQ venues or scene, but no hostility noted.

ABW.name: Aruba
ABW.summary:
Aruba stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

An autonomous constituent country within a Western European kingdom, Aruba legislates positively rather than merely tolerating: its parliament voted 11-5 in 2016 to open registered unions carrying married-couple benefits (pension succession, emergency medical decisions) — the first island in the Caribbean to act, by its own government's account — and the official tourism authority runs a dedicated LGBT programme marketing the island as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly a hundred nationalities resident.

Travel-culture reporting through the kingdom's networks characterises Aruba, with its two sister islands, as quiet, tolerant and mostly open — a small, stable, tourism-dependent society. The parliamentary vote's own record notes religious and cultural opposition to full equal marriage, which remains unlegislated, and no local gender-recognition or specialist-care pathway is evidenced. No enforcement against trans or same-sex visitors is documented anywhere in the record: protection by registered partnership and tourism economics rather than full equality.
ABW.outOfScopeNotes: Part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. Whether the registered-union pathway is ever exercised by visitors, and whether the absence of documented enforcement reflects absence or non-reporting, is unresolved: the record rests on official tourism self-description and kingdom-network travel reporting, with no independent local enforcement data.

sources.summary: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

CUW.name: Curaçao
CUW.summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

Also an autonomous constituent country of the same kingdom, the island's audited record is one of official intent colliding with friction: representatives of all kingdom governments agreed in 2015 on an equal-rights package for Caribbean-country LGBT residents — yet the same reporting documents Pride permit difficulties as recently as 2013 and organised parliamentary opposition that the island's own government publicly opposed while supporting the community.

Travel-culture surveys place the island inside the region's quiet tolerant mainstream. For a visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin infrastructure: no documented state hostility, an active but negotiating community in the capital, and no evidenced local gender-recognition pathway or care capacity. The record is brief; what exists shows institutions contested rather than hostile.
CUW.outOfScopeNotes: Part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.
