BES.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
BES.summary:
Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba) stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

These are not autonomous countries but special municipalities of the kingdom itself, so metropolitan equality law applies directly: same-sex marriage has been performed on the islands since 2012 — one small island hosted the region's first such wedding after the 2010 status change and markets civil ceremonies openly — with the state's penal-code discrimination grounds and partnership frameworks in force, and a current-status review confirming no later change.

The caveats are the kingdom's own, and they are real: legal gender change still requires a medical expert's statement (the self-declaration act was withdrawn at kingdom level in July 2025), non-binary markers demand months-long court procedure, and three tiny church-dense communities leave service depth thin — the same rights overview that documents these gaps rates them with the metropolitan standard attached. Travel-side evidence is warm and wedding-positive; no adverse enforcement is documented.
BES.outOfScopeNotes: Special municipalities of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. The dossier records same-sex marriage performed since 2012 while the freshness confirmation cites 2018 — the earliest-performed date is unresolved; how the medical-expert gender-change statement is applied in practice is unverified.

For this record: travel-facing evidence that the island markets itself as equality-friendly with statutory protection behind it.

Dutch Caribbean Legal Portal (5 Dec 2012): the Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union — Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27) on 4 Dec 2012, two visiting residents. For this record: same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012, and the territory has a track record of performing them for visitors.

For this record: practical logistics for a couple — civil ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry.

FRO.name: Faroe Islands
FRO.summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

A self-governing archipelago in the Realm of Denmark: domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after church-state friction.

The climate is measured by politics rather than prosecution: in 2006 activists gathered some 20,000 signatures — a large share of a ~50,000 population — demanding anti-discrimination protection after surveys found violence and discrimination against out gay people 'not uncommon' and legally unaddressed; a Centre Party MP who refused to share a state banquet with Iceland's gay premier (2010, 'a direct provocation') was still demanding Pride bans in 2015, when a nationally beloved singer urged the public to ignore him. For a visitor: low violence risk, thin legal protection, and high-profile political hostility to visibility.
FRO.outOfScopeNotes: Self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark; local deviations noted in the summary. The record's reporting is dated (2006-2015); no later evidence confirms whether the political hostility persists, and the petition figure is described as 'some', not exact.

sources.summary: PinkNews (9 Nov 2006): LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at the time the Faroes (population ~47,000, self-governing within Denmark) had neither protection, leaving homophobia legally unaddressed.

PinkNews (7 Sep 2010): Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic PM Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion — signals the prominence of religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures in Faroese politics.

Gay Iceland (Jul 2015): when Faroese MP Jenis av Rana demanded Pride be banned (held two days before the national holiday), singer Eivor Palsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality — documents anti-Pride pressure and organised public pushback.

GRL.name: Greenland
GRL.summary:
Greenland stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

A self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law. Its LGBT record is quiet and consensual: partnership law came from the Danish model in 1996 with virtually no debate; marriage equality was adopted from Danish legislation in 2016, passed unanimously by the local parliament with the established church's bishop supportive; and in 2016 the territory took a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, ahead of the metropole's own practice.

For a visitor the picture is low-friction: gay life is described as 'almost a non-event' — integrated, non-violent, modest, with a small Pride since 2010 and a national equality association (Qaamaneq, 2014). The counterweight is capacity, not hostility: some 56,000 people across remote settlements means thin institutional reach, and anonymity comes from isolation rather than crowds.
GRL.outOfScopeNotes: Self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark; local deviations noted in the summary. The dossier's reporting dates to 2014-2016; whether the self-declaration practice and service levels persist is not confirmed by later evidence, and the population figure derives from the travel reporting rather than official statistics.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz 'Gay Greenland - Past and Present' (May 2015): gay life is 'almost a non-event' — low-key, integrated, non-violent; modest Pride march since 2010; the 1996 same-sex partnership law passed with virtually no debate — a picture of quiet tolerance.

PinkNews (Apr 2016): Greenland's same-sex marriage law came into effect — adopted Danish legislation, passed unanimously twice (first bill lapsed due to Danish elections); replaces the 1996 partnership law; the established church's bishop supported it.

KNR Greenlandic Broadcasting (Aug 2014): new national association LGBT Qaamaneq founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people — political, cultural and social equality, open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.

PRI.name: Puerto Rico
PRI.summary:
Puerto Rico stands under the full the United States federal regime: the United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker has been eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor arriving on the United States documents faces that mismatch at entry; airport screening follows federal procedure; the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions here, so care access during a visit cannot be assumed; and in February 2025 the the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sports.

A US territory: the federal anti-trans turn of 2025–26 (document/marker rules, TSA screening friction) applies in full — and unlike some territories, local law compounds rather than softens it. In July 2025 Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent — up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed; civil-rights groups announced court challenges, and the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly.

Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the federal courts after local couples sued (2014), while religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure. For a trans visitor today: federal paperwork friction, the country's harshest local care-crime regime, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.

Court challenges to the care ban were announced but their outcomes are unresolved, and how the deliberately vague provisions will be enforced in practice is unverified; the 2014 marriage ruling and the 2019 bill episodes are history, not current law.

An unincorporated US territory, so the 2025–26 federal turn — marker/document policy, TSA screening, the trans military-exclusion order — lands hard on an island whose economy and society carry a large permanent US military presence. ASM.name: American Samoa
ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies, including the orders on sex classification in documents and federal facilities (EO 14168), gender-affirming care funding (EO 14187) and athletic participation (EO 14201), the last of which is paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all US identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth, new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; Lambda Legal and the Human Rights Campaign document how name and gender changes now interact with federal records. A trans visitor holding US documents faces that mismatch at Pago Pago, where screening follows US federal procedure.

The same January 2025 order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities used in accordance with their gender identity. The territory's hospital is federally funded, and the orders halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reach it, so a trans visitor who needs emergency or inpatient care may be placed in a ward or room corresponding to sex assigned at birth, or be separated from care that was previously funded.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in territory employment has produced federal enforcement. In September 2023 the US Department of Justice secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and in June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen, one of the documented trans-specific violence records for the territory.

Marriage recognition remains contested on the ground. The Fono Senate voted down a bill in March 2003 that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed. In January 2016 the newly confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told the Senate he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling, and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws changed. As of July 2024 an on-island constitutional survey by Professor Daniel Hall was still testing whether the territory's same-sex marriage ban would survive a Fourteenth Amendment challenge, indicating the local ban is treated as operative. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; no same-sex couple has applied for a licence to date, and the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar and then the US Department of the Interior.

Social climate differs from the legal posture. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, is described in university research as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association on an explicitly cultural-pride footing. Contemporary commentary reports homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, so visible nonconformity attracts comment more readily than official sanction.
ASM.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Obergefell is operative in American Samoa in practice is asserted in both directions by sourced material, a 2016 judicial statement and a 2026 law review conclusion, and no case has tested it; the territory's own marriage statute and its constitutional durability after the July 2024 survey are not settled in the sources.

Not sourced: whether the territory's hospital has actually altered ward assignment or care-funding practice since the January 2025 orders, and whether any trans visitor has been refused entry, detained or referred at Pago Pago on document grounds.

Unverified in the inventory: the current status of the ACLU suit against the State Department, the outcome of the Lambda Legal guidance as litigation proceeds, and the precise scope of the SWS25 visa restriction as applied to arrivals in this territory.

Open: whether the September 2023 DOJ settlement terms have been implemented, and whether any hate-crime or employment complaint by a trans person has been filed since February 2023.

I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. For this record: documents that the territory deliberately declined a formal marriage ban pre-Obergefell, and gives contemporaneous local fa'afafine voices on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. For this record: direct evidence that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise it did not automatically apply, with named actors and dates.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. For this record: the freshest dated authority on the exact open question (is the 2015 ruling operative in ASM?), and it separates the law from the practical reality (no licenses sought/issued).

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). For this record: as of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

Marriage recognition remains contested on the ground. The jurisdictional legislature voted down a bill in March 2003 that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the lower chamber's judiciary committee recommended it be killed. In January 2016 the newly confirmed trial judge told the Senate he had not read the national supreme court's 2015 marriage decision and that his court did not deal with the ruling, and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws changed. As of July 2024 an on- constitutional survey by a law professor was still testing whether the state/province same-sex marriage ban would survive an equal-protection challenge, indicating the local ban is treated as operative. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in the state/province concludes that the 2015 decision does apply and that the state/province would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; no same-sex couple has applied for a licence to date, and the litigation path runs through the state/province high court against the registrar and then the national interior department.

Social climate differs from the legal posture. The local cultural category of people born male who embody both male and female traits is described in university research as a recognised and integral part of traditional local culture, and a residents' association for that community was formed in 2010 by merging two earlier organisations on an explicitly cultural-pride footing. Contemporary commentary reports same-sex relations as widely accepted locally while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, so visible nonconformity attracts comment more readily than official sanction.

MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
MNP.summary:
Northern Mariana Islands stands under the full the United States federal regime: the United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker has been eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor arriving on the United States documents faces that mismatch at entry; airport screening follows federal procedure; the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions here, so care access during a visit cannot be assumed; and in February 2025 the the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sports.

A US commonwealth in political union: federal document, immigration and screening policy applies (including 2025–26 marker restrictions), while marriage recognition reached Saipan in 2015 by operation of the federal constitution — recognition exists, and nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression. In 2023 the legislature enacted a hate-crimes statute whose sentencing criteria expressly cover sexual orientation and gender identity — a formal, if recent, protection.

The policy accounting is nonetheless near-bottom: a comprehensive US equality index scores the commonwealth's gender-identity law in negative territory (sexual-orientation law 'low'), citing family-law gaps — no second-parent adoption, no assisted-reproduction recognition, no family-services protection. Visitor reality: no documented legal danger, a fresh hate-crime shield, minimal other institutional support, and high social visibility in small, church-influenced islands.
MNP.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of the United States; local deviations noted above.

COK.name: Cook Islands
COK.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islands; local criminal law governs conduct.

A self-governing island state in free association with New Zealand, the Cook Islands criminalised male same-sex acts under a 1969 colonial-era Crimes Act (terms to seven or ten years, consent no defence) until parliament repealed the provisions in April 2023, effective 1 June 2023 — after a decade of stalled bills, NZ-assisted drafting, and sustained advocacy by the local Te Tiare Association, whose spokespeople called the laws 'draconian' colonial relics. Enforcement in living memory was essentially absent; the repeal removed a held-over risk rather than an active prosecution threat.

Pre-contact history reframes the present: 2020 coverage noted a nation 'historically accepting of same-sex relationships' whose anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonisation. Post-decriminalisation there is still no marriage equality and no general non-discrimination statute; public life is strongly church-inflected; the islands are some 15,000 people where everyone is known — decriminalised, unequal, and small.
COK.outOfScopeNotes: In free association with New Zealand; local deviations noted above. Population figures vary across the audited sources — roughly 15,000 in the record text, 21,000 in a 2017 source; the church-inflected climate's practical weight for an outed visitor is unquantified.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

NIU.name: Niue
NIU.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Niue; local criminal law governs conduct.

One of the world's smallest self-governing states, in free association with New Zealand, Niue carries neither criminalisation nor protection on LGBT matters. Colonial-era offences were removed with the age of consent reported equalised by 2011, and no audited source documents enforcement against queer people at all; equally there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination statute — and the principal 1966 act still shows uneven ages of majority by sex (21 men/19 women) on its face into the 2010s.

Culturally, UN regional documentation lists Niue's fakafifine among the Pacific's pre-colonial third-gender identities — 'cultural treasure' framing that signals deep family embedding, coexisting with church-led conservatism. Legacy public-health law provided for HIV testing of visitors staying beyond about two months: rarely invoked, but on the books. With a population near 1,500, anonymity is impossible — the question is community reaction, not arrest, and it is quietly unresolved.
NIU.outOfScopeNotes: In free association with New Zealand; local deviations noted above.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust history of criminalisation, Niue section: the Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May (in force June), removing 'buggery', 'attempted buggery' and 'indecent assault on males' — offences under ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code carrying up to 10 years. The law was inherited from New Zealand via 1901 annexation, retained on self-governance in 1974, and survived New Zealand's own 1986 decriminalisation (which changed NZ law only). For this record: documented legal decriminalisation and its colonial-law chain.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fakafifine of Niue among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

GayLawNet Niue laws page: age of majority is 21 for men and 19 for women under the Niue Act 1966 (Part 21, Marriage of Minors); the age of consent was reportedly equalised in May 2011 (per ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia, May 2011); the page flags limited information available on Niue topics. For this record: dated consent-equality and the sex-asymmetric age of majority still on the books.

HKG.name: Hong Kong
HKG.summary:
A special administrative region running its own legal system under a constitutional settlement: trans claims here have been fought in court more than legislated. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the apex court in 2023 ruled full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a precondition for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card — reversing a 2019 high-court loss in the same litigation. Beyond the card, however, recognition still runs on surgery; and where the executive has chosen, it has chosen against: in September 2025 the legislature voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14 after court deadlines, so relationship recognition and any SOGI equality ordinance remain absent.

Corporate visibility invites backlash (a bank's rainbow installations drew a homophobic campaign in 2016), and open activism operates in a space tightened since the 2020 security law. Visitor arithmetic: no criminal law, dense urban anonymity, a functioning marker-change route on cards — inside a system that still demands surgery for most recognition and whose politicians recently voted inclusion down.
HKG.outOfScopeNotes: Special administrative region of China; local deviations noted above.

sources.summary: AP (Feb 2023): 'Hong Kong transgender men win appeal over status change' — the Court of Final Appeal rules full sex-reassignment surgery should not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on official identity cards, a far-reaching win in the Henry Tse case.

PinkNews (1 Feb 2019): HK High Court ruled against trans men Henry Tse, Q and R — Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the 'only objectively ascertainable criterion', rejecting self-ID as leading to 'uncertainty and arbitrariness'; the men had already changed legal gender in Britain; counsel called the requirement 'out of proportion'. Current status (2026 re-check): legal gender recognition still requires full sex-reassignment surgery; Sept 2025 LegCo voted the government's registered-partnerships bill down 71-14.

HKFP opinion by Nury Vittachi (7 Dec 2016), 'HSBC's rainbow lions: Can we have our homophobia back please?': documents the 2016 backlash to HSBC's rainbow-lion installations — a viral local campaign insisting homophobia is homegrown or foreign-imported, framed satirically. Useful as climate evidence: corporate LGBT visibility provokes organised pushback in Hong Kong.

HK Court of Appeal, Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005, Sept 2006): judicial review of Crimes Ordinance provisions setting the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 vs 16 for heterosexual acts — the applicant (21, in same-sex relationships since 16) argued the disparity unjustifiably discriminated; the judgment examines whether facially neutral laws can breach equality. Landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong.

MAC.name: Macau
MAC.summary:
A small southern Chinese territory with its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation: nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression, and almost nothing protects them either. There is no legal gender-recognition pathway — the first organised push (2015) got only a hearing at the identification bureau, with the trans claimant speaking behind a screen; when government legislated on domestic violence in 2016 it knowingly excluded same-sex partners as non-'family', against a 2015 UN Committee-Against-Torture direction that protection be non-discriminatory — an exclusion a local association and an internationally known campaigner publicly accused the administration of choosing, warning it signals SOGI bias is justifiable.

For a visitor: zero legal risk, near-zero legal recourse, and the compression of a very small city where casinos, churches and old resident networks all know their own. The administration treats the subject as a non-issue — which is both the mercy and the void.
MAC.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of China; local deviations noted above. The 2026 official statement leaves reform timing unset; the employment-only protection's enforcement practice is undocumented; the April 2026 appeal by four trans residents has no reported outcome in the audited material.

Jason Chao / Rainbow of Macau statement (May 2016): the government knowingly enacted a discriminatory domestic-violence law despite the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination; warns the law signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

sources.summary: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Macau': same-sex activity decriminalised 1996; no recognition of same-sex unions; Basic Law Art. 25 discrimination list omits sexual orientation — SOGI protection only in employment (Law 7/2008 Art. 6/2); the 2012 domestic-violence draft dropped same-sex cohabitants for 'lack of social consensus'; the 2015 gender-marker-change study never produced a law.

sources.title: Transgenders don't exist in the eyes of the law
sources.summary: Plataforma Media (8 Sep 2023): transgender residents cannot change sex on Macau ID cards — no data-change policy exists — causing border-crossing confusion (a trans man holding a Hong Kong card marked male is still registered female in Macau); activists press the long-promised legislative reform.

sources.title: Macau: legal recognition of gender identity requires 'prudent study'
sources.summary: Plataforma Media (7 Apr 2026): the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) says gender-identity legal recognition still needs 'prudent study' of core societal values, civil and family law, and states there are 'no plans to revise the framework' — Macau remains the only area in China without ID gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions (both possible in mainland China and Hong Kong), despite a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents.

ESH.name: Western Sahara
ESH.summary:
A disputed North African territory under military administration by a neighbouring state, whose penal code governs any visitor: same-sex intimacy is criminalised (six months to three years) with wide police discretion, and morality articles are the tool turned on visibly trans people — rights reviews document involuntary outing, expression discrepancies at checkpoints and registries, no gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition (a 2021 path covers intersex people only); the administering state's religious establishment has condemned transition.

Occupation stacks the risk: 170 charged in the administering state in one year, a 2020 organised outing campaign, rights defenders tried at the territory's own court (a 2005 case of eight Sahrawis remains a landmark), and a 2018 legal study recording LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike. For an outed visitor: criminalisation, morality enforcement and occupation policing, with no civil space and negligible accountability.
ESH.outOfScopeNotes: Disputed territory administered by the neighbouring state; local deviations noted above; see the entry on the administering state for the underlying legal analysis. The 2005 trials are reported as both seven and eight defenders in the audited material; the count is unverified.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch dispatch (9 Dec 2005): trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; HRW called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. Documents Moroccan state authority exercised over the territory (security services, courts) and detention of Sahrawi activists - the legal framework a visitor to the territory stands under.

PinkNews global legality roundup (Jul 2017): lists the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, noting it has been illegal for decades and that the partially-recognised state (AU member since 2016) governs the territory claim. Date-stamps the 2017 status as criminalised.

GMB.name: Gambia
GMB.summary: Gambia is dangerous for trans visitors. There is no LGR and no visible community.

sources.summary: Outright International country profile (updated Mar 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised since the colonial era; the 2014 'aggravated homosexuality' life clause was removed by the March 2025 Criminal Code, which instead sets a five-year minimum for 'unnatural offences' (defined as any homosexual act) with no stated maximum, plus three years for 'gross indecency'; the Barrow government has not typically enforced the provisions.

West Africa Democracy Radio: reports The Gambia's new criminal-law package raising the minimum sentence for homosexual acts to five years — broadcast corroboration of the penalty change now on the books.

Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2024: The Gambia rated 'Partly Free' (50/100); political freedoms improved under Barrow after 22 years of Jammeh's rule, with severe discrimination against LGBT+ people listed among ongoing concerns.

UK Home Office CPIN on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia (v3.0, Feb 2023): systematic assessment of risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information on law and treatment — the fullest English-language documentation of conditions on the ground.

HRW report 'State of Fear' (Sept 2015): arbitrary arrests, torture and killings in Gambia under Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people — the enforcement climate of the previous regime, relevant to how police treat visibly LGBT visitors.
US State Dept 2020 human-rights report on Gambia: same-sex conduct criminalised (up to life under the 2013 amendment); documents arrests and societal discrimination.
US State Dept 2021 report: continued criminalisation with no prosecutions reported; significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons.

GMB.tangentialFactors: The Criminal Code criminalises same-sex conduct, the 2014 amendment added an “aggravated homosexuality” offence (life imprisonment for “serial offenders”), and in 2024 the National Assembly raised the minimum sentence for homosexual acts to 5 years — the trajectory is towards harsher penalties, not reform. Under Jammeh, LGBTI people faced documented persecution (his infamous “slit throats” rhetoric); the Barrow era has seen some improvement in general freedoms but no decriminalisation and continued severe discrimination (Freedom House). Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; trans people captured via birth-sex status and indecency provisions.
GMB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Egypt/Uzbekistan/Burkina Faso (0.22), above Tunisia (0.19), below Ghana (0.24).
